subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define child health (paediatric) nursing. (2 marks) (b) Explain the philosophy and modern concepts of child care. (6 marks) (c) Describe the changing trends in paediatric care and the role of the paediatric nurse. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Roles of the paediatric nurse
labels: central circle "child and family" surrounded by care provider

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Child health (paediatric) nursing is the specialised branch of nursing concerned with the care of children from birth to adolescence (0–18 years), in health and illness, together with their families. It aims to promote the optimum growth and development of every child, prevent illness, care for the sick child, and help children with disability or chronic disease reach their fullest potential. The word "paediatrics" comes from the Greek pais (child) and iatros (healer).

(b) Philosophy and modern concepts of child care (6 marks) Philosophy

  • Children are not miniature adults – they differ anatomically, physiologically, psychologically and immunologically, and their needs change with each stage of development.
  • Every child has the right to survival, development, protection and participation – care respects these rights.
  • The family is the constant in the child's life – parents are partners in care, not visitors.
  • Health care should be holistic (physical, emotional, social, intellectual and spiritual), preventive and promotive as well as curative.

Modern concepts

  1. Family-centred care – parents are involved in planning and giving care; open visiting and rooming-in; respect for the family's culture and decisions.
  2. Atraumatic care – care that minimises physical and psychological distress: preparation before procedures, presence of parents, local anaesthetic creams and sucrose for painful procedures, play, avoidance of unnecessary separation and restraint.
  3. Holistic and child-friendly care – attention to play, schooling, nutrition and emotional needs, not only to the disease.
  4. Growth and development-based care – care adapted to the child's age and developmental level.
  5. Preventive paediatrics – immunisation, growth monitoring, nutrition, safe environment and accident prevention are as important as treatment.
  6. Comprehensive care for the whole child population – special attention to newborns, the girl child, children with disability, and children in difficult circumstances (street children, orphans, victims of abuse).
  7. Child rights-based approach – the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and national laws guide care.
  8. Evidence-based, team-based care – paediatricians, nurses, nutritionists, social workers, teachers and community workers work together.

(c) Changing trends in paediatric care and the role of the paediatric nurse (7 marks) A. Changing trends

  1. From disease-oriented curative care to preventive, promotive and family-centred care.
  2. From long hospital stays to day care, short stay and home-based care (home-based newborn and young child care by ASHAs).
  3. Growth of neonatology – special newborn care units (SNCUs), newborn stabilisation units and newborn care corners; survival of very preterm babies.
  4. Integrated approaches – Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (screening for the "4 Ds").
  5. Focus on early childhood development – stimulation, early detection of developmental delay, early intervention centres.
  6. Technology – non-invasive monitoring, CPAP, surfactant, telemedicine, digital immunisation records (U-WIN).
  7. Specialisation – paediatric intensive care, oncology, nephrology, surgery and palliative care.
  8. Respect for child rights – child-friendly hospitals, protection from abuse, consent and assent.
  9. Community participation – Anganwadi workers, ASHAs and self-help groups in child health.
  10. Expanded roles of nurses – paediatric nurse practitioners and specialist nurses.

B. Role of the paediatric nurse

  1. Care provider – skilled, safe, developmentally appropriate nursing care to sick children.
  2. Health promoter and educator – teaching parents about nutrition, immunisation, hygiene, growth, development and safety.
  3. Advocate – protecting the rights, safety and best interests of the child; recognising and reporting abuse.
  4. Counsellor and supporter – helping children and families cope with illness, hospitalisation, disability and death.
  5. Coordinator and case manager – linking the child with the health team, schools, social services and government schemes.
  6. Preventive role – immunisation, growth monitoring, screening, accident prevention.
  7. Rehabilitator – helping children with chronic illness or disability achieve maximum independence.
  8. Researcher and leader – evidence-based practice, quality improvement, training of junior staff.
  9. Community nurse – work in under-five clinics, schools, Anganwadis and homes.

D. Principles of paediatric nursing

  1. Child and family are the unit of care – the parents' knowledge of the child, their culture and their concerns are respected, and they are involved in every stage of care.
  2. Care is based on growth and development – the nurse adapts communication, explanations, play, diet, safety measures and procedures to the child's age and developmental stage.
  3. Safety first – children cannot protect themselves; cots with side rails, safe storage of medicines, supervision during feeding and bathing, and correct identification are essential.
  4. Prevention of infection – children's immunity is immature, so hand hygiene, aseptic technique, isolation and immunisation are strictly followed.
  5. Accurate, weight-based treatment – drugs and fluids are calculated by weight or surface area and double-checked.
  6. Minimum trauma – painful procedures are reduced, pain is relieved, and separation from parents is avoided (atraumatic care).
  7. Continuity and individualised care – a consistent nurse, a written care plan and attention to the child's routines (sleep, feeding, toileting).
  8. Play, education and normal life – play and schooling continue during illness wherever possible.
  9. Honesty and respect – truthful explanations, privacy, consent from parents and assent from the child.
  10. Health promotion at every contact – every visit is used to check immunisation, growth and nutrition and to teach the family.

E. Qualities of a paediatric nurse

  • Love for children, patience, cheerfulness and a calm, gentle manner.
  • Sound knowledge of normal growth and development and of childhood illnesses.
  • Skill in paediatric procedures – venepuncture, medication calculation, resuscitation and newborn care.
  • Keen observation, because children often cannot express what they feel; quick recognition of deterioration.
  • Good communication with children of all ages and with anxious parents; ability to use play.
  • Respect for culture, confidentiality and children's rights; emotional stability in situations such as the death of a child.

F. Present challenges in child health in India

  • A continuing burden of newborn deaths, undernutrition (stunting and underweight) and anaemia, together with a rising problem of childhood obesity, diabetes and screen-related problems.
  • Injuries (road traffic, drowning, burns), child abuse, child labour and child marriage.
  • Mental health and developmental disorders, and the needs of children with disability.
  • Antimicrobial resistance, new and re-emerging infections, and the effects of air pollution and climate change.
  • Gaps between rural and urban areas, and between richer and poorer states – which the paediatric nurse helps to close through community-based care.

G. Scope of child health nursing

  • Hospital – paediatric wards, NICU and SNCU, paediatric ICU, emergency, surgical and oncology units, outpatient and immunisation clinics.
  • Community – sub-centres and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, Anganwadis, under-five clinics, home visits, school health services and RBSK teams.
  • Special settings – child guidance clinics, early intervention centres, homes for children in need of care, palliative care services.
  • Education, administration and research – teaching students, managing paediatric units and studying better ways of caring for children.

Conclusion Child health nursing is the specialised care of children from birth to adolescence and their families. Its philosophy recognises that children are not miniature adults and that the family is central; modern care is family-centred, atraumatic, holistic, preventive and rights-based. With trends moving towards newborn care, integrated programmes, community and home care and specialisation, the paediatric nurse acts as care provider, educator, advocate, counsellor, coordinator and researcher.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Explain the impact of hospitalisation on the child and the family. (8 marks) (b) Describe the nursing measures to reduce the stress of hospitalisation, including atraumatic and family-centred care. (7 marks)
tags: fear of bodily injury and pain

diagram.caption: Stages of separation anxiety in hospitalised young children
labels: superficial relationships) – with arrow showing prevention by parental presence

answer_html:
Introduction Hospitalisation is a major crisis for a child and family. Children have limited coping abilities and understanding of illness, and they face a strange environment, painful procedures and separation from familiar people. The reactions depend on the child's age and developmental level, previous experience, seriousness of illness, family support and the hospital environment.

(a) Impact of hospitalisation (8 marks) A. Major stressors for the child

  1. Separation anxiety – most marked between 6 months and 30 months; the young child goes through three stages:
    • Protest – cries loudly, clings to the parent, searches for the mother, refuses others' attention.
    • Despair – becomes quiet, sad, withdrawn, uninterested in play or food; may show regression.
    • Detachment (denial) – seems to adjust and shows interest in surroundings, but relationships are superficial; it is a sign of resignation and can damage attachment if separation is prolonged.
  2. Loss of control – loss of routines, independence and choices; toddlers react with temper tantrums and regression (bed-wetting, thumb-sucking, baby talk); school-age children and adolescents feel a loss of independence, privacy and peer contact.
  3. Fear of bodily injury and pain – preschoolers may see illness or procedures as punishment and fear injections, mutilation and the dark; adolescents worry about body image.
  4. Fear of the unknown – strange people, equipment, sounds and smells.

B. Reactions according to age

  • Infants – distress at separation after 6 months; feeding and sleep disturbances.
  • Toddlers – strongest separation anxiety, regression, resistance to procedures.
  • Preschoolers – magical thinking, fear of mutilation, guilt.
  • School-age children – fear of losing control, missing school and friends; may hide fears.
  • Adolescents – concern about privacy, body image, separation from peers; may be angry or withdrawn.

C. Effects on the family

  • Parents – shock, disbelief, anxiety, fear, guilt ("Did I cause this?"), anger, helplessness, frustration with hospital routines; financial burden and loss of wages; difficulty caring for other children; exhaustion from staying in hospital.
  • Siblings – jealousy, resentment, fear of getting ill, guilt, loneliness and changes in behaviour or school performance.
  • Family functioning – disruption of roles and routines; strain on relationships; need for information and support.

D. Possible long-term effects

  • Behavioural changes after discharge (clinging, sleep problems, fears), especially after long or repeated admissions without parental presence; on the positive side, well-managed hospitalisation can build coping skills and confidence.

(b) Nursing measures to reduce stress (7 marks) 1. Preparation for hospitalisation and procedures

  • Pre-admission visits where possible; explanation in age-appropriate language; picture books, dolls and therapeutic play to rehearse procedures; honest information ("it will pinch for a moment").

2. Minimising separation – family-centred care

  • Rooming-in and open visiting for parents; mother allowed to stay with young children.
  • Involve parents in care – feeding, bathing, comforting, simple procedures.
  • Respect the family's culture, beliefs and decisions; keep them informed; include them in ward rounds and care planning.
  • Encourage familiar objects – favourite toy, blanket, photographs; maintain home routines (bedtime, feeding).

3. Atraumatic care

  • Minimise pain – topical anaesthetic creams (EMLA), oral sucrose for neonates, breastfeeding during procedures, distraction, skilled staff to reduce repeated pricks.
  • Do painful procedures in a treatment room, not in the child's bed (keeps the bed a "safe place").
  • Avoid unnecessary restraint; use comfort positioning on the parent's lap.
  • Limit unnecessary examinations and procedures; cluster care to allow sleep.

4. Promoting control and normal development

  • Offer simple choices (which arm, which cup); maintain routines; encourage self-care.
  • Provide play – playroom, toys, drawing and storytelling; continue schooling (hospital school or homework).
  • Allow adolescents privacy and contact with friends (phone, visits).

5. Child-friendly environment

  • Bright, colourful wards, child-sized furniture, safe beds with side rails, a play area, reduced noise, staff in friendly uniforms.

6. Support for parents and siblings

  • Explain the illness and treatment; listen to concerns; provide counselling and social-work support for financial and practical problems.
  • Help siblings visit and understand; suggest ways to involve them.

7. Planning for discharge

  • Teach parents home care, medicines and warning signs; prepare the child for going home; arrange follow-up.

8. Factors that influence the child's reaction

  • Age and developmental level – toddlers react most strongly to separation.
  • Previous experience of illness and hospital – a bad experience increases fear.
  • Seriousness and duration of illness, number of painful procedures and length of stay.
  • Preparation given before admission and procedures.
  • Coping skills and temperament of the child.
  • Presence and anxiety of parents – anxious parents transmit anxiety to the child; calm, involved parents reduce it.
  • Hospital environment – noise, lack of privacy, adult wards, and the attitude of staff.

9. Admission of the child to the ward

  • Welcome the child and parents by name; show the ward, toilet, playroom and call bell; introduce the nurse who will care for the child.
  • Allow the child to keep personal clothes and a favourite toy; record the child's routines (feeding, sleep, toileting words, likes and fears) so that the same routines can be continued.
  • Explain the ward rules, visiting, meals for the parent who stays, and what will happen next.
  • Carry out admission assessment gently, with the child on the parent's lap if possible.
  • Put on the identity band, record weight and allergies, and make sure the cot sides are raised before leaving the bedside.

10. Therapeutic play in hospital

  • Emotional outlet (dramatic) play – children act out their experiences with dolls, toy syringes and stethoscopes, which releases fear and anger.
  • Instructional play – the nurse uses dolls and equipment to explain a procedure before it is done.
  • Physiologically enhancing play – blowing bubbles or a windmill for deep breathing, games to encourage movement of a joint, competitions to encourage drinking fluids.
  • A play specialist or nurse supervises play; toys must be washable and safe; play is not stopped as a punishment.

11. Benefits of a well-managed hospital stay

  • Recovery from illness and relief of pain; the child learns new coping skills, gains confidence and independence (self-care), and meets other children; parents learn more about their child's care. These benefits are greatest when parents stay with the child and staff practise family-centred care.

12. Guidance to parents at discharge about behaviour changes

  • Explain that some children show post-hospital behaviour – clinging, fear of strangers, sleep disturbances, temper tantrums, bed-wetting or anger towards the mother – which usually settles within a few weeks.
  • Advise parents to give extra attention and reassurance, keep routines regular, avoid punishment for regression, encourage play about the hospital experience, and seek help if problems persist.

Conclusion Hospitalisation causes separation anxiety, loss of control, fear of pain and injury, and regression in children, and anxiety, guilt and disruption in families. Nurses reduce this stress by preparing children, keeping parents with them through family-centred care, practising atraumatic care, providing play and choices, creating a child-friendly environment, supporting parents and siblings, and planning discharge carefully.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the national programmes and agencies for child health and welfare in India, and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Children are about one-third of India's population, and their survival and development are national priorities. Under the National Health Mission, child health services are delivered through the RMNCH+A (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health) strategy (2013), which follows a continuum of care from pregnancy to adolescence. Other ministries add nutrition, education and protection services. India's child mortality has fallen steadily – the infant mortality rate was 25, the neonatal mortality rate 19 and the under-five mortality rate 29 per 1,000 live births in 2023 (SRS) – but much remains to be done.

A. Newborn health programmes

  1. India Newborn Action Plan (INAP, 2014) – aims at single-digit neonatal mortality and stillbirth rates by 2030.
  2. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011) – free delivery and free care of sick infants in public facilities, including drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood and transport.
  3. Facility-Based Newborn Care (FBNC)
    • Newborn Care Corners (NBCC) at every delivery point – resuscitation and essential newborn care.
    • Newborn Stabilisation Units (NBSU) at first referral units.
    • Special Newborn Care Units (SNCU) at district hospitals for sick and small newborns.
  4. Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC, 2011) – ASHAs visit every newborn (days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 after institutional delivery, with an extra visit on day 1 after home delivery) to promote breastfeeding, warmth, cord care and to detect danger signs.
  5. Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC, 2018) – ASHA visits at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 months for nutrition, growth, development and immunisation.
  6. MAA – Mothers' Absolute Affection (2016) – promotion of early and exclusive breastfeeding.
  7. Kangaroo mother care, newborn screening and Vitamin K prophylaxis in facilities.

B. Child health programmes

  1. Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) – free vaccines against childhood diseases; Mission Indradhanush (2014) and its intensified rounds to reach unvaccinated children; U-WIN digital registration and tracking of every vaccination.
  2. Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) and facility-based IMNCI – standard management of common illnesses by health workers.
  3. SAANS (2019) – Social Awareness and Action to Neutralise Pneumonia Successfully – early detection and treatment of childhood pneumonia.
  4. Stop Diarrhoea Campaign (earlier the Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight) – ORS and zinc distribution, sanitation and hygiene promotion.
  5. Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK, 2013) – screening of children from birth to 18 years for the "4 Ds" – Defects at birth, Deficiencies, Diseases and Developmental delays including disability – by mobile health teams in Anganwadis and schools, with referral to District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC) and free treatment.
  6. Anemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – iron-folic acid supplementation (biweekly IFA syrup for 6–59 months, weekly tablets for older children), deworming, testing and treatment.
  7. National Deworming Day (2015) – albendazole twice a year for children and adolescents aged 1–19 years.
  8. Vitamin A supplementation – from 9 months to 5 years.
  9. Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK, 2014) – adolescent health (nutrition, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, substance misuse, injuries).
  10. MusQan (2021) – child-friendly, quality services for children in public health facilities.

C. Nutrition and development programmes

  1. Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS, 1975) – through Anganwadi centres: supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, immunisation, health check-ups, referral, and nutrition and health education; now under Saksham Anganwadi and Mission Poshan 2.0.
  2. POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) – reduction of stunting, wasting, underweight and anaemia.
  3. PM POSHAN (earlier Mid-Day Meal) – hot cooked meals for school children.

D. Child protection and welfare

  1. Mission Vatsalya – child protection services (earlier the Integrated Child Protection Scheme): child welfare committees, children's homes, foster care, sponsorship, adoption through CARA.
  2. Childline 1098 – 24-hour emergency helpline for children in distress (now linked with the national emergency number 112).
  3. Beti Bachao Beti Padhao – survival, protection and education of the girl child.
  4. Samagra Shiksha – elementary and secondary education under the Right to Education.

E. Agencies working for child welfare

  • International – UNICEF (child survival, immunisation, nutrition, protection), WHO (technical guidance), UNFPA, World Bank, Save the Children.
  • National – Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Women and Child Development, National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD), Indian Council for Child Welfare (ICCW), Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), and voluntary organisations such as CRY, SOS Children's Villages and Bal Bhavan.

F. Role of the nurse

  1. Service delivery – immunisation sessions, newborn care, IMNCI case management, growth monitoring, IFA and deworming, ORS–zinc distribution.
  2. Identification and referral – danger signs in newborns, malnourished children, children with the "4 Ds", abused children.
  3. Health education – breastfeeding, complementary feeding, hygiene, immunisation, warmth, early childhood development, accident prevention.
  4. Supervision and training of ANMs, ASHAs and Anganwadi workers; coordination with ICDS and schools.
  5. Records and reports – MCP card, immunisation registers, U-WIN, HMIS reports.
  6. Advocacy and community mobilisation – Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days, mothers' meetings, campaigns.
  7. Monitoring and evaluation of programme coverage and quality.

G. Supporting services and platforms

  • Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Health and Wellness Centres) – comprehensive primary health care, including newborn and child health services, close to the community.
  • Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days (VHSND) – monthly platform at the Anganwadi for immunisation, growth monitoring, antenatal care and health education.
  • Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres (NRC) – facility-based care for children with severe acute malnutrition with medical complications.
  • Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) and LaQshya – quality antenatal and labour-room care, which also improve newborn survival.
  • Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) – cash benefit to pregnant and lactating mothers, supporting nutrition and rest.

H. Achievements and challenges

  • Achievements (NFHS-6, 2023–24) – institutional deliveries above 90%, full immunisation of children aged 12–23 months about 87%, and stunting reduced to 29.3%.
  • Challenges – still high newborn mortality in some states, wasting and underweight, anaemia, gaps in quality of care in SNCUs, urban slum and tribal populations, and delayed care-seeking. Strengthening home visits, referral transport, community participation and the skills of nurses is the way forward.

I. Important child health days and weeks (used for mass awareness)

  • World Breastfeeding Week (1–7 August); National Newborn Week (15–21 November); World Prematurity Day (17 November); National Deworming Day (10 February and 10 August); Children's Day (14 November); World Children's Day (20 November, the day the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted).

Conclusion India's child health services, organised under RMNCH+A, include newborn programmes (INAP, JSSK, FBNC, HBNC, HBYC, MAA), child health programmes (UIP and Mission Indradhanush, IMNCI, SAANS, Stop Diarrhoea, RBSK, Anemia Mukt Bharat, deworming), nutrition schemes (ICDS, POSHAN), and protection services (Mission Vatsalya, Childline). Supported by UNICEF, WHO and national agencies, nurses deliver, coordinate and monitor these services and educate families, helping India move towards its 2030 child survival goals.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Write a note on the under-five clinic.
answer_html:
Introduction Children below five years form a vulnerable group – most child deaths and much of the malnutrition occur in this age group. The under-five clinic (well-baby clinic) provides comprehensive, preventive, promotive and curative care to these children at one place, usually at the PHC, sub-centre (Ayushman Arogya Mandir), urban health centre or hospital OPD. The concept was introduced by Dr. David Morley.

1. Objectives

  • To reduce morbidity and mortality among children under five years.
  • To promote optimum growth and development.
  • To detect and treat illness and malnutrition early.
  • To protect against communicable diseases by immunisation.
  • To educate mothers in child care, nutrition and family planning.

2. Services offered

  1. Care in illness – diagnosis and treatment of common illnesses (diarrhoea, pneumonia, fever, worms, skin infections) using IMNCI; referral of serious cases.
  2. Preventive care
    • Immunisation according to the national schedule.
    • Growth monitoring – regular weighing and plotting on the growth chart of the Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card ("road to health"); early detection of growth faltering.
    • Nutrition surveillance – detection of underweight, wasting, stunting and anaemia; nutrition counselling; supplementation (Vitamin A, IFA), deworming.
    • Oral rehydration therapy – ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, and teaching mothers to prepare ORS.
  3. Family planning – advice on spacing of births, which itself improves child survival.
  4. Health education – breastfeeding, complementary feeding, hygiene, sanitation, home care of minor illnesses, danger signs, accident prevention, early childhood stimulation.
  5. Screening and referral – for developmental delay, congenital defects and disabilities (linked with RBSK).

3. Organisation

  • Fixed day and time, with registration, weighing, examination, immunisation, treatment and counselling stations; records maintained on the MCP card and registers; follow-up of defaulters by ASHAs and ANMs.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Weighing and plotting growth, immunisation, assessment and treatment using IMNCI, distribution of ORS, IFA and Vitamin A, health education, counselling, record keeping, home visits for defaulters and referral.

Conclusion The under-five clinic offers care in illness, immunisation, growth monitoring, nutrition surveillance, oral rehydration, family planning and health education to children below five years under one roof. Run largely by nurses, it is one of the most effective ways of reducing child morbidity and mortality.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the internationally accepted rights of the child and the role of the nurse in protecting them.
tags: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
Declaration of the Rights of the Child 1959
answer_html:
Introduction Children need special protection because of their physical and mental immaturity. The UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child (1959) listed ten principles, and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), adopted on 20 November 1989, made these rights legally binding on the countries that ratified it. India ratified the UNCRC in 1992. A child is defined as every person below 18 years of age.

1. Guiding principles of the UNCRC

  • Non-discrimination – all rights apply to every child, whatever the sex, caste, religion, disability, birth or status.
  • Best interests of the child – a primary consideration in all actions concerning children.
  • Right to life, survival and development to the maximum extent possible.
  • Respect for the views of the child – children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, given due weight according to age and maturity.

2. Groups of rights

  1. Right to survival – life, a name and nationality from birth, adequate nutrition, safe water, health care, immunisation, shelter.
  2. Right to development – education, play and leisure, cultural activities, information, freedom of thought and religion, early childhood care.
  3. Right to protection – from abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, trafficking, sexual exploitation, harmful traditional practices (child marriage), armed conflict; special protection for refugee, disabled and orphaned children and children in conflict with law.
  4. Right to participation – freedom of expression, to be heard, to form associations, and to take part in decisions that affect them.

3. Rights of children in health care (applied)

  • To receive the best available care; to have parents present; to be informed in language they understand and to give assent; to privacy and dignity; to play and education in hospital; to be protected from unnecessary procedures and pain; to be cared for in a child-friendly environment by trained staff.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Provide equal, non-discriminatory care, especially to the girl child and children with disability.
  • Promote breastfeeding, immunisation and nutrition (survival rights).
  • Encourage play, schooling and stimulation (development rights).
  • Recognise and report abuse, neglect, child labour and child marriage; know Childline (1098) and the child protection system (protection rights).
  • Involve children in decisions, explain procedures and seek assent (participation rights).
  • Advocate child-friendly policies in hospitals and the community.

Conclusion The UNCRC, ratified by India in 1992, guarantees every child the rights to survival, development, protection and participation, guided by non-discrimination and the child's best interests. Nurses uphold these rights through equal care, health promotion, protection from abuse and respect for children's views.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the legislations related to child health and welfare in India.
tags: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005
answer_html:
Introduction The Constitution of India directs the State to protect children – Article 21A (free and compulsory education for children of 6–14 years), Article 24 (no employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work), and Article 39(e) and (f) (children must not be abused and must be given opportunities to develop in a healthy manner). These are supported by policies and laws.

1. National Policy for Children, 2013

  • Recognises every person below 18 years as a child; priorities – survival, health and nutrition; education and development; protection; and participation.

2. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (amended 2021)

  • Care, protection, treatment and rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection and children in conflict with law; Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards; adoption through CARA; punishment for cruelty to children.

3. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 (amended 2019)

  • Defines sexual offences against children; child-friendly reporting, recording of evidence and special courts; mandatory reporting by any person (including doctors and nurses) who knows of an offence; stricter punishments after 2019.

4. Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

  • Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years; 25% seats for disadvantaged children in private schools.

5. Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016)

  • No employment of children below 14 years (except helping in family enterprises outside school hours); adolescents (14–18) barred from hazardous occupations.

6. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006

  • Marriage below 18 years for girls and 21 years for boys is a child marriage; it is voidable and punishable; Child Marriage Prohibition Officers.

7. Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994

  • Prohibits sex selection and disclosure of the sex of the foetus – protects the girl child.

8. Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (IMS) Act, 1992 (amended 2003)

  • Prohibits advertisement and promotion of infant milk substitutes, feeding bottles and infant foods, to protect breastfeeding.

9. Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005

  • Set up the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and State Commissions to monitor child rights and laws.

10. Others

  • Maternity benefit of 26 weeks for working mothers (now under the Code on Social Security, 2020) and crèche facilities – supporting breastfeeding.
  • National Food Security Act, 2013 – nutritional support for pregnant women and children (through ICDS and school meals).
  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 – rights of children with disability, inclusive education.
  • Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 – offences such as infanticide, abandonment and cruelty to children.

Role of the nurse – know these laws; promote breastfeeding and discourage formula promotion; never take part in sex determination; recognise and report abuse and child marriage; guide families about education and disability benefits.

Conclusion Child welfare in India is protected by the Constitution, the National Policy for Children 2013 and laws such as the JJ Act 2015, POCSO Act 2012, RTE Act 2009, Child Labour Act, Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, PCPNDT Act and IMS Act, monitored by the NCPCR. Nurses help implement these laws in daily practice.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the concept of preventive paediatrics and the preventive measures for child health.
answer_html:
Definition Preventive paediatrics is the branch of paediatrics that aims at preventing disease, disability and death in children and promoting their optimal physical, mental and social growth and development. It begins even before conception and continues through childhood and adolescence.

1. Levels of prevention in children

  • Primary – health promotion (nutrition, hygiene, stimulation) and specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt, safety measures).
  • Secondary – early diagnosis and treatment (newborn screening, growth monitoring, developmental screening, IMNCI).
  • Tertiary – limiting disability and rehabilitation (early intervention for developmental delay, physiotherapy, special education).

2. Preventive measures by stage A. Antenatal (before birth)

  • Pre-conception care – folic acid, avoidance of consanguineous marriage where genetic disease runs in the family, genetic counselling.
  • Regular antenatal check-ups, maternal nutrition, IFA and calcium, tetanus–diphtheria (Td) immunisation, prevention and treatment of anaemia, infections (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B) and hypertension – to prevent low birth weight, prematurity and congenital infections.

B. Intranatal (at birth)

  • Institutional, clean and safe delivery; skilled birth attendance; prevention of birth asphyxia (newborn resuscitation), hypothermia and infection.

C. Postnatal and childhood

  1. Essential newborn care – warmth, early and exclusive breastfeeding, cord care, Vitamin K, newborn screening.
  2. Immunisation according to the national schedule.
  3. Nutrition – exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, appropriate complementary feeding, Vitamin A, IFA, deworming, iodised salt; growth monitoring to detect faltering early.
  4. Early childhood development – responsive caregiving, play and stimulation; developmental screening (RBSK).
  5. Hygiene and environmental sanitation – safe water, toilets, handwashing, clean homes.
  6. Prevention of common illnesses – ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, early care for pneumonia, mosquito nets.
  7. Prevention of accidents – age-appropriate safety (falls, burns, drowning, poisoning, road accidents).
  8. Dental care, vision and hearing screening in school.
  9. Adolescent health – nutrition, menstrual hygiene, prevention of substance use and early pregnancy.

D. Social preventive paediatrics

  • Family planning and birth spacing; parental education; poverty alleviation; protection from abuse, child labour and child marriage; welfare services for children in difficult circumstances.

3. Role of the nurse – antenatal and newborn care, immunisation, growth monitoring, nutrition and hygiene education, developmental screening, accident prevention teaching, home visits and referral.

Conclusion Preventive paediatrics protects children from conception to adolescence through antenatal care, safe delivery, newborn care, immunisation, nutrition, growth and developmental monitoring, hygiene, accident prevention and social measures. Nurses are key providers of these low-cost, high-impact services.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain child morbidity and mortality in India – the indicators, major causes and strategies for reduction.
answer_html:
Introduction Child mortality indicators reflect the health of a nation and the quality of its health services. India has made steady progress, but newborn deaths still form the largest share of child deaths.

1. Indicators (per 1,000 live births)

  • Perinatal mortality rate – stillbirths (after 28 weeks) plus early neonatal deaths (first 7 days) per 1,000 live births and stillbirths.
  • Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) – deaths in the first 28 days; divided into early (0–7 days) and late (7–28 days) neonatal deaths.
  • Post-neonatal mortality – deaths from 28 days to 1 year.
  • Infant mortality rate (IMR) – deaths below 1 year.
  • Under-five mortality rate (U5MR) – deaths before 5 years.

2. Current situation in India (SRS 2023)

  • IMR 25 (rural 28, urban 18), NMR 19 (rural 21, urban 13), U5MR 29 – all declining steadily since 2014.
  • About three-quarters of infant deaths occur in the neonatal period, mostly in the first week.
  • Targets – SDG 2030: NMR 12 or less and U5MR 25 or less; India Newborn Action Plan: single-digit NMR by 2030.

3. Major causes of child deaths

  • Neonatal – complications of prematurity and low birth weight, birth asphyxia, neonatal sepsis and pneumonia, congenital anomalies, hypothermia.
  • Post-neonatal and under-five – pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, injuries (drowning, burns, road accidents), with malnutrition as an underlying factor in many deaths.

4. Child morbidity

  • Acute respiratory infections, diarrhoea, worm infestations, skin infections, anaemia, vitamin deficiencies, malnutrition, injuries and developmental disabilities.
  • NFHS-6 (2023–24) showed improvement: stunting fell to 29.3% (from 35.5% in NFHS-5) and severe wasting to 5.2%, while overall wasting (about 19%) and underweight (about 32%) remain high; anaemia in young children was very high in NFHS-5 (67%).

5. Contributing factors

  • Poverty, low maternal education, early marriage and teenage pregnancy, short birth intervals, home deliveries, poor sanitation, lack of breastfeeding, incomplete immunisation, delayed care-seeking and geographical inaccessibility.

6. Strategies for reduction

  • Antenatal care and institutional delivery (JSY, JSSK); essential newborn care, resuscitation, kangaroo mother care and SNCUs.
  • Early and exclusive breastfeeding; complementary feeding; nutrition programmes (ICDS, POSHAN).
  • Full immunisation (UIP, Mission Indradhanush) – full immunisation coverage reached about 87% in NFHS-6.
  • IMNCI, SAANS (pneumonia), Stop Diarrhoea (ORS–zinc), malaria control.
  • Home-based newborn and young child care by ASHAs; RBSK screening.
  • Safe water, sanitation and hygiene; female education; birth spacing.

Conclusion NMR, IMR and U5MR are the key indicators of child health; in 2023 India's IMR was 25, NMR 19 and U5MR 29. Prematurity, asphyxia, sepsis, pneumonia, diarrhoea and malnutrition are the main causes. Continued focus on newborn care, nutrition, immunisation, management of common illnesses and social development will help India reach its 2030 targets.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the differences between an adult and a child that affect the child's response to illness.
answer_html:
Introduction "A child is not a miniature adult." Children differ from adults anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, psychologically and socially, and these differences change how they become ill, how illness presents and how they must be cared for.

1. Anatomical differences

  • Large head relative to body, with open fontanelles in infants – head injuries are common; heat loss is high from the head.
  • Airway – narrow airway, large tongue, high and anterior larynx, funnel-shaped narrowest part below the vocal cords; infants breathe mainly through the nose – small swellings cause severe obstruction.
  • Chest wall – soft, compliant ribs and horizontal ribs; breathing is mainly diaphragmatic.
  • Bones – softer with growth plates; fractures are different (greenstick) and may affect growth.
  • Larger body surface area to weight ratio – more heat and fluid loss.

2. Physiological differences

  • Higher metabolic rate, heart rate and respiratory rate; higher need for oxygen, calories and fluids per kg.
  • More body water (about 75–80% in newborns) and immature kidneys – rapid dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.
  • Immature temperature regulation – newborns easily become hypothermic; children develop high fever quickly and may have febrile seizures.
  • Limited glycogen stores – risk of hypoglycaemia with fasting or illness.
  • Immature liver and kidneys – different drug absorption, metabolism and excretion; doses are calculated by weight or body surface area.
  • Compensation then sudden collapse – children maintain blood pressure until late in shock, then deteriorate rapidly.

3. Immunological differences

  • Immature immune system; newborns depend on maternal antibodies; frequent infections until immunity develops; need for immunisation.

4. Psychological and developmental differences

  • Limited understanding of illness and procedures; fear of separation, pain and strangers; regression under stress; limited ability to describe symptoms (pain is often expressed by crying, irritability or refusal to feed).

5. Social differences

  • Dependence on parents for care and decisions; consent is given by parents with the child's assent; schooling and play are affected by illness.

6. Nursing implications

  • Careful, frequent observation using age-specific normal values; weight-based drug and fluid calculations; prevention of hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and dehydration; airway vigilance; family-centred, developmentally appropriate and atraumatic care; communication through play.

Conclusion Children differ from adults in body proportions, airway, metabolism, body water, temperature control, organ maturity, immunity, psychology and dependence on family. These differences make them more vulnerable to dehydration, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, airway obstruction and rapid deterioration, and they require age-specific nursing care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the communication techniques used with children of different ages.
answer_html:
Introduction Good communication reduces children's fear, gains their cooperation, helps assess their needs and builds trust with the family. It must be adapted to the child's age and developmental level.

1. General principles

  • Introduce yourself; use the child's name; come down to the child's eye level; smile and use a calm, warm voice.
  • Be honest – do not say a procedure "won't hurt" if it will.
  • Use simple, concrete words and short sentences; avoid frightening words ("cut", "take blood out"); give choices only when real choices exist.
  • Allow time; listen; respect privacy; involve parents.

2. Communication by age

  • Infants – non-verbal communication: holding, cuddling, rocking, gentle touch, eye contact, soothing voice; respond quickly to crying; keep the mother nearby; approach slowly and avoid sudden movements.
  • Toddlers (1–3 years) – approach through the parent; talk while the child sits on the parent's lap; simple words, short explanations just before the procedure; allow a security object; use play (let the child touch the stethoscope); expect "no" and offer simple choices.
  • Preschoolers (3–6 years) – play, puppets, dolls, picture books, drawing and storytelling; explain using concrete terms; demonstrate on a doll; reassure that illness is not a punishment; praise cooperation.
  • School-age children (6–12 years) – explain the reason and steps of procedures; use diagrams and models; answer questions honestly; involve the child in care decisions; respect modesty.
  • Adolescents – treat with respect as young adults; interview alone as well as with parents; ensure privacy and confidentiality within legal limits; be non-judgemental; discuss body image, school, friends and health risks; involve them in decisions.

3. Special techniques

  • Third-person technique – "Some children feel scared when…" helps the child express feelings indirectly.
  • Storytelling and mutual storytelling, drawing ("draw your family"), "three wishes", rating scales (faces), therapeutic play with medical equipment.
  • "I" messages for feelings; praise and rewards (stickers).

4. Communicating with parents

  • Listen to their observations (they know the child best); give clear, consistent information; show empathy; use interpreters when needed; involve them in care; address their fears and guilt.

Conclusion Communication with children must match their development – touch and voice for infants, simple words and choices for toddlers, play and stories for preschoolers, explanations for school-age children, and respect and confidentiality for adolescents – along with honest, empathic communication with parents.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the reactions of children of different ages to death and dying, and the nursing care of the dying child and the family.
tags: care of family of dying child
answer_html:
Introduction The death of a child is one of the most painful experiences for a family and for staff. Children's understanding of death develops with age, and their care at the end of life must be honest, comforting and family-centred.

1. Children's concept of death by age

  • Infants and toddlers (below 3 years) – no concept of death; react to separation from parents and changes in routine; may become irritable or withdrawn.
  • Preschoolers (3–6 years) – see death as temporary and reversible (like sleep or going away); magical thinking – may believe they caused the death by bad thoughts; may ask repeatedly when the person will return.
  • School-age children (6–12 years) – gradually understand that death is final, universal and inevitable; younger ones may imagine death as a person ("bogeyman"); fear of pain and mutilation; interested in details.
  • Adolescents – adult-like understanding but may feel invulnerable; concerned about body image, losing independence and friends; may feel anger or depression.

2. Nursing care of the dying child

  1. Comfort and symptom control – pain relief (regular analgesics, including opioids when needed), relief of breathlessness, nausea, secretions, fever and itching; mouth, eye and skin care; positioning.
  2. Honest, age-appropriate communication – answer questions truthfully; allow the child to express fears through play, drawing or stories; do not leave the child alone.
  3. Normal activities as long as possible – play, favourite toys, music, contact with friends and school.
  4. Presence of parents – unrestricted visiting; parents encouraged to hold, cuddle and care for the child; privacy.
  5. Spiritual and cultural needs – prayers, rituals and religious practices respected.
  6. Choice of place of care – home-based palliative care where the family wishes, with support.

3. Care of the family

  • Anticipatory grief – help parents express feelings (shock, denial, anger, guilt, sadness); provide clear information and involve them in decisions (including limitation of treatment).
  • Siblings – explain in simple words; allow visits; reassure that they did not cause the illness; watch for behaviour changes.
  • At the time of death – allow the family time with the child; respectful care of the body as per customs; help with formalities.
  • Bereavement support – follow-up contact, counselling, support groups; watch for complicated grief.

4. Care of staff – debriefing and support, as caring for a dying child is emotionally demanding.

Conclusion Children's understanding of death changes from separation fears in infancy, to death as reversible in preschoolers, to final and universal in school-age children and adolescents. Nursing care of the dying child focuses on comfort, honesty, normal activities and the presence of parents, while the family, including siblings, is supported before and after the death.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the principles of pre-operative and post-operative care of infants and children.
answer_html:
Introduction Surgery in children carries special risks – airway problems, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, dehydration and fear. Careful preparation and close monitoring make surgery safe and less traumatic.

A. Pre-operative care

  1. Psychological preparation – age-appropriate explanation using dolls, pictures or a visit to the theatre area; honest information; allow questions; parents involved and, where possible, present until induction.
  2. Consent and assent – written informed consent from parents or guardian; the child's assent sought.
  3. Assessment – history (allergies, previous anaesthesia, recent infections, bleeding tendency), vital signs, accurate weight (for drug and fluid doses), hydration and nutrition status, investigations as ordered (Hb, blood group, others).
  4. Fasting – as per anaesthetist's instructions; current guidance allows clear fluids up to 1–2 hours, breast milk up to 4 hours, formula and other milk up to 6 hours and solid food up to 6–8 hours before anaesthesia; avoid unnecessarily long fasting, which causes hypoglycaemia and dehydration; IV fluids if fasting is prolonged.
  5. Physical preparation – bath, clean clothes, identification band, removal of jewellery, nail polish and loose teeth checked; bladder emptied (older child); skin preparation as ordered; premedication.
  6. Pre-operative checklist – identity, consent, fasting, site marking, records, investigations, blood availability.

B. Post-operative care

  1. Airway and breathing – position on the side or as ordered until awake; suction secretions; oxygen as needed; monitor respiratory rate and SpO2; watch for laryngospasm and respiratory depression.
  2. Circulation – heart rate, BP, capillary refill, bleeding from the wound or drains.
  3. Temperature – prevent hypothermia (warm blankets, radiant warmer for infants) and monitor for fever.
  4. Fluids and blood sugar – IV fluids by infusion pump with strict intake–output; monitor urine output and blood glucose (especially in infants); start oral feeds early when allowed.
  5. Pain relief – regular assessment with age-appropriate pain scales; analgesics as ordered (paracetamol, NSAIDs where appropriate, opioids with monitoring); non-drug measures (cuddling, distraction).
  6. Wound and drain care – aseptic dressing; prevent the child from touching the wound (mittens or elbow splints only if needed); watch for infection.
  7. Prevention of complications – deep breathing through play (blowing bubbles), early mobilisation, positioning.
  8. Emotional care – parents present when the child wakes; comfort objects; play.
  9. Discharge teaching – wound care, medicines, diet, activity, warning signs and follow-up.

Conclusion Pre-operative care of children includes psychological preparation, consent and assent, weight-based assessment, safe fasting and physical preparation; post-operative care focuses on airway, circulation, warmth, fluids and blood sugar, pain relief, wound care, emotional support and discharge teaching.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the administration of medications to children, including the calculation of paediatric drug dosage.
answer_html:
Introduction Children are at high risk of medication errors because doses are calculated individually by weight or surface area, and a small decimal error can mean a ten-fold overdose. Medicines must be given with accurate calculation, correct technique and attention to the child's development.

1. Calculation of paediatric doses

  • By body weight (most common and accurate) – dose (mg) = dose per kg × weight (kg); e.g. paracetamol 15 mg/kg for a 12 kg child = 180 mg.
  • By body surface area (BSA) – used for chemotherapy and some drugs: child's dose = (BSA in m² ÷ 1.73) × adult dose; BSA (Mosteller) = √(height in cm × weight in kg ÷ 3600).
  • Rules based on age or weight (older methods, approximate):
    • Young's rule – child's dose = age (years) ÷ (age + 12) × adult dose.
    • Clark's rule – child's dose = weight (lb) ÷ 150 × adult dose.
    • Fried's rule (infants) – child's dose = age (months) ÷ 150 × adult dose.
  • Always double-check high-alert drugs (insulin, digoxin, opioids, potassium) with a second nurse; check the maximum dose.

2. Oral medicines

  • Use liquid preparations; measure with an oral syringe or dropper (not a kitchen spoon).
  • Infants – hold semi-upright, place the syringe at the side of the mouth (inner cheek) and give slowly to prevent choking; allow sucking.
  • Toddlers and preschoolers – give choices (juice afterwards), praise; never call medicine "sweets"; do not mix with milk or essential foods (may cause refusal).
  • Older children – tablets if they can swallow; check that the medicine was swallowed.

3. Intramuscular injections

  • Vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh) – preferred site in infants and children below 2–3 years.
  • Deltoid – small volumes in older children.
  • Ventrogluteal – safe in older children; avoid the dorsogluteal site in infants (sciatic nerve).
  • Small volumes (about 0.5–1 mL in infants), short needles, quick technique; restrain gently with the parent's help; comfort afterwards.

4. Intravenous medicines and fluids

  • Peripheral veins of the hand, foot or scalp (infants); secure and protect the cannula; give drugs and fluids through infusion or syringe pumps or burette sets; check the site hourly for infiltration and phlebitis.

5. Other routes – eye, ear (in children below 3 years pull the pinna down and back), nasal drops, inhalers with spacer and mask, nebulisation, rectal suppositories.

6. Safety measures

  • Follow the rights of medication administration (right child, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response); check identity band; know allergies; observe for side effects; never leave medicines at the bedside; teach parents correct home administration.
  • Avoid aspirin (Reye's syndrome) and codeine in young children.

Conclusion Paediatric doses are calculated mainly by weight or body surface area (older rules such as Young's, Clark's and Fried's are approximate). Oral, IM, IV and other routes need age-appropriate techniques, and strict safety checks, double-checking and parent education prevent medication errors in children.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the calculation of fluid requirements and the nursing care of a child receiving intravenous fluids.
answer_html:
Introduction Children have a higher body water content, higher metabolic rate and immature kidneys, so they dehydrate quickly and are also easily overloaded. Fluids must be calculated precisely and given with careful monitoring.

1. Maintenance fluid requirement (Holliday–Segar method)

  • First 10 kg – 100 mL/kg/day (4 mL/kg/hour).
  • Next 10 kg (11–20 kg) – 50 mL/kg/day (2 mL/kg/hour).
  • Each kg above 20 kg – 20 mL/kg/day (1 mL/kg/hour).
  • Example – a 25 kg child: 1,000 + 500 + 100 = 1,600 mL/day, about 65 mL/hour (4 × 10 + 2 × 10 + 1 × 5 = 65).
  • Newborns – about 60–80 mL/kg/day on day 1, increased gradually to about 150 mL/kg/day by the end of the first week (more for preterm babies and those under phototherapy or radiant warmers).
  • Isotonic fluids (with dextrose) are generally preferred for maintenance to reduce the risk of hyponatraemia; type and rate are prescribed by the doctor.

2. Deficit (replacement) fluids

  • Fluid deficit (mL) = % dehydration × weight (kg) × 10; e.g. 10 kg child with 5% dehydration = 500 mL.
  • For diarrhoeal dehydration, ORS or IV plans are used as per IMNCI/WHO guidelines (Plan A, B, C); ongoing losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, drains, fever) are added.

3. Calculating drop rates

  • Drops per minute = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ (time in minutes).
  • With a microdrip (60 drops/mL) set, drops per minute = mL per hour.
  • Infusion pumps or burette (measured-volume) sets are used in young children so that no more than a set volume can run in accidentally.

4. Nursing care of a child on IV fluids

  1. Verify the order – type, volume, rate; label the bag and line.
  2. Secure the cannula with a transparent dressing and splint; protect from pulling (with minimum restraint).
  3. Hourly checks – rate, volume infused, site (redness, swelling, pain, coolness – infiltration or phlebitis), connections.
  4. Strict intake–output chart – weigh nappies (1 g = 1 mL); urine output (normal about 1–2 mL/kg/hour in infants and 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour in older children).
  5. Monitor for dehydration (dry mouth, sunken eyes and fontanelle, poor skin turgor, reduced urine) and overload (puffiness, weight gain, tachypnoea, crackles, raised heart rate, enlarged liver).
  6. Daily weight; blood glucose and electrolytes as ordered.
  7. Aseptic technique; change sets as per policy; start oral feeds as soon as allowed and taper IV fluids.
  8. Comfort and play; explain to parents and involve them in watching the site.

Conclusion Maintenance fluids in children are calculated by the Holliday–Segar method (100/50/20 mL per kg per day, or 4-2-1 mL per kg per hour), with deficit and ongoing losses added. Accurate pumps or burette sets, hourly monitoring of the site and rate, strict intake–output, daily weight and watchfulness for dehydration and overload are essential nursing responsibilities.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the assessment and management of pain in children.
answer_html:
Introduction Children, including newborns, feel pain, and poorly treated pain has lasting effects on behaviour and pain sensitivity. Because young children cannot describe pain, nurses must assess pain regularly with age-appropriate tools and treat it promptly.

1. Signs of pain in children

  • Infants – high-pitched cry, grimacing (brow bulge, eye squeeze, deepened nasolabial furrow), rigid body, poor feeding, changes in heart rate and SpO2.
  • Toddlers and preschoolers – crying, restlessness, guarding, refusing to move, irritability, clinging, regression.
  • Older children – verbal complaints, withdrawal, reduced play, sleep disturbance.

2. Pain assessment tools

  • Neonates – NIPS (Neonatal Infant Pain Scale), PIPP (Premature Infant Pain Profile), CRIES (for post-operative pain).
  • Infants, young children and non-verbal children – FLACC scale – Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability, each scored 0–2 (total 0–10).
  • Children aged about 3 years and above – Wong–Baker FACES scale (0 – no hurt to 10 – hurts worst) or the Oucher scale.
  • Children above about 7–8 years – numerical rating scale (0–10) or visual analogue scale.
  • Also note parents' observations, the location, type and duration of pain, and response to treatment.

3. Non-pharmacological measures

  • Neonates – oral sucrose or breastfeeding during procedures, non-nutritive sucking, skin-to-skin (kangaroo) care, swaddling, facilitated tucking.
  • Older children – presence of parents, distraction (toys, bubbles, cartoons, music), guided imagery, breathing exercises, play, positioning, cold or warm packs, massage.
  • Atraumatic procedures – skilled staff, fewer pricks, treatment room for painful procedures.

4. Pharmacological measures (as prescribed)

  • Paracetamol (about 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, within the maximum daily dose).
  • Ibuprofen (about 5–10 mg/kg every 6–8 hours; not in young infants or in dehydration).
  • Opioids (morphine, fentanyl) for severe pain, with monitoring of respiration and sedation.
  • Local anaesthetics – EMLA cream applied about 60 minutes before venepuncture; local infiltration.
  • Avoid aspirin (Reye's syndrome) and codeine in children.
  • Regular dosing rather than "as needed" for continuous pain; route by mouth whenever possible (avoid IM injections for pain relief).

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Assess and record pain as a "vital sign"; reassess after interventions; educate parents; prevent procedural pain; advocate for adequate analgesia.

Conclusion Pain in children is assessed with age-appropriate tools – NIPS, PIPP or CRIES for neonates, FLACC for young or non-verbal children, FACES for preschoolers and numerical scales for older children – and managed with sucrose, breastfeeding, distraction and parental presence along with safe weight-based analgesics.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the nurse's responsibilities in the immunisation of children.
answer_html:
Introduction Immunisation is one of the most cost-effective child survival interventions. Under the Universal Immunisation Programme, nurses plan and conduct immunisation sessions and ensure that every child receives safe and timely vaccines.

1. Before the session

  • Planning – prepare the due list from registers and U-WIN; inform families through ASHAs and Anganwadi workers; arrange the session site with seating, privacy and handwashing.
  • Vaccines and logistics – collect vaccines in a vaccine carrier with conditioned ice packs; check expiry dates and the vaccine vial monitor (VVM); carry diluents of the same manufacturer, auto-disable (AD) syringes, hub cutter, waste bags, emergency (anaphylaxis) kit with adrenaline, MCP cards and records.

2. At the session

  1. Screening of each child – age, previous doses, current illness and history of reaction.
    • Genuine contraindications – severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or vaccine component; live vaccines are avoided in severe immunodeficiency; progressive neurological illness for pertussis-containing vaccine.
    • False contraindications (vaccinate) – mild fever, cough and cold, diarrhoea, malnutrition, prematurity, low birth weight, child on antibiotics, breastfeeding, family history of reactions.
  2. Explain to the mother which vaccines are being given, the diseases they prevent and possible minor reactions.
  3. Correct vaccine, dose, route and site – for example, BCG intradermal on the left upper arm; oral vaccines (OPV, rotavirus) as drops; pentavalent and PCV intramuscular in the anterolateral thigh; fractional IPV intradermal on the upper arm; measles–rubella subcutaneous on the right upper arm.
  4. Safe injection practices – one AD syringe per injection, no recapping, immediate cutting with the hub cutter, segregation of waste as per biomedical waste rules.
  5. Positioning and comfort – child held securely on the mother's lap; breastfeeding or cuddling after injection.
  6. Reconstituted vaccines (BCG, MR, JE) are used within the time limit and kept on ice; the open vial policy is followed for eligible liquid vaccines.

3. After vaccination

  • Observe the child for 30 minutes for any immediate adverse event; manage anaphylaxis promptly.
  • Advise the mother – mild fever, local pain or swelling may occur; do not apply anything on the BCG site; seek care for high fever, persistent crying or convulsions.
  • Record the vaccination on the MCP card, register and U-WIN; tell the mother the next due date.
  • Return unopened vaccines to the cold chain point; dispose of waste safely.

4. Follow-up and community role

  • Trace drop-outs and left-outs through ASHAs; organise catch-up (Mission Indradhanush); report adverse events following immunisation; educate the community to remove myths and fear.

Conclusion The nurse ensures successful immunisation by planning the session, maintaining the cold chain at the site, screening for true contraindications, giving the correct vaccine by the correct route and site with safe injection practices, observing for 30 minutes, advising and recording, and tracing defaulters.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Define neonatal mortality rate. Give its current value in India.
answer_html:
Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) is the number of deaths of babies within the first 28 completed days of life per 1,000 live births in a given year: NMR = (number of deaths of infants under 28 days in a year ÷ number of live births in the same year) × 1,000.

  • It includes early neonatal deaths (first 7 days) and late neonatal deaths (7–28 days).
  • India (SRS 2023): NMR 19 per 1,000 live births (rural 21, urban 13); the SDG target is 12 or less by 2030.
  • Main causes – prematurity and low birth weight, birth asphyxia, neonatal sepsis and congenital anomalies.
  • It reflects the quality of antenatal, intranatal and newborn care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: List four differences between an adult and a child.
answer_html:
Differences between an adult and a child

  1. Airway – a child's airway is narrow, the tongue is large and infants breathe mainly through the nose, so small swellings cause serious obstruction; in adults the airway is wider and more rigid.
  2. Body water and fluids – children have more body water (about 75–80% in newborns) and immature kidneys, so they dehydrate quickly; adults have about 60% body water.
  3. Temperature regulation – children, especially newborns, lose heat easily and develop hypothermia or high fever quickly; adults regulate temperature better.
  4. Drug doses – children's doses are calculated by body weight or surface area because liver and kidney function are immature; adults receive standard doses.
  5. Psychological and social – children depend on parents, have limited understanding of illness and react with fear and regression; adults can understand, decide and consent for themselves.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Define infant mortality rate and under-five mortality rate. Give India's current figures.
answer_html:
• Infant mortality rate (IMR) – the number of deaths of children under one year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year. India: 25 (SRS 2023) – rural 28, urban 18; it has fallen from 40 in 2013.
  • Under-five mortality rate (U5MR) – the number of deaths of children before reaching five years of age per 1,000 live births. India: 29 (SRS 2023); the SDG target is 25 or less by 2030.
  • Both are sensitive indicators of a country's health status, maternal and child health services, nutrition and socio-economic development.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is atraumatic care?
answer_html:
Atraumatic care is the provision of therapeutic care in settings, by personnel and through interventions that eliminate or minimise the psychological and physical distress experienced by children and their families in the health-care system. Principles

  1. Prevent or minimise separation of the child from the family (rooming-in, parental presence during procedures).
  2. Promote a sense of control (preparation, choices, routines).
  3. Prevent or minimise bodily injury and pain (EMLA cream, sucrose for neonates, distraction, skilled staff, fewer pricks). Examples – explaining procedures through play, doing painful procedures in a treatment room, allowing the parent to hold the child, avoiding unnecessary restraint.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What are the stages of separation anxiety in a hospitalised child?
answer_html:
Separation anxiety is the distress shown by young children (especially 6 months to 3 years) when separated from their parents, as in hospital. It occurs in three stages:

  1. Protest – the child cries loudly, screams for the parent, clings, searches and rejects strangers.
  2. Despair – the child becomes quiet, sad, withdrawn and inactive; loses interest in play and food; may regress (bed-wetting, thumb-sucking).
  3. Detachment (denial) – the child seems to adjust and becomes interested in surroundings, but relationships are superficial; it reflects resignation and can harm the parent–child bond if separation is prolonged. Prevention – rooming-in, open visiting and involvement of parents in care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is family-centred care?
answer_html:
Family-centred care is a philosophy of care that recognises the family as the constant in a child's life and treats parents as partners with the health team in planning, giving and evaluating the child's care. Key elements

  • Respect and dignity – honouring the family's culture, values and choices.
  • Information sharing – complete, honest and timely information.
  • Participation – parents encouraged to take part in care and decisions at the level they choose.
  • Collaboration – families involved in policies and programmes. Examples – rooming-in, open visiting, parents present during procedures and ward rounds, teaching parents home care before discharge.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the Holliday–Segar formula?
answer_html:
The Holliday–Segar formula is used to calculate maintenance fluid requirements in children according to body weight:

  • First 10 kg – 100 mL/kg/day (4 mL/kg/hour).
  • Next 10 kg – 50 mL/kg/day (2 mL/kg/hour).
  • Each kg above 20 kg – 20 mL/kg/day (1 mL/kg/hour). Example – for an 18 kg child: (10 × 100) + (8 × 50) = 1,000 + 400 = 1,400 mL/day, about 58 mL/hour (the hourly 4-2-1 rule gives 40 + 16 = 56 mL/hour – nearly the same). Deficits and ongoing losses are added to the maintenance volume.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define growth and development. (2 marks) (b) List the principles of growth and development and explain the factors influencing it. (5 marks) (c) Describe the developmental milestones of a toddler. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Developmental milestones of a toddler (1–3 years)
labels: 12–15 months walks alone; 15 months tower of 2 cubes
feeds self with spoon; 2 years climbs stairs

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (2 marks)

  • Growth is the increase in the physical size of the body or any of its parts due to multiplication and enlargement of cells. It is quantitative and can be measured – weight, length/height, head and chest circumference, and dentition.
  • Development is the progressive increase in skill and capacity of function – motor, language, cognitive, social and emotional. It is qualitative, related to maturation of the nervous system, and assessed by observing milestones. Growth and development are interdependent and continue from conception to adulthood.

(b) Principles and factors (5 marks) Principles of growth and development

  1. Continuous and orderly process – it occurs in a predictable sequence, though not always at the same rate (rapid in infancy and adolescence).
  2. Cephalocaudal direction – from head to tail: the infant controls the head before the trunk and legs.
  3. Proximodistal direction – from the centre of the body outwards: shoulder and arm control before fine finger movements.
  4. General to specific – mass, generalised responses (whole-body movements) come before specific, skilled ones.
  5. Sequence is the same for all children, but the rate varies – each child is unique.
  6. Different parts grow at different rates – the brain grows fastest in early years, the reproductive organs at puberty.
  7. Development depends on maturation and learning – a child walks only when the nervous system is ready, but practice and stimulation help.
  8. Critical (sensitive) periods – periods when the child is most responsive to particular stimuli or most vulnerable to harm (e.g. the first 1,000 days).
  9. All areas of development are interrelated – physical, mental, emotional and social development influence one another.

Factors influencing growth and development

  • Heredity (genetic factors) – parental height, body build, sex (boys are heavier and taller after puberty), race, genetic and chromosomal disorders.
  • Prenatal factors – maternal nutrition, anaemia, infections (rubella, CMV, toxoplasmosis), drugs, alcohol, smoking, radiation, maternal illness (diabetes, hypertension), placental insufficiency leading to low birth weight.
  • Nutrition – adequate breastfeeding and complementary feeding, protein, energy and micronutrients; malnutrition causes stunting and delayed development.
  • Hormones – growth hormone, thyroxine, insulin, sex hormones.
  • Illness and infections – repeated diarrhoea, respiratory infections, worms, chronic disease.
  • Environment – sanitation, safe water, housing, pollution, sunlight.
  • Socio-economic status – income, parental education, family size and access to health care.
  • Emotional environment and stimulation – love, security, play, talking and reading to the child; neglect and abuse retard development.
  • Culture, birth order and family relationships.

(c) Developmental milestones of a toddler (8 marks) The toddler period extends from 1 to 3 years. It is a period of rapid motor and language development and of growing independence.

1. Physical growth

  • Growth slows compared with infancy: weight increases by about 2–2.5 kg per year (birth weight is about quadrupled by 2–2.5 years); height increases by about 12 cm in the second year and 6–8 cm in the third year; head circumference is about 48 cm at 2 years.
  • All 20 deciduous (milk) teeth erupt by about 2½–3 years.
  • Characteristic pot-belly and lumbar lordosis; "physiological anorexia" – appetite decreases as growth slows.

2. Gross motor development

  • 12–15 months – walks alone with a wide-based gait; creeps upstairs.
  • 18 months – runs stiffly, walks upstairs with one hand held, pulls toys, sits on a small chair.
  • 2 years – runs well, goes up and down stairs alone placing both feet on each step, kicks a ball, jumps.
  • 3 years – rides a tricycle, climbs stairs with alternate feet, stands on one foot momentarily, jumps from a step.

3. Fine motor (adaptive) development

  • 15 months – builds a tower of 2 cubes; scribbles spontaneously; puts small objects into a bottle.
  • 18 months – tower of 3–4 cubes; turns pages of a book (2–3 at a time); feeds self with a spoon (with spilling); takes off shoes and socks.
  • 2 years – tower of 6–7 cubes; turns pages one at a time; copies a vertical line; opens doors.
  • 3 years – tower of 9–10 cubes; copies a circle; dresses and undresses with help (unbuttons); eats well with a spoon.

4. Language development

  • 15 months – uses a few meaningful words (jargon); points to what he wants.
  • 18 months – vocabulary of about 10–20 words; names familiar objects; points to body parts.
  • 2 years – about 300 words; two-word phrases ("mummy go"); uses "me", "mine".
  • 3 years – about 900 words; three-word sentences; asks many questions ("why?"); tells name, age and gender.

5. Personal–social and emotional development

  • Erikson – autonomy versus shame and doubt – the toddler wants to do things himself; success brings self-confidence, too much control or criticism brings shame and doubt.
  • Negativism ("no" to everything), ritualism (insists on routines), temper tantrums, possessiveness ("mine").
  • Separation anxiety remains strong; fear of strangers decreases gradually.
  • Play – solitary and parallel play (plays beside, not with, other children); imitation of household activities (18 months); enjoys push–pull toys, blocks, sand and water.
  • Self-help – drinks from a cup (15 months), uses a spoon (18 months), helps in dressing (2–3 years).
  • Toilet training – bowel control usually by 18–24 months, daytime bladder control by 2–3 years, night-time control by 3–4 years (or later).

6. Cognitive development

  • Piaget – end of sensorimotor stage (up to 2 years) and beginning of the preoperational stage – object permanence is complete; the child begins to use symbols, words and pretend play; thinking is egocentric.

7. Needs of the toddler and anticipatory guidance to parents

  • Safety – the toddler is curious and mobile: prevent falls (stairs, windows), burns (hot liquids, stoves), drowning (buckets, tanks), poisoning (kerosene, medicines, cleaning agents kept locked), choking (small objects, nuts); road safety.
  • Nutrition – family foods in small, frequent meals; avoid forcing food; continue breastfeeding up to 2 years; avoid junk food.
  • Toilet training when the child shows readiness, with patience and praise.
  • Discipline – consistent, simple limits; ignore tantrums when safe, praise good behaviour; avoid harsh punishment.
  • Sibling rivalry – prepare the toddler for a new baby; give individual attention.
  • Immunisation – boosters at 16–24 months (DPT, OPV, MR second dose, JE where applicable); Vitamin A every 6 months.
  • Dental care, play, language stimulation (talking, reading, singing), and adequate sleep.

Nursing importance
