  • Knowledge of normal milestones helps the nurse to detect developmental delay early (e.g. not walking by 18 months or not speaking two-word phrases by 2 years needs evaluation) and to guide parents on safety, nutrition and behaviour.

Conclusion Growth is quantitative increase in size and development is qualitative increase in function; both follow orderly principles and are influenced by heredity, nutrition, hormones, illness, environment and emotional stimulation. The toddler walks, runs and climbs, builds towers, speaks in phrases and sentences, seeks autonomy and begins toilet training, and needs safety, nutrition, patient discipline and stimulation from parents.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Describe the physical growth of an infant during the first year. (5 marks) (b) Explain the motor, language and social milestones of an infant. (6 marks) (c) Write the anticipatory guidance for parents of an infant. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Gross motor milestones in the first year
labels: 3 months head control; 4–5 months rolls over; 6 months sits with support; 8 months sits without support; 9 months crawls and stands with support; 10–11 months cruises; 12–13 months stands alone and walks

answer_html:
Introduction Infancy is the period from birth to one year. It is the period of the fastest growth and development after birth, and of the greatest vulnerability to infection and malnutrition.

(a) Physical growth during infancy (5 marks)

  1. Weight
    • Average birth weight is about 2.8–3 kg in India; babies lose up to about 10% in the first week and regain birth weight by 10–14 days.
    • Gain is about 25–30 g per day in the first 3 months, then slower.
    • Weight doubles by about 5 months and triples by 1 year (about 9–10 kg).
  2. Length
    • About 50 cm at birth, about 75 cm at 1 year (an increase of about 50%).
  3. Head circumference
    • About 33–35 cm at birth, increasing by about 2 cm per month in the first 3 months; about 45–46 cm at 1 year. It reflects brain growth; very small or rapidly enlarging heads need evaluation.
  4. Chest circumference
    • Less than the head circumference at birth (by about 2 cm); equal to the head circumference at about 1 year, and larger thereafter.
  5. Fontanelles
    • Posterior fontanelle closes by about 6–8 weeks; anterior fontanelle closes by 12–18 months. A bulging fontanelle suggests raised intracranial pressure, a sunken one dehydration.
  6. Teeth
    • The first teeth (lower central incisors) appear at about 6–7 months; about 6–8 teeth by 1 year.
  7. Other changes
    • Vital signs: heart rate falls from about 120–160/min at birth to about 100–140/min at 1 year; respiratory rate from 30–60/min to 25–40/min.
    • Primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, grasp, stepping) disappear by 3–6 months as voluntary control develops.
    • Physiological anaemia at 2–3 months; immunity from maternal antibodies wanes after 6 months.

(b) Developmental milestones (6 marks) 1. Gross motor

  • 1 month – lifts head momentarily in prone.
  • 3 months – holds head steady (neck control).
  • 4–5 months – rolls over.
  • 6 months – sits with support; bears weight on legs.
  • 8 months – sits without support.
  • 9 months – crawls; stands holding furniture.
  • 10–11 months – cruises (walks holding furniture).
  • 12–13 months – stands alone and takes first steps.

2. Fine motor

  • 3 months – hands open; grasp reflex disappears; plays with hands.
  • 4–5 months – reaches for and grasps objects with the whole palm (palmar grasp).
  • 6–7 months – transfers objects from hand to hand.
  • 9 months – pincer grasp (thumb and finger) begins; bangs two cubes.
  • 12 months – neat pincer grasp; releases objects on request; tries to scribble.

3. Language

  • 1–2 months – responds to sounds; cooing (vowel sounds) by 2–3 months.
  • 4 months – laughs aloud.
  • 6 months – monosyllables ("ba", "da").
  • 9 months – bisyllables ("mama", "dada", without meaning); understands "no".
  • 12 months – 1–2 meaningful words; understands simple commands.

4. Personal–social

  • 6–8 weeks – social smile.
  • 3 months – recognises the mother.
  • 6–9 months – stranger anxiety; enjoys mirror image.
  • 9 months – waves "bye-bye", plays peek-a-boo.
  • 12 months – plays simple ball games; drinks from a cup with help; cooperates in dressing.
  • Erikson – trust versus mistrust – consistent, loving care builds basic trust.
  • Piaget – sensorimotor stage – learning through senses and movement; object permanence develops at about 9–10 months.

(c) Anticipatory guidance for parents (4 marks)

  1. Feeding – exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; complementary feeding from 6 months with continued breastfeeding; hygiene in preparing food; no bottle feeding.
  2. Immunisation – complete all doses according to the national schedule (birth, 6, 10, 14 weeks and 9 months), and Vitamin A at 9 months.
  3. Growth monitoring – monthly weighing and plotting on the MCP card.
  4. Safety
    • Never leave the baby alone on a bed or table (falls); keep small objects, coins and buttons away (choking); keep hot liquids, stoves and lamps out of reach (burns); never leave the baby alone near water or buckets (drowning); keep medicines and kerosene locked (poisoning); place the baby on the back to sleep.
  5. Stimulation and play – talk, sing and smile; bright toys, rattles; tummy time; respond promptly to crying (builds trust).
  6. Hygiene and care – daily bath, cord and nappy care, clean clothes, handwashing before handling the baby.
  7. Teething – offer a clean teething ring; clean gums and teeth; see a doctor if fever or diarrhoea occurs (not caused by teething alone).
  8. Warning signs – poor feeding, fast breathing, fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, convulsions – seek care immediately.
  9. Developmental concerns – report if the baby does not smile by 2–3 months, hold the head by 4 months, sit by 9 months or respond to sounds.

Newborn reflexes and the age at which they disappear

  • Moro (startle) reflex – present at birth, disappears by about 3–6 months.
  • Rooting and sucking reflexes – rooting disappears by about 3–4 months (sucking becomes voluntary).
  • Palmar grasp – disappears by about 3–4 months; plantar grasp by about 9–12 months.
  • Stepping (walking) reflex – disappears by about 2 months.
  • Asymmetric tonic neck reflex – disappears by about 4–6 months.
  • Babinski sign (fanning of toes) – normal up to about 12–18 months. Persistence of these reflexes beyond the expected age, or their absence at birth, suggests a neurological problem.

Measuring the growth of an infant

  • Weight – on an electronic or beam infant weighing scale, naked or with minimal clothing, at the same time of day; recorded to the nearest 10 g.
  • Length – with an infantometer (lying down) with the head against the fixed board and legs straightened; height is measured standing after 2 years.
  • Head and chest circumference – with a non-stretchable tape.
  • Values are plotted on the WHO growth charts in the MCP card (weight-for-age, length-for-age, weight-for-length); a falling or flat growth curve (growth faltering) is an early warning sign of illness or malnutrition.

Developmental red flags in infancy

  • No social smile by 3 months; no head control by 4 months; not reaching for objects by 5–6 months; not sitting without support by 9 months; no babbling by 9–12 months; not responding to name or sounds; loss of skills already learnt; persistent squint after 6 months. Such infants are referred for developmental assessment (RBSK, District Early Intervention Centre).

Nursing importance

  • Regular growth and developmental assessment at immunisation and under-five clinics allows early detection of malnutrition, hearing and vision problems, and developmental delay.

Conclusion In the first year an infant doubles the birth weight by about 5 months and triples it by 1 year, grows about 25 cm in length and 12 cm in head circumference, and progresses from head control to standing and first steps, from cooing to first words and from social smile to stranger anxiety. Anticipatory guidance on feeding, immunisation, safety, stimulation and warning signs helps parents raise a healthy infant.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define play. (2 marks) (b) Explain the values (functions) and types of play. (7 marks) (c) Describe the selection of play materials for children of different ages and the role of the nurse in play. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of play according to social character
labels: organised group play with rules and roles)

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Play is a spontaneous, voluntary and enjoyable activity that a child engages in for its own sake, without any purpose other than the pleasure it gives. Play is the work of children – through play they learn about themselves and the world, develop skills and express their feelings.

(b) Values and types of play (7 marks) A. Values (functions) of play

  1. Sensorimotor (physical) development – running, climbing, throwing and handling toys develop muscles, coordination, balance and fine motor skills; play burns energy and builds fitness.
  2. Intellectual (cognitive) development – children learn colours, shapes, sizes, textures, numbers and cause and effect; puzzles and games develop problem-solving, memory and language.
  3. Socialisation and moral development – children learn to share, take turns, follow rules, cooperate, compete fairly and accept others; they learn right and wrong.
  4. Creativity – drawing, clay, building and imaginative play develop creativity and imagination.
  5. Self-awareness – children discover their abilities, test limits and develop self-confidence and a sense of identity, including gender roles.
  6. Emotional release and therapeutic value – play allows children to express fear, anger and anxiety safely, to master frightening experiences and to cope with stress such as hospitalisation.
  7. Communication – play is the child's language; nurses use it to understand feelings and to explain procedures.

B. Types of play 1. According to social character (Parten)

  • Onlooker play – the child watches others play and may talk to them but does not join (toddlers).
  • Solitary (independent) play – the child plays alone with own toys (infants and young toddlers).
  • Parallel play – the child plays beside other children with similar toys, but not with them (toddlers, 2–3 years).
  • Associative play – children play together in a loosely organised way, sharing toys, without fixed rules or goals (preschoolers).
  • Cooperative play – organised group play with rules, roles and a common goal, such as team games (school-age children).

2. According to content

  • Social–affective play – the infant enjoys interaction with adults (smiling, cooing, peek-a-boo).
  • Sense-pleasure play – enjoyment of sensory experiences – water, sand, mud, music, colours.
  • Skill play – repeated practice of a new skill (stacking blocks, cycling).
  • Dramatic (pretend, imaginative) play – acting out roles ("mother", "doctor", "teacher"); common in preschoolers.
  • Games – play with rules (hide-and-seek, kho-kho, carrom, cricket, board and computer games) – school-age children.
  • Unoccupied behaviour – the child seems to be doing nothing but is observing and exploring.

(c) Selection of play materials and the role of the nurse (6 marks) A. Principles of selecting toys

  • Safety – non-toxic paint, no sharp edges or points, no small detachable parts for children below 3 years (choking), strong and durable, washable; no toys with long strings near infants.
  • Suited to age, developmental level and interests; should be stimulating but not frustrating.
  • Simple, inexpensive and locally available (traditional Indian toys, household articles); allow creativity rather than passive watching.
  • Variety – to develop physical, mental and social skills; limit screen time.

B. Play materials by age

  • 0–3 months – bright, moving mobiles, rattles, soft music, the mother's face and voice.
  • 4–6 months – rattles, squeeze toys, teething rings, soft balls, a mirror.
  • 7–12 months – blocks, nesting cups, push–pull toys, big balls, picture books, peek-a-boo games.
  • Toddlers (1–3 years) – push–pull toys, large blocks, simple puzzles, crayons, sand and water play, dolls and soft toys, toy telephone, simple musical instruments; tricycle at about 3 years.
  • Preschoolers (3–6 years) – tricycle, dolls and doll-house, kitchen sets, doctor sets, dress-up clothes, clay, paints, picture and story books, jigsaw puzzles, swings and slides.
  • School-age children (6–12 years) – board games (snakes and ladders, carrom, chess), sports (cricket, football, badminton), bicycle, skipping rope, craft and science kits, books, hobbies such as collections and gardening.
  • Adolescents – team sports, music, reading, computer and creative hobbies, social and community activities.

C. Role of the nurse in play

  1. Educating parents about the value of play and suitable, safe toys for each age.
  2. Providing play in hospital – a playroom or play corner, toys for bed-bound children, play with the child during care; children with infections are given toys that can be disinfected or discarded.
  3. Therapeutic play – using dolls and equipment to prepare children for procedures (instructional play), allowing them to act out their experiences (emotional outlet), and games that encourage deep breathing, exercise or drinking (physiologically enhancing play).
  4. Observation – noting how a child plays to assess development and emotional state.
  5. Adapting play to the child's condition – quiet play for children on bed rest, play suited to children with disabilities.
  6. Safety – checking toys for damage and hazards, supervising play.

D. Factors influencing play

  • Age and development – the type of play changes with motor, cognitive and social maturity.
  • Health – sick or malnourished children play less; play returns as the child recovers (a useful sign of improvement).
  • Intelligence and personality – bright children prefer creative and problem-solving play; shy children prefer solitary play.
  • Sex and culture – gender roles and cultural norms influence choice of play and toys.
  • Environment – space, safety, playgrounds and time available; urban crowding limits outdoor play.
  • Socio-economic status – availability of toys, books and leisure; simple household articles can be equally effective.
  • Companions – siblings and friends encourage social play.

E. Play for children with special needs

  • Children with disability need adapted toys (large, easy-to-grip, sound-making toys for visually impaired children; visual toys for hearing-impaired children; toys that encourage movement for children with cerebral palsy), with goals set by the therapist.
  • Children on bed rest or with limited energy need quiet play – books, puzzles, drawing, music, storytelling.
  • Children in isolation need toys that can be disinfected or given to keep.
  • Children with chronic illness benefit from play that gives them a sense of control and a normal childhood, such as caring for a doll that has the same illness.

F. Problems of excessive screen use

  • Long hours with mobile phones, television and video games reduce physical activity, outdoor and social play, sleep and language development, and increase obesity and behaviour problems. The nurse advises parents to avoid screens for children below 2 years (except video calls with family), to limit screen time to about one hour a day of good-quality content for 2–5-year-olds, and to encourage active, creative play.

Conclusion Play is the child's natural, enjoyable activity and the "work of childhood". It promotes physical, intellectual, social, moral, creative and emotional development and has great therapeutic value. Play progresses from solitary and parallel play in infants and toddlers to associative and cooperative play in older children, and toys must be safe, age-appropriate and stimulating. Nurses guide parents, provide play and therapeutic play in hospital, and use play to assess and help children.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the growth and development of the preschool child, with the needs and parental guidance.
answer_html:
Introduction The preschool period extends from 3 to 6 years. Growth is steady, motor skills are refined, language expands rapidly, and the child develops initiative, imagination and readiness for school.

1. Physical growth

  • Weight increases by about 2 kg per year and height by about 6–7 cm per year; birth length doubles by about 4 years.
  • The child becomes slimmer and taller as the pot-belly disappears; bladder and bowel control are usually achieved.

2. Motor development

  • Gross motor – rides a tricycle (3 years), hops on one foot (4 years), skips and balances on one foot for several seconds (5 years), climbs and runs well, catches a ball.
  • Fine motor – copies a circle (3 years), cross (4 years), square (about 4½ years) and triangle (5 years); uses scissors; draws a person with several body parts; dresses alone; ties shoelaces by 5–6 years.

3. Language and cognitive development

  • Vocabulary grows from about 900 words at 3 years to about 2,000 words by 5 years; speaks in full sentences; asks "why" and "how"; tells stories; knows colours and counts.
  • Piaget – preoperational stage – egocentrism (sees things only from own point of view), magical thinking (thoughts can cause events), animism (lifeless objects are alive), centration; the child may believe illness is punishment.

4. Psychosocial development

  • Erikson – initiative versus guilt – the child plans and starts activities; too much criticism causes guilt.
  • Freud – phallic stage – curiosity about body differences; identification with the parent of the same sex.
  • Play – associative and imaginative play, dress-up, role play; imaginary playmates are common and normal.
  • Fears – of the dark, animals, ghosts and bodily injury (mutilation).
  • Common problems – bed-wetting, thumb-sucking, stuttering, temper tantrums, sibling rivalry, curiosity about sex.

5. Needs and parental guidance

  1. Nutrition – balanced family diet with milk, pulses, vegetables, fruits; avoid junk food and sweet drinks; family meals.
  2. Safety – road safety, playground and water safety, no matches or medicines within reach, teach the child his name, address and parents' phone number, body safety (good touch–bad touch).
  3. Preparation for school – reading stories, drawing, simple counting; develop self-care skills and social skills.
  4. Discipline – consistent rules, praise for good behaviour, time-out rather than beating.
  5. Answer questions honestly, including simple sex education.
  6. Dental care – brushing twice daily, regular dental check-up.
  7. Immunisation – DPT booster at 5–6 years; Vitamin A up to 5 years; deworming.
  8. Adequate sleep (10–13 hours) and limited screen time; plenty of outdoor play.

Conclusion The preschool child grows steadily, hops, skips and copies shapes, speaks fluently, thinks magically and egocentrically, and develops initiative through imaginative and associative play. Parents need guidance on nutrition, safety, school readiness, discipline, honest answers, dental care, immunisation and play.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the growth and development of the school-age child, with the needs and parental guidance.
answer_html:
Introduction The school-age period extends from 6 to 12 years (up to puberty). Growth is slow and steady, the child becomes increasingly skilled and independent, and school and friends become very important.

1. Physical growth

  • Weight increases by about 2–3 kg per year and height by about 5–6 cm per year; boys and girls are of similar size until girls' growth spurt begins at about 10–11 years.
  • Permanent teeth begin to erupt at about 6 years (first molars); deciduous teeth are shed.
  • Body proportions become more adult-like; muscle strength and coordination improve; vision matures.

2. Motor development

  • Rides a bicycle, swims, plays team sports, skips rope; fine motor skills allow neat writing, drawing, craft work and playing musical instruments.

3. Cognitive development

  • Piaget – concrete operational stage – logical thinking about concrete objects; understands conservation (quantity remains the same when shape changes), classification, reversibility and cause and effect; can understand simple explanations of illness and treatment.

4. Psychosocial and moral development

  • Erikson – industry versus inferiority – the child enjoys learning, achieving and being productive; repeated failure or criticism leads to feelings of inferiority.
  • Freud – latency stage – sexual interests are quiet; energy is directed to school and friendships.
  • Kohlberg – conventional level – follows rules to be "good" and to maintain social order.
  • Peer group ("gang age") – friends of the same sex, clubs, team games, collections and hobbies; cooperative play with rules; competition.

5. Common problems

  • School phobia, learning difficulties, attention problems, bullying, accidents and sports injuries, dental caries, refractive errors, worm infestations, obesity and excessive screen time, early puberty.

6. Needs and parental guidance

  1. Nutrition – balanced diet with breakfast, healthy school lunch (PM POSHAN in government schools), limited junk food and sugary drinks.
  2. Physical activity – at least one hour of active play daily; limit screen time; adequate sleep (9–11 hours).
  3. School support – interest in homework without pressure; communication with teachers; attention to vision, hearing and learning problems.
  4. Safety – road and cycling safety (helmets), swimming safety, safe use of the internet, protection from abuse.
  5. Personal hygiene and dental care – handwashing, bathing, brushing, regular check-ups.
  6. Preparation for puberty – age-appropriate information on body changes and menstruation.
  7. Immunisation – Td at 10 and 16 years; HPV vaccine for girls (9–14 years) under the national campaign; deworming.
  8. Encouragement and praise for effort; responsibility through small household tasks.

Conclusion The school-age child grows slowly and steadily, gets permanent teeth, thinks logically about concrete things, develops industry through learning and peer activities, and follows rules. Parents need guidance on nutrition, activity, sleep, schooling, safety, hygiene, puberty and immunisation.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain Kohlberg's theory of moral development and its implications for child health nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Lawrence Kohlberg (an American psychologist), building on Piaget's work, described how children's moral reasoning – their ideas about right and wrong – develops in three levels with two stages each. He studied how children answered moral dilemmas such as the "Heinz dilemma" (whether a man should steal a drug to save his dying wife).

1. Level I – Preconventional morality (about 4–10 years)

  • Morality is based on external consequences – punishment and reward.
  • Stage 1 – Punishment and obedience orientation – an act is wrong if it is punished; the child obeys to avoid punishment.
  • Stage 2 – Instrumental-relativist (individualism and exchange) orientation – right is what satisfies one's own needs; "you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours".

2. Level II – Conventional morality (about 10–13 years and adolescence)

  • Morality is based on conforming to the expectations of family and society.
  • Stage 3 – Good boy–nice girl (interpersonal concordance) orientation – good behaviour is what pleases or helps others and earns approval.
  • Stage 4 – Law and order orientation – respect for authority, rules and duty to maintain social order.

3. Level III – Postconventional (principled) morality (adolescence and adulthood; not reached by everyone)

  • Morality is based on self-chosen principles.
  • Stage 5 – Social contract orientation – laws are agreements that can be changed for the greater good; individual rights are respected.
  • Stage 6 – Universal ethical principles orientation – decisions are guided by conscience and universal principles of justice, equality and human dignity.

4. Criticisms

  • Based mainly on male subjects; Carol Gilligan argued that women's morality emphasises care and relationships (ethics of care) rather than justice alone; moral reasoning does not always predict behaviour; cultural differences.

5. Implications for child health nursing

  • Preschool and young school children understand rules in terms of punishment and reward – explain ward rules simply, use praise and rewards (stickers) rather than threats; reassure them that illness or procedures are not punishment.
  • School-age children want to be "good" and follow rules – involve them in setting simple rules, praise cooperation, explain the reasons for treatment.
  • Adolescents reason about rights, fairness and principles – respect their opinions, involve them in decisions about their care, discuss consent, confidentiality and risky behaviours openly.
  • Nurses and parents act as role models of honesty, fairness and caring; moral education through stories, discussion and consistent discipline.

Conclusion Kohlberg described moral development in three levels – preconventional (punishment and self-interest), conventional (approval and law and order) and postconventional (social contract and universal principles). Nurses use this understanding to explain rules, reassure children that illness is not punishment, use praise, and involve older children and adolescents in decisions.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain how developmental theories guide the nursing care of children of different ages.
answer_html:
Introduction The theories of Freud (psychosexual), Erikson (psychosocial) and Piaget (cognitive) describe what children of each age need, fear and understand. Applying them helps the nurse give developmentally appropriate care, especially when a child is ill or in hospital.

1. Infant (0–1 year)

  • Erikson – trust vs mistrust; Freud – oral stage; Piaget – sensorimotor.
  • Nursing care – consistent caregiver, prompt response to crying, keep the mother with the baby (rooming-in, breastfeeding); allow non-nutritive sucking (pacifier during procedures, especially if nil by mouth); cuddling, eye contact and soothing talk; bright toys and mobiles for stimulation.

2. Toddler (1–3 years)

  • Erikson – autonomy vs shame and doubt; Freud – anal stage (toilet training); Piaget – late sensorimotor/early preoperational.
  • Nursing care – allow choices and self-care (feeding self, holding the cup); maintain home routines and toileting words; do not insist on toilet training during illness and accept regression; limit restraint; parents present; simple explanations just before procedures; push–pull toys and parallel play.

3. Preschooler (3–6 years)

  • Erikson – initiative vs guilt; Freud – phallic stage; Piaget – preoperational (magical thinking, egocentrism).
  • Nursing care – explain with dolls and pictures; avoid frightening words; reassure that illness is not a punishment; cover wounds with bandages (fear of mutilation); allow play and simple tasks; give praise; protect modesty.

4. School-age child (6–12 years)

  • Erikson – industry vs inferiority; Freud – latency; Piaget – concrete operations.
  • Nursing care – explain the illness and procedures logically with diagrams and models; involve the child in care (keeping an intake chart, choosing menus); continue schoolwork and hobbies; allow contact with friends; respect privacy; recognise achievements.

5. Adolescent (12–18 years)

  • Erikson – identity vs role confusion; Freud – genital stage; Piaget – formal operations (abstract thinking).
  • Nursing care – respect privacy and confidentiality; involve in decisions and explain fully; allow own clothes and belongings; consider body-image concerns; facilitate contact with peers (phone, visits); discuss sensitive health issues without judgement; place in adolescent or age-appropriate wards.

6. General applications

  • Choosing appropriate toys, communication, explanations, pain assessment tools and discipline; recognising regression as a normal response to stress; teaching parents what to expect.

Conclusion Developmental theories guide nursing care by showing that infants need trust and comfort, toddlers need autonomy and routines, preschoolers need reassurance and play, school-age children need explanation and achievement, and adolescents need privacy, identity and participation. Care planned with these needs in mind reduces stress and promotes normal development during illness.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain toilet training – the signs of readiness, the method and the guidance to parents.
answer_html:
Introduction Toilet training is the process of teaching a child to control bladder and bowel and to use the potty or toilet. It is a major task of the toddler period (Freud's anal stage; Erikson's autonomy stage). Success depends on the child's physical and psychological readiness, not on age alone.

1. Signs of readiness (usually between 18 months and 3 years)

  • Physical – voluntary control of anal and urethral sphincters (usually after 18–24 months); stays dry for about 2 hours; regular bowel movements; can walk, sit and squat, and pull pants up and down.
  • Mental – recognises the urge to pass urine or stool; can communicate it by words or gestures; understands and follows simple instructions.
  • Psychological – wants to please the parents, shows interest in the toilet and in imitating others, dislikes wet or soiled nappies.
  • Parental readiness – parents have time and patience; no major stress (new baby, moving house, illness).

2. Method

  1. Choose a suitable time and a potty chair (or a child seat on the toilet) on which the feet touch the floor.
  2. Use simple, consistent words for urine and stool.
  3. Let the child sit on the potty, fully clothed at first, to become familiar with it; then at regular times – after waking, after meals and before bed – for a few minutes only.
  4. Watch for signs of need (squatting, grunting) and take the child to the potty.
  5. Praise success; never punish accidents.
  6. Use easy-to-remove clothes; move to training pants when the child is dry for most of the day.
  7. Teach hygiene – wiping front to back (girls), flushing, handwashing. - Bowel control is usually achieved before bladder control; daytime bladder control by about 2–3 years, and night-time dryness by about 3–5 years.

3. Guidance to parents

  • Do not start too early or force the child; avoid scolding, shaming or punishment – it causes fear, constipation and resistance.
  • Expect accidents and regression during stress (illness, hospitalisation, birth of a sibling) – stay calm.
  • Be consistent among all caregivers (grandparents, crèche).
  • Night-time wetting up to 5 years is normal; seek advice if the child is still wet after 5–6 years or if there is pain, dribbling or constipation.
  • In hospital, the nurse continues the child's home routine and words and does not insist on training during illness.

Conclusion Toilet training succeeds when the child is physically, mentally and psychologically ready, usually between 18 months and 3 years. A patient, consistent, praise-based approach with a potty chair and regular sitting times, without punishment, helps the child achieve bowel and bladder control.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain dentition in children and the care of teeth.
answer_html:
Introduction Healthy teeth are needed for chewing, speech, appearance and the correct placement of permanent teeth. Dental caries is the commonest chronic disease of childhood and is largely preventable.

1. Deciduous (milk, primary) teeth – 20 in number

  • Eruption begins at about 6–7 months with the lower central incisors; followed by upper central incisors (7–8 months), lateral incisors (8–10 months), first molars (12–16 months), canines (16–20 months) and second molars (20–30 months).
  • All 20 are present by about 2½–3 years.
  • A rough guide for the number of milk teeth up to 2 years: age in months minus 6.
  • Delayed eruption (no teeth by 13 months) may occur with rickets, hypothyroidism or Down syndrome.

2. Permanent teeth – 32 in number

  • Begin to erupt at about 6 years (first molars, the "six-year molars"), followed by the incisors (6–8 years); shedding of milk teeth continues up to about 12 years; second molars at about 12 years and third molars (wisdom teeth) at 17–25 years.

3. Teething

  • May cause drooling, irritability, desire to bite and mild gum swelling; it does not cause high fever, diarrhoea or convulsions – such symptoms need medical evaluation.
  • Relief – a clean, cool teething ring, gentle gum massage with a clean finger; avoid teething powders and sugary syrups.

4. Dental caries in children

  • Early childhood caries (nursing bottle caries) – caused by prolonged bottle feeding, especially at bedtime with milk or sweet drinks, frequent sugary snacks and poor oral hygiene; affects the upper front teeth first.
  • Effects – pain, infection, abscess, poor feeding, loss of teeth and malpositioned permanent teeth.

5. Care of teeth

  1. Infants – clean the gums with a soft, moist cloth after feeds; avoid putting the baby to sleep with a bottle; no sweet dummies.
  2. From the first tooth – brush twice daily with a soft child's toothbrush and a smear (rice-grain size) of fluoride toothpaste up to 3 years, and a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6 years; parents should brush for young children and supervise until about 7–8 years.
  3. Diet – limit sugary foods and drinks, especially between meals; encourage fruits, vegetables and milk; rinse the mouth after meals.
  4. Fluoride – use of fluoride toothpaste; professional fluoride varnish where advised (avoid excess fluoride in areas with high fluoride in water – fluorosis).
  5. Regular dental check-ups – first visit by the first birthday or within 6 months of the first tooth, then every 6 months; pit-and-fissure sealants for permanent molars.
  6. Prevent injury – mouth guards in contact sports; seek immediate dental care for knocked-out permanent teeth (keep the tooth in milk).
  7. Discourage prolonged thumb-sucking beyond 4–5 years.

Conclusion Children have 20 milk teeth, beginning at about 6–7 months and complete by 2½–3 years, and 32 permanent teeth, beginning at about 6 years. Teething causes only mild symptoms. Early childhood caries is prevented by avoiding bedtime bottles and frequent sweets, brushing with fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth, and regular dental check-ups.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: List the gross motor milestones in the first year of life.
answer_html:
Gross motor milestones (first year)

  1. 3 months – holds the head steady (neck control).
  2. 4–5 months – rolls over.
  3. 6 months – sits with support.
  4. 8 months – sits without support.
  5. 9 months – crawls; stands holding on to furniture.
  6. 10–11 months – cruises (walks holding furniture).
  7. 12–13 months – stands alone and takes the first steps. Failure to hold the head by 4 months, sit without support by 9 months or walk by 18 months needs developmental evaluation.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: List the milestones of language development up to 3 years.
answer_html:
Language milestones

  1. 2–3 months – cooing (vowel sounds).
  2. 4 months – laughs aloud.
  3. 6 months – monosyllables ("ba", "da").
  4. 9 months – bisyllables ("mama", "dada") without meaning; understands "no".
  5. 12 months – 1–2 meaningful words.
  6. 18 months – about 10–20 words; names familiar objects.
  7. 2 years – two-word phrases; about 300 words.
  8. 3 years – three-word sentences; asks questions; tells name, age and gender; about 900 words. A child who does not babble by 12 months, has no words by 16–18 months or no two-word phrases by 2 years should have a hearing test and developmental assessment.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is Tanner staging?
answer_html:
Tanner staging (sexual maturity rating) is a five-stage scale, described by J. M. Tanner, used to assess the physical development of secondary sexual characteristics during puberty.

  • In girls – based on breast development and pubic hair.
  • In boys – based on genital (testicular and penile) development and pubic hair.
  • Stage 1 is prepubertal (childlike) and stage 5 is adult; stages 2–4 are intermediate.
  • Uses – to assess whether puberty is normal, early (precocious) or delayed; to interpret growth (the growth spurt occurs at about Tanner stages 2–3 in girls and 3–4 in boys); and to guide health education of adolescents.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST-II)?
answer_html:
The Denver Developmental Screening Test (Denver II) is a widely used screening tool to identify children from birth to 6 years who may have developmental delay.

  • It assesses four domains – personal–social, fine motor–adaptive, language and gross motor – using 125 items, plus behaviour during the test.
  • The child's performance is compared with the age at which 25%, 50%, 75% and 90% of children pass each item; items failed that most younger children pass are "delays".
  • Results are normal, suspect or untestable; suspect results need re-testing and full developmental assessment.
  • It is a screening, not a diagnostic test. In India, simpler tools such as the Trivandrum Developmental Screening Chart and RBSK checklists are also used.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Differentiate between parallel play and associative play.
answer_html:
Parallel play

  • Typical of toddlers (2–3 years).
  • Children play beside each other with similar toys, but not with each other – there is little interaction or sharing.

  • Example – two toddlers each playing with their own blocks side by side. Associative play

  • Typical of preschoolers (3–5 years).

  • Children play together, share toys and talk about the activity, but the play is loosely organised, without fixed rules, roles or a common goal.
  • Example – a group of children riding tricycles and following one another around.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Give the normal head circumference at different ages and its significance.
answer_html:
Head (occipitofrontal) circumference is measured with a non-stretchable tape around the head just above the eyebrows and over the most prominent part of the occiput. Normal values (approximate)

  • Birth – 33–35 cm.
  • 3 months – about 40 cm (increase of about 2 cm per month in the first 3 months).
  • 1 year – about 45–46 cm.
  • 2 years – about 48 cm.
  • 5 years – about 50–51 cm. Significance – it reflects brain growth; a small head (microcephaly) suggests poor brain growth (e.g. congenital infections, genetic causes), while a large or rapidly increasing head (macrocephaly) suggests hydrocephalus or other conditions; head circumference is plotted regularly on growth charts in the first two years.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define a neonate and classify newborns according to gestational age and birth weight. (3 marks) (b) Explain the assessment (appraisal) of a newborn, including the APGAR score, physical examination and assessment of gestational age. (12 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of newborns by gestational age and birth weight
labels: post-term ≥ 42 weeks); vertical axis birth weight with 10th and 90th percentile curves dividing SGA
AGA and LGA; weight bands LBW < 2500 g

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) A neonate (newborn) is a baby from birth to 28 days of life. The first week is the early neonatal period and 7–28 days the late neonatal period.

Classification

  1. By gestational age
    • Preterm – born before 37 completed weeks (late preterm 34–36+6 weeks; very preterm below 32 weeks; extremely preterm below 28 weeks).
    • Term – 37 to 41+6 weeks.
    • Post-term – 42 weeks or more.
  2. By birth weight
    • Low birth weight (LBW) – below 2,500 g (irrespective of gestational age).
    • Very low birth weight (VLBW) – below 1,500 g.
    • Extremely low birth weight (ELBW) – below 1,000 g.
  3. By weight for gestational age (intrauterine growth)
    • Small for gestational age (SGA) – below the 10th percentile.
    • Appropriate for gestational age (AGA) – 10th to 90th percentile.
    • Large for gestational age (LGA) – above the 90th percentile (e.g. infants of diabetic mothers).

(b) Assessment (appraisal) of the newborn (12 marks) The newborn is assessed immediately at birth, again within 24 hours (detailed examination) and before discharge, to detect problems early and plan care.

A. History

  • Maternal age, parity, blood group, illnesses (diabetes, hypertension, infections), drugs, antenatal care; duration of labour, rupture of membranes, liquor (meconium), mode of delivery, need for resuscitation; family history of genetic disorders.

B. APGAR score Developed by Dr. Virginia Apgar; assessed at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth (and every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if the score is below 7). | Sign | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---|---|---| | Appearance (colour) | Blue or pale all over | Body pink, extremities blue | Completely pink | | Pulse (heart rate) | Absent | Below 100/min | 100/min or more | | Grimace (reflex irritability) | No response | Grimace | Cry, cough, sneeze | | Activity (muscle tone) | Limp | Some flexion | Active movement | | Respiration | Absent | Slow, irregular, weak cry | Good, strong cry | - 7–10 – normal; 4–6 – moderate depression; 0–3 – severe depression. - Resuscitation is not delayed to calculate the APGAR score; it is decided by breathing, heart rate and tone.

C. Vital signs and measurements

  • Temperature – 36.5–37.5 °C (axillary).
  • Heart rate – 120–160/min (apical, counted for a full minute).
  • Respiratory rate – 40–60/min (counted for a full minute; periodic breathing is normal, but apnoea above 20 seconds is abnormal).
  • Weight – average 2.8–3 kg; length about 50 cm; head circumference 33–35 cm; chest circumference about 2 cm less than head circumference.

D. General examination

  • Posture – flexed limbs (term baby); poor tone suggests prematurity, asphyxia or sepsis.
  • Cry – strong; a weak or high-pitched cry is abnormal.
  • Colour – pink; acrocyanosis (blue hands and feet) in the first 24–48 hours is normal; central cyanosis, pallor or jaundice in the first 24 hours is abnormal.
  • Skin – vernix caseosa, lanugo (more in preterm), milia, mongolian spots, erythema toxicum (normal); look for rashes, petechiae, oedema, birthmarks.

E. Head-to-toe examination

  1. Head – shape (moulding), anterior and posterior fontanelles (size, tension), sutures; caput succedaneum (oedema crossing suture lines, disappears in a few days) versus cephalhaematoma (blood under the periosteum, limited by sutures, takes weeks to resolve).
  2. Face – symmetry (facial palsy), features suggesting syndromes (e.g. Down syndrome).
  3. Eyes – discharge, subconjunctival haemorrhage, red reflex (cataract), size.
  4. Ears – shape, position (low-set ears), patency; hearing screening before discharge.
  5. Nose – patency of both nostrils (choanal atresia).
  6. Mouth – cleft lip and palate, tongue-tie, natal teeth, Epstein pearls, ability to suck.
  7. Neck – swellings, webbing, sternomastoid tumour, clavicle fracture (crepitus).
  8. Chest – shape, symmetry, retractions, breath sounds, breast enlargement (normal), heart sounds and murmurs.
  9. Abdomen – soft, slightly protuberant; liver palpable 1–2 cm; masses; umbilical cord – two arteries and one vein, bleeding or discharge.
  10. Genitalia – male: testes in the scrotum, position of urethral opening (hypospadias), hydrocele; female: labia, vaginal discharge or bleeding (normal); ambiguous genitalia.
  11. Anus – patency (imperforate anus); passage of meconium within 24–48 hours and urine within 24 hours.
  12. Spine – swellings or dimples (neural tube defects), tufts of hair.
  13. Limbs – number of fingers and toes, palmar creases (single crease), movements (Erb's palsy), hips for developmental dysplasia (Barlow and Ortolani tests), club foot.

F. Neurological assessment – primitive reflexes

  • Moro, rooting, sucking, swallowing, palmar and plantar grasp, stepping, tonic neck and Babinski reflexes – their absence or asymmetry suggests neurological injury, prematurity or nerve palsy.

G. Assessment of gestational age

  • New Ballard Score – assesses six neuromuscular signs (posture, square window at the wrist, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel to ear) and six physical signs (skin, lanugo, plantar creases, breast, eye and ear, genitalia); the total score gives the gestational age (about 20–44 weeks).
  • Physical clues of a term baby – creases over the whole sole, well-formed breast bud (5–10 mm), firm ear cartilage with quick recoil, testes in the scrotum with rugae, labia majora covering labia minora; the preterm baby has thin, red skin, plenty of lanugo, few sole creases, soft ears and poor tone.

H. Screening before discharge

  • Blood glucose in at-risk babies; congenital hypothyroidism and other metabolic screening where available; hearing screening; pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease; check for jaundice; weight and feeding.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Examine in a warm place (radiant warmer), quickly and gently, with clean hands; explain findings to the mother; record findings; report abnormalities (malformations, respiratory distress, jaundice in the first 24 hours, poor feeding, absent meconium) promptly.

I. Assessment of feeding and behaviour

  • Observe a breastfeed – position and attachment, effective sucking and swallowing, number of feeds (8–12 in 24 hours); urine 6 or more times a day after the first few days.
  • States of the newborn – deep sleep, light sleep, drowsy, quiet alert, active alert and crying; a healthy baby moves between these states, can be consoled and shows interest in faces and voices.
  • Mother–baby interaction – bonding, comfort with handling, confidence; identify mothers who need extra support.

J. Danger signs that may be found during appraisal (refer immediately)

  • Not feeding well or unable to suck; convulsions; fast breathing (60 or more per minute), severe chest indrawing, grunting; temperature below 35.5 °C or above 37.5 °C; lethargy or no movement; jaundice within 24 hours or on the palms and soles; central cyanosis; bleeding; umbilical redness extending to the skin; many skin pustules; major malformations; no passage of urine or meconium in 24–48 hours.

Conclusion A neonate is a baby up to 28 days old, classified by gestational age (preterm, term, post-term), birth weight (LBW, VLBW, ELBW) and growth (SGA, AGA, LGA). Appraisal includes history, the APGAR score at 1 and 5 minutes, vital signs and measurements, a systematic head-to-toe examination, reflexes, gestational age assessment by the New Ballard Score and screening tests – enabling early detection of problems and planning of care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define low birth weight and list the problems of preterm babies. (5 marks) (b) Describe the nursing management of a preterm, low birth weight baby. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Characteristics of a preterm baby
labels: thin red shiny skin with visible veins
undescended testes or prominent labia minora

answer_html:
(a) Definition and problems (5 marks) Low birth weight (LBW) is defined by WHO as a birth weight below 2,500 g, irrespective of gestational age. LBW babies are either preterm (born before 37 completed weeks), small for gestational age (growth-restricted), or both. LBW is the single most important cause of neonatal death in India.

Characteristics of a preterm baby

  • Small size with a relatively large head; thin, shiny, red skin with visible veins; plenty of lanugo; little subcutaneous fat; soft, flat ear cartilage; few or no plantar creases; small breast buds; undescended testes or prominent labia minora; extended limbs and poor muscle tone; weak cry and poor suck.

Problems of preterm babies

  1. Hypothermia – large surface area, thin skin, little brown fat.
  2. Respiratory problems – respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency), apnoea of prematurity, weak cough.
  3. Hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia – poor stores.
  4. Feeding difficulties – weak or uncoordinated suck and swallow (coordinated after about 34 weeks), small stomach, risk of aspiration; necrotising enterocolitis (NEC).
  5. Infections – immature immunity, invasive procedures.
  6. Jaundice – immature liver.
  7. Neurological – intraventricular haemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia.
  8. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).
  9. Anaemia of prematurity, metabolic bone disease.
  10. Long-term – developmental delay, cerebral palsy, hearing and vision problems, poor growth.

(b) Nursing management (10 marks) 1. Immediate care at birth

  • Deliver in a warm room; resuscitation by a trained team if needed; dry and wrap immediately; delayed cord clamping (at least 60 seconds) when the baby does not need resuscitation; start skin-to-skin contact; give Vitamin K (0.5 mg for babies below 1,000 g; 1 mg above).
  • Shift sick or very small babies to the SNCU in a warm transport.

2. Maintenance of temperature

  • Keep the baby in the thermoneutral range (36.5–37.5 °C) – kangaroo mother care for stable babies; radiant warmer or incubator for sick or very small babies; cap, socks and warm clothes; avoid bathing until stable (sponge only); keep the room warm and draught-free.
  • Check temperature every 2–4 hours (more often under a warmer); avoid overheating.

3. Respiratory care

  • Position with the neck slightly extended; clear secretions gently only when needed.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, colour and SpO2 (target about 90–95% in preterm babies on oxygen); oxygen through nasal prongs or CPAP as ordered; gentle stimulation for apnoea, caffeine as prescribed; record apnoea episodes.

4. Nutrition

  • Breast milk is the best food; feeding method according to maturity – direct breastfeeding (usually at about 34 weeks or more), cup or paladai with expressed breast milk (about 30–34 weeks), orogastric or nasogastric tube (younger or weak babies), and IV fluids for very small or sick babies.
  • Feed every 2–3 hours; increase volumes gradually as ordered; burp; position on the right side or prone with monitoring after feeds; check for abdominal distension and vomiting (NEC).
  • Help the mother express breast milk every 2–3 hours; use donor milk from a human milk bank if needed; supplements (Vitamin D, iron, calcium and phosphorus, multivitamins) as prescribed.
  • Daily weight – expected gain of about 15–20 g/kg/day after the initial loss.

5. Prevention of infection

  • Strict hand hygiene before and after handling; minimal handling; aseptic technique for procedures and IV lines; separate equipment; clean cord care; breast milk; limit visitors with infections; prompt recognition of signs of sepsis.

6. Monitoring and prevention of complications

  • Vital signs, colour, activity, feeding, urine and stools; blood glucose as per protocol; jaundice (serum bilirubin and phototherapy as needed).
  • Developmentally supportive care – reduce light and noise, cluster care, nesting and flexed positioning, minimal painful procedures (sucrose, skin-to-skin).
  • Careful oxygen therapy and ROP screening (babies below 34 weeks or below 2,000 g); hearing screening.

7. Kangaroo mother care and family involvement

  • Continuous skin-to-skin contact with the mother (or father) for as many hours as possible; it maintains temperature, promotes breastfeeding and weight gain, reduces infections and supports bonding.
  • Teach the mother to recognise danger signs and care for the baby.

8. Discharge and follow-up

  • Discharge criteria – stable temperature in room air or KMC, feeding well by breast or cup, gaining weight, no illness, mother confident.
  • Teaching – warmth, exclusive breastfeeding, hygiene, KMC at home, immunisation (on schedule by chronological age), danger signs (poor feeding, cold, fast breathing, lethargy, convulsions, jaundice).
  • Follow-up – weight, growth and development, eye and hearing checks, through high-risk follow-up clinics and home visits by ASHAs.

9. Causes of preterm birth and low birth weight (for prevention)

  • Maternal – young (teenage) or older mothers, short stature, undernutrition and anaemia, low pregnancy weight gain, short birth interval, heavy physical work, tobacco use (smoking or chewing), alcohol, hypertension and pre-eclampsia, diabetes, infections (urinary tract infection, malaria, syphilis), previous preterm birth, poor antenatal care, poverty.
  • Fetal – multiple pregnancy, congenital anomalies and chromosomal disorders, intrauterine infections.
  • Placental and uterine – placental insufficiency, placenta praevia, abruption, uterine anomalies, cervical incompetence, premature rupture of membranes, polyhydramnios.

10. Prevention of LBW and preterm birth

  • Adequate maternal nutrition, IFA and calcium, treatment of anaemia, spacing of births, avoidance of teenage pregnancy.
  • Regular antenatal care (PMSMA), early detection and treatment of hypertension, diabetes and infections.
  • Avoidance of tobacco and alcohol; rest and reduced heavy work in late pregnancy.
  • Antenatal corticosteroids for women at risk of preterm birth (to mature the baby's lungs) and referral to a facility with newborn care.

11. Nursing diagnoses (examples)

  • Ineffective thermoregulation related to large surface area and little subcutaneous fat.
  • Ineffective breathing pattern related to surfactant deficiency and immature respiratory centre.
  • Imbalanced nutrition, less than body requirements, related to weak suck and small stomach capacity.
  • Risk for infection related to immature immunity and invasive procedures.
  • Risk for impaired parent–infant attachment related to separation in the SNCU.
  • Anxiety of parents related to the critical condition and long hospital stay.

12. Community follow-up

  • LBW babies receive extra home visits by ASHAs under home-based newborn care; the ASHA checks weight, temperature, feeding and KMC practice, counsels the family, and refers the baby at once if any danger sign appears. Families are advised to keep the baby away from smoke and sick contacts and to use mosquito nets.

Nursing importance

  • Simple measures – warmth, breast milk, hand hygiene and kangaroo mother care – delivered by nurses prevent most deaths in LBW babies.

Conclusion A low birth weight baby weighs less than 2,500 g; preterm babies have thin skin, little fat, poor tone and immature organs, and suffer from hypothermia, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, feeding problems, infection, jaundice, ROP and neurological complications. Nursing care focuses on warmth, respiratory support, breast-milk feeding by the right method, infection prevention, monitoring, developmentally supportive care, kangaroo mother care, parent education and follow-up.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) List the preparations needed for neonatal resuscitation. (3 marks) (b) Explain the steps of neonatal resuscitation according to current guidelines. (9 marks) (c) Describe the post-resuscitation care of the newborn. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Neonatal resuscitation algorithm
labels: birth – term? breathing or crying? good tone? – if yes
routine care with mother; if no
gasping or HR < 100: positive pressure ventilation
SpO2 monitor – HR < 100 despite PPV: ventilation corrective steps (MR SOPA) – HR < 60: intubate or laryngeal mask
chest compressions 3:1 with 100% oxygen – HR < 60: IV epinephrine

answer_html:
Introduction About one in ten newborns needs some help to begin breathing, and about 1% need extensive resuscitation. Birth asphyxia is a major cause of neonatal death and disability. Neonatal resuscitation follows the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) of the American Academy of Pediatrics and American Heart Association (updated in 2025), and in India is taught through Navjaat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK). The first 60 seconds after birth are the "Golden Minute".

(a) Preparation (3 marks)

  1. Anticipation – identify risk factors (prematurity, meconium-stained liquor, fetal distress, maternal diabetes or hypertension, multiple pregnancy, breech, prolonged labour, general anaesthesia).
  2. Trained team – at least one person skilled in resuscitation at every birth; a full team for high-risk births; a pre-birth briefing with roles.
  3. Warm environment – delivery room at about 25–28 °C; radiant warmer switched on; warm towels; plastic wrap or bag for babies below 32 weeks.
  4. Equipment checked – self-inflating bag (about 240 mL) with masks of sizes 0 and 1, oxygen source and blender, suction (bulb and machine), mucus extractor, laryngoscope with straight blades (00, 0, 1), endotracheal tubes (2.5–4 mm), laryngeal mask, umbilical catheter, pulse oximeter, ECG monitor, stethoscope, clock or timer.
  5. Drugs – epinephrine (1:10,000 – 0.1 mg/mL), normal saline, 10% dextrose, syringes and needles.

(b) Steps of resuscitation (9 marks) Step 1 – Rapid assessment at birth

  • Ask: Is the baby term? Is the baby breathing or crying? Is the tone good?
  • If yes – routine care: delayed cord clamping for at least 60 seconds, dry, skin-to-skin contact with the mother, continued observation.
  • If no – bring the baby to the radiant warmer for initial steps.

Step 2 – Initial steps (within about 30 seconds)

  • Warm (radiant warmer; plastic wrap for very preterm), dry thoroughly and remove wet linen, position the head in a slightly extended "sniffing" position, clear secretions only if the airway is obstructed (mouth first, then nose; routine suction, including for meconium, is not recommended), and stimulate by rubbing the back or flicking the soles.
  • Assess breathing and heart rate (stethoscope or ECG); attach a pulse oximeter on the right hand (pre-ductal).

Step 3 – Positive pressure ventilation (PPV)

  • Start PPV within 60 seconds if the baby is apnoeic or gasping, or the heart rate is below 100/min.
  • Bag-and-mask ventilation at 40–60 breaths per minute, with a well-fitting mask covering the nose and mouth.
  • Oxygen – start with room air (21%) for babies of 35 weeks or more and 21–30% for those below 35 weeks; adjust to reach the target pre-ductal SpO2 – about 60–65% at 1 minute, 70–75% at 3 minutes, 80–85% at 5 minutes and 85–95% by 10 minutes.
  • If the chest does not rise, use the corrective steps MR SOPA – Mask adjustment, Reposition the airway, Suction mouth and nose, Open the mouth, Pressure increase, Alternative airway (endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask).
  • Check the heart rate after 15 seconds and after 30 seconds of effective ventilation (chest moving).
  • Heart rate rising above 100/min – continue PPV until spontaneous breathing, then stop gradually; consider CPAP for laboured breathing.

Step 4 – Chest compressions

  • If the heart rate remains below 60/min after at least 30 seconds of effective PPV (preferably through an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask), start chest compressions and increase oxygen to 100%.
  • Two-thumb technique on the lower third of the sternum, depth about one-third of the chest diameter.
  • Ratio 3:1 – 3 compressions to 1 breath, giving 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute (one cycle every 2 seconds).
  • Check the heart rate after 60 seconds; stop compressions when the heart rate is 60/min or more.

Step 5 – Medication

  • If the heart rate remains below 60/min despite 60 seconds of compressions with effective ventilation:
    • Epinephrine (adrenaline) 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) – intravenous (umbilical venous catheter) or intraosseous 0.02 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg), repeated every 3–5 minutes; while IV access is obtained, an endotracheal dose of 0.1 mg/kg (1 mL/kg) may be given.
    • Volume expander – normal saline 10 mL/kg over 5–10 minutes if there is blood loss or shock.
  • Consider other causes – pneumothorax, congenital anomalies (diaphragmatic hernia), airway obstruction.

Step 6 – When to stop

  • If there is no heart rate after about 20 minutes of full resuscitation, the team discusses stopping with the family, according to policy.

(c) Post-resuscitation care (3 marks)

  • Shift to the SNCU/NICU with continuous monitoring of heart rate, breathing, SpO2, BP and temperature.
  • Maintain normal temperature and avoid hyperthermia; therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) within 6 hours of birth for babies of 36 weeks or more with moderate to severe hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, in units able to provide it.
  • Check and maintain blood glucose, fluids (often restricted initially) and electrolytes; watch for seizures, poor urine output, feeding intolerance and infection.
  • Start feeds cautiously when stable; continue breastfeeding support.
  • Document the resuscitation (times, interventions, APGAR scores, drugs); counsel and support the parents; plan follow-up for neurodevelopment.

Special situations

  • Meconium-stained liquor – if the baby is vigorous, routine care; if not vigorous, initial steps and PPV within the first minute; tracheal suction is done only if the airway is obstructed.
  • Very preterm babies (below 32 weeks) – place in a polythene bag or wrap without drying the body, cap on the head, use lower oxygen concentrations, gentle ventilation, early CPAP for breathing difficulty.
  • Suspected diaphragmatic hernia – avoid prolonged bag-and-mask ventilation; intubate early and insert an orogastric tube.

Role of the nurse in the resuscitation team

  • Anticipating high-risk births and informing the team; daily checking of the warmer, bag and masks, suction and oxygen; drying and warming; ventilating or giving chest compressions; preparing and giving drugs; keeping time and recording events; communicating with the family; restocking after use; taking part in regular NSSK skill drills.

Signs of effective ventilation and recovery

  • Visible, gentle chest rise with each breath; rising heart rate (the most important sign); improving SpO2 and colour; return of tone and spontaneous breathing.
  • Most babies recover with effective ventilation alone; only a few need chest compressions or drugs, which is why the quality of bag-and-mask ventilation matters most.

Conclusion Successful neonatal resuscitation depends on anticipation, a trained team and checked equipment. The steps are rapid assessment, initial steps of warming, drying, positioning and stimulation, positive pressure ventilation within the Golden Minute with corrective steps, chest compressions at 3:1 when the heart rate stays below 60/min, and epinephrine and volume when needed, followed by careful post-resuscitation care including temperature control, glucose, seizure monitoring and family support.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Differentiate between physiological and pathological jaundice in the newborn. (4 marks) (b) Explain the causes and assessment of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a newborn under phototherapy and exchange transfusion. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Kramer's dermal zones of neonatal jaundice
labels: zone 4 arms and legs below knees
zone 5 palms and soles – increasing serum bilirubin from zone 1 to zone 5

answer_html:
Introduction Neonatal jaundice is yellow colouring of the skin and sclera due to raised serum bilirubin; it becomes visible when bilirubin exceeds about 5–7 mg/dL. About 60% of term and 80% of preterm babies develop jaundice in the first week. Most cases are physiological, but very high unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood–brain barrier and cause kernicterus, a permanent brain injury.

(a) Physiological versus pathological jaundice (4 marks) | Feature | Physiological jaundice | Pathological jaundice | |---|---|---| | Onset | After 24 hours (day 2–3) | Within the first 24 hours, or at any time with high levels | | Peak | Day 3–5 in term babies (later in preterm) | Variable | | Level | Below phototherapy thresholds for age (usually below 12–15 mg/dL in term babies) | Above phototherapy thresholds; rises rapidly (more than 5 mg/dL per day) | | Duration | Disappears by 10–14 days (up to 3 weeks in preterm) | Persists beyond 2 weeks in term (3 weeks in preterm) | | Type | Unconjugated | Unconjugated or conjugated (direct bilirubin above about 1 mg/dL) | | Other signs | Baby well, feeding normally | Pale stools, dark urine, poor feeding, lethargy, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly | - Physiological jaundice is due to high red cell mass, shorter red cell life, immature liver enzymes (glucuronyl transferase) and increased enterohepatic circulation.

(b) Causes and assessment (4 marks) Causes of pathological jaundice

  • Haemolytic – Rh incompatibility, ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Increased bilirubin load – cephalhaematoma, bruising, polycythaemia (IDM, SGA), swallowed blood.
  • Infection – sepsis, urinary infection, intrauterine infections (TORCH).
  • Decreased conjugation – prematurity, congenital hypothyroidism, Crigler–Najjar syndrome.
  • Breastfeeding-related – breastfeeding (suboptimal intake) jaundice in the first week, and breast milk jaundice (prolonged, mild, after the first week in a thriving baby).
  • Conjugated (cholestatic) jaundice – biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis – needs urgent evaluation (pale stools).

Assessment

  • Clinical – examine in daylight by pressing the skin; jaundice spreads from head to toe (Kramer's rule: zone 1 face and neck, zone 2 upper trunk, zone 3 lower trunk and thighs, zone 4 arms and legs, zone 5 palms and soles – the lower the spread, the higher the bilirubin). Clinical estimation is unreliable, so measurement is needed.
  • Transcutaneous bilirubinometer (screening) and total serum bilirubin (TSB) with direct fraction.
  • Bilirubin is interpreted against hour-specific nomograms and phototherapy/exchange charts according to gestational age and risk factors.
  • Other tests – mother's and baby's blood groups, direct Coombs' test, haemoglobin and haematocrit, reticulocyte count, peripheral smear, G6PD, sepsis screen, thyroid function, urine tests.
  • Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy – lethargy, poor sucking, hypotonia, then hypertonia, arching (opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, fever, seizures.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks) A. General management

  • Ensure adequate breastfeeding (8–12 feeds a day); treat the cause (antibiotics for sepsis, thyroxine for hypothyroidism); IV immunoglobulin in severe isoimmune haemolysis as prescribed.

B. Phototherapy

  • Principle – blue–green light (wavelength about 430–490 nm) converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble isomers (photo-isomerisation) that are excreted in bile and urine without conjugation.
  • Types – conventional, LED phototherapy (commonly used), double-surface or intensive phototherapy, fibre-optic blankets.

Nursing care during phototherapy

  1. Place the baby naked except for a nappy, under the light at the distance recommended by the manufacturer (about 30–45 cm for conventional units); expose maximum skin surface; change position if the light is from one side.
  2. Protect the eyes with opaque eye shields (not too tight; check for discharge and remove during feeds); cover the gonads lightly if advised.
  3. Monitor temperature every 2–4 hours – risk of hyperthermia or hypothermia; keep the unit in a thermoneutral environment.
  4. Hydration – continue breastfeeding (short breaks from the light for feeds are allowed in moderate jaundice); watch for dehydration (weight, urine output); extra fluids only as ordered.
  5. Skin care – no oils or lotions (they may burn); watch for rashes; loose green stools are common – keep the perineum clean.
  6. Monitor bilirubin (every 12–24 hours or as ordered); skin colour is not a reliable guide under phototherapy.
  7. Watch for complications – dehydration, hyperthermia, skin rash, eye injury, and bronze baby syndrome (grey-brown skin in babies with conjugated jaundice).
  8. Check the irradiance and bulbs; keep the baby within the light; minimise interruption in severe jaundice.
  9. Support the mother – explain, allow her to touch and feed the baby; reduce anxiety.

C. Exchange transfusion

  • Indications – bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold for age and risk, bilirubin rising despite intensive phototherapy, signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, and severe haemolytic disease (low cord haemoglobin, high cord bilirubin).
  • Procedure – double-volume exchange (about 160–170 mL/kg) through the umbilical vein in small aliquots (withdraw then infuse), using fresh, cross-matched blood (for Rh disease, O-negative blood compatible with the mother's serum); it removes about 85% of the baby's red cells and about half of the bilirubin and antibodies.
  • Nursing care
    • Before – consent; stop feeds for 3–4 hours or empty the stomach; radiant warmer, monitor, resuscitation equipment; warm the blood (blood warmer); baseline vitals, glucose, calcium.
    • During – strict asepsis; maintain temperature; continuous monitoring of heart rate, breathing, SpO2 and colour; record each aliquot withdrawn and infused; give calcium gluconate as ordered; watch for arrhythmias, apnoea, air embolism.
    • After – monitor vital signs, blood glucose, calcium, potassium, platelets and bilirubin; observe the umbilical site for bleeding; watch for complications – hypocalcaemia, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia, thrombocytopenia, infection, necrotising enterocolitis, volume overload; restart feeds as ordered; continue phototherapy.

D. Prevention and follow-up

  • Anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh-negative mothers; early and frequent breastfeeding; risk assessment and bilirubin check before discharge; teach parents to watch for yellow palms and soles, pale stools, poor feeding or lethargy; hearing (BERA) and developmental follow-up after severe jaundice.

E. Kernicterus (bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction)

  • Unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei; risk is higher in preterm, sick, acidotic or hypoalbuminaemic babies.
  • Phases – early (lethargy, hypotonia, poor suck), intermediate (irritability, high-pitched cry, hypertonia, arching, fever) and advanced (opisthotonus, apnoea, seizures, coma).
  • Long-term sequelae – athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward gaze palsy, dental enamel defects and intellectual disability – hence the importance of early detection and treatment.

F. Prolonged jaundice (beyond 2–3 weeks)

  • Needs evaluation for direct (conjugated) bilirubin, stool colour, thyroid function, urine infection and G6PD; pale stools or dark urine suggest biliary atresia, which must be operated on early (ideally before about 60 days) for a good result.

Conclusion Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours and settles within two weeks, while pathological jaundice appears early, rises fast, reaches high levels or persists. Causes include haemolysis (Rh, ABO, G6PD), infection, hypothyroidism, breastfeeding problems and cholestasis. Bilirubin is measured and plotted on age-specific charts; phototherapy with careful eye protection, temperature, hydration and bilirubin monitoring treats most babies, and exchange transfusion is used for very high levels or encephalopathy, to prevent kernicterus.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define neonatal sepsis and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the risk factors, clinical features and investigations. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management, nursing care and prevention of neonatal sepsis. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Sepsis screen in the newborn
labels: 000/mm³; absolute neutrophil count low; immature-to-total neutrophil ratio > 0.2; micro-ESR > 15 mm in first hour; CRP > 1 mg/dL – two or more positive = positive screen; blood culture is the gold standard

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Neonatal sepsis is a clinical syndrome of systemic illness caused by bacterial (or fungal) infection in the first 28 days of life, with or without a positive blood culture. It includes septicaemia, pneumonia, meningitis, osteomyelitis and urinary tract infection of the newborn and is one of the leading causes of neonatal death in India.

  • Early-onset sepsis (EOS) – within the first 72 hours; acquired from the mother's genital tract before or during delivery; organisms – E. coli, Klebsiella, Group B Streptococcus; presents often with respiratory distress and pneumonia.
  • Late-onset sepsis (LOS) – after 72 hours; acquired from the hospital environment (nosocomial) or the community; organisms – Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Candida; meningitis is more common.

(b) Risk factors, clinical features and investigations (5 marks) Risk factors

  • Maternal / EOS – prolonged rupture of membranes (more than 18 hours), maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, foul-smelling liquor, frequent vaginal examinations (more than 3), prolonged or difficult labour, maternal urinary infection.
  • Neonatal / LOS – prematurity and LBW, birth asphyxia, invasive procedures (IV lines, ventilation), prolonged hospital stay, lack of breastfeeding, bottle feeding, poor hand hygiene, overcrowded nurseries, unhygienic cord care.

Clinical features (often non-specific)

  • Lethargy, refusal to feed or poor suck, "not doing well".
  • Temperature instability – hypothermia (common, especially in preterm) or fever.
  • Respiratory – fast breathing, grunting, chest retractions, apnoea, cyanosis.
  • Gastrointestinal – vomiting, abdominal distension, diarrhoea, feed intolerance.
  • Circulatory – poor perfusion, capillary refill above 3 seconds, mottling, shock.
  • Neurological – irritability, high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, convulsions (suggest meningitis).
  • Others – jaundice, sclerema, bleeding, umbilical redness, skin pustules, hypoglycaemia.

Investigations

  • Blood culture (before antibiotics) – the gold standard.
  • Sepsis screen – total leucocyte count below 5,000/mm³, low absolute neutrophil count, immature-to-total neutrophil ratio above 0.2, micro-ESR above 15 mm in the first hour, CRP above 1 mg/dL; two or more positive parameters suggest sepsis.
  • Lumbar puncture (CSF) – in suspected or culture-positive sepsis to rule out meningitis.
  • Urine culture (LOS), chest X-ray, blood glucose, electrolytes, blood gas.

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (7 marks) A. Medical management (as prescribed)

  • Antibiotics started promptly after cultures – commonly ampicillin (or cloxacillin) plus gentamicin as first line; cefotaxime, amikacin, piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem for hospital-acquired or resistant infections, according to the unit's antibiogram; duration about 7–10 days for sepsis (stopped at 36–48 hours if cultures are negative and the baby is well) and 14–21 days for meningitis.
  • Supportive care – warmth, oxygen and ventilation as needed, IV fluids and glucose, correction of shock (fluid boluses, inotropes), treatment of hypoglycaemia, jaundice and bleeding.
  • In the community, when referral is not possible, simplified antibiotic regimens for possible serious bacterial infection are used as per national guidelines.

B. Nursing care

  1. Monitoring – temperature, heart rate, respiration, SpO2, colour, capillary refill, BP, activity, feeding tolerance, urine output, blood glucose; signs of shock or meningitis.
  2. Thermoregulation – radiant warmer or incubator; avoid hypothermia and hyperthermia.
  3. Respiratory support – positioning, gentle suction, oxygen or CPAP as ordered.
  4. Nutrition – expressed breast milk by tube or cup when stable; IV fluids when the baby is very sick; gradual return to breastfeeding.
  5. Antibiotic administration – correct dose by weight, timing, dilution and route; maintain IV access aseptically; watch for side effects (gentamicin – kidney and hearing); record.
  6. Infection control – hand hygiene, isolation of babies with resistant organisms, aseptic care of lines and catheters, care of the cord and skin.
  7. Collection of specimens – correct technique for blood culture (adequate volume, aseptic) and CSF.
  8. Support of parents – explain the condition; involve the mother in care and breastfeeding; reduce anxiety.

C. Prevention

  • Antenatal and intrapartum – treat maternal infections, clean and safe delivery, limit vaginal examinations, antibiotics for prolonged rupture of membranes, the "six cleans" of delivery.
  • Postnatal – hand hygiene (the most important), exclusive breastfeeding and colostrum, kangaroo mother care, clean cord care (keep dry), rooming-in, minimal handling, avoidance of unnecessary procedures, strict asepsis for lines, regular cleaning of equipment, rational use of antibiotics, adequate staffing and space in nurseries.
  • Educate mothers on hygiene and danger signs, and early care-seeking.

D. Routes of infection and pathophysiology

  • Ascending infection from the vagina after rupture of membranes; transplacental (syphilis, Listeria, viruses); during passage through the birth canal; and after birth through hands of caregivers, contaminated equipment, IV lines, the umbilical stump and skin.
  • The newborn's immature immunity (low IgM and IgA, weak neutrophil and complement function, thin skin) allows organisms to spread rapidly into the blood and meninges, causing inflammation, poor perfusion and organ dysfunction.

E. Complications

  • Meningitis, septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrotising enterocolitis, hypoglycaemia, jaundice, multi-organ failure and death.
  • Long-term – hydrocephalus, cerebral palsy, deafness (also from aminoglycosides) and developmental delay after meningitis.

F. Nursing diagnoses (examples)

  • Risk for hypothermia related to illness and immature thermoregulation.
  • Ineffective breathing pattern related to sepsis and apnoea.
  • Imbalanced nutrition related to poor sucking and feed intolerance.
  • Risk for injury (seizures) related to meningitis.
  • Parental anxiety related to the critical illness of the baby.

G. Care of a baby with meningitis

  • Monitor head circumference, fontanelle, level of consciousness and seizures; seizure precautions and anticonvulsants as ordered; fluid balance (avoid overload); longer course of antibiotics; hearing test and developmental follow-up after recovery.

H. Antibiotic stewardship in the newborn unit
