  • Start antibiotics only when infection is likely; take cultures first; choose antibiotics according to the unit's own antibiogram; review at 36–48 hours and stop if cultures are negative and the baby is well; avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics (which select resistant organisms and fungal infections).

I. Signs of improvement

  • Stable temperature, better activity and sucking, normal breathing and perfusion, falling CRP, negative repeat cultures, and weight gain – after which feeds are increased and the baby is moved to the step-down or KMC area.

J. Discharge teaching for the family

  • Continue exclusive breastfeeding; keep the baby warm (KMC); wash hands before handling; keep the cord clean and dry; avoid applying oil, ash or cow dung to the cord; follow the immunisation schedule; return immediately if the baby feeds poorly, becomes cold or hot, breathes fast, has convulsions, becomes yellow or less active; attend follow-up for hearing and development after meningitis.

Conclusion Neonatal sepsis is systemic infection in the first 28 days, classified as early-onset (within 72 hours, maternal origin) or late-onset (after 72 hours, hospital or community origin). It presents with non-specific signs such as lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia, apnoea and poor perfusion, and is confirmed by blood culture and a sepsis screen. Prompt antibiotics, supportive care and meticulous nursing save lives, while hand hygiene, breastfeeding, KMC, clean delivery and cord care, and rational antibiotic use prevent it.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Describe the organisation of a neonatal care unit (SNCU/NICU), including levels of newborn care, physical set-up, equipment, staffing and infection control.

diagram.caption: Layout of a special newborn care unit
labels: entry with hand-washing area and gowning
sick newborn care area with radiant warmers and monitors
nursing station with view of all beds

answer_html:
Introduction Sick and small newborns need special care in well-organised units. Under the Facility-Based Newborn Care (FBNC) programme of the National Health Mission, India has built a network of newborn care facilities linked by referral transport, so that every newborn receives care at the appropriate level.

A. Levels of newborn care

  1. Level I – Newborn Care Corner (NBCC) – in every delivery room and operation theatre; radiant warmer, resuscitation equipment, essential newborn care.
  2. Level II – Newborn Stabilisation Unit (NBSU) – at first referral units and CHCs; about 4 beds; stabilisation, warmth, oxygen, IV fluids, phototherapy and referral.
  3. Level II–III – Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) – at district hospitals; usually 12 or more beds; care of sick and small newborns except those needing ventilation (CPAP, phototherapy, IV antibiotics, KMC).
  4. Level III – Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) – in medical colleges and tertiary hospitals; mechanical ventilation, surfactant, surgery and super-specialty care.

B. Physical set-up

  • Location – close to the labour room and operation theatre, with easy access for referred babies; separate from adult areas; restricted entry.
  • Areas – entry with hand-washing and gowning area, triage/admission, sick newborn care area (warmers and monitors), isolation area for infected babies (and separate area for outborn babies where possible), step-down area, phototherapy area, kangaroo mother care ward, breastfeeding and milk expression room, nursing station with a clear view of all babies, doctors' room, store, clean and dirty utility, and a parents' waiting area.
  • Space – adequate space around each bed (so that equipment and staff can move and infection spread is reduced), with at least 1 metre between warmers.
  • Environment – temperature about 26–28 °C, good ventilation and lighting (dimmable at night), low noise, washable floors and walls; uninterrupted power supply with generator back-up; piped or concentrator oxygen with an air–oxygen blender.
  • Hand-washing stations with elbow-operated taps and alcohol hand-rub at every bed.

C. Equipment

  • Thermal care – radiant warmers with servo control, incubators, room warmers, low-reading thermometers.
  • Respiratory care – oxygen concentrators/cylinders, blenders, nasal prongs and hoods, CPAP machines, ventilators (NICU), bag-and-mask devices with masks of sizes 0 and 1, laryngoscopes with straight blades, suction machines.
  • Monitoring – pulse oximeters, multi-parameter monitors, glucometers, bilirubinometers, weighing scales.
  • Treatment – phototherapy units (LED), syringe and infusion pumps, IV cannulae and fluids, exchange transfusion sets, emergency drug tray.
  • Feeding – breast pumps, feeding cups and paladais, feeding tubes, refrigerator for expressed milk.
  • Others – KMC chairs and binders, autoclave and sterilisation equipment, computer for records, and a mobile phone or telemedicine link for consultation with higher centres.
  • Emergency equipment is kept ready on a resuscitation trolley at every warmer cluster and checked every shift.

D. Staffing

  • Doctors – paediatricians or neonatologists and medical officers trained in FBNC, available round the clock.
  • Nurses – trained in newborn care (FBNC, NSSK and IMNCI); about one nurse for every 3–4 sick babies in an SNCU, and one nurse for one or two babies on ventilators in an NICU; a nurse in charge for each shift.
  • Support staff – housekeeping, attendants, data entry operator, lab technician, biomedical engineer, and counsellors for breastfeeding and family support.
  • Regular training, skill drills and performance review.

E. Policies and protocols

  • Admission and discharge criteria; standard treatment protocols (resuscitation, thermal care, feeding, jaundice, sepsis, hypoglycaemia); referral and transport policy; family participatory care – mothers trained to take part in feeding, KMC and hygiene; open access for parents; consent; death review; records and the online SNCU database.

F. Infection control

  • Hand hygiene before and after touching every baby (the single most important measure); gowns and slippers at entry; limited entry of visitors.
  • Separate area for infected and outborn babies; one baby per warmer or incubator; individual equipment (thermometer, stethoscope) where possible.
  • Daily cleaning and disinfection of warmers, incubators and surfaces; proper sterilisation of equipment; safe handling of linen; biomedical waste segregation.
  • Asepsis for IV lines and procedures; minimal handling; breast milk feeding; rational antibiotic use; surveillance of infection rates and periodic culture surveillance.

G. Follow-up and continuity

  • Step-down and KMC wards before discharge; high-risk follow-up clinics for growth, development, eyes and hearing; home visits by ASHAs under HBNC/HBYC.

Role of the nurse

  • Admission and assessment, thermal and respiratory care, feeding, medication, monitoring, infection control, equipment maintenance, parent education and participation, records, and quality improvement.

H. Admission and discharge

  • Admission criteria (SNCU) – very small babies (birth weight below about 1,800 g or gestation below 34 weeks), respiratory distress, apnoea, central cyanosis, suspected sepsis, perinatal asphyxia, seizures, hypothermia or hyperthermia, refusal to feed, jaundice needing phototherapy or exchange, hypoglycaemia, shock, bleeding, abdominal distension and major malformations needing care.
  • Discharge criteria – stable temperature in room air or KMC, feeding well by breast or cup, gaining weight, off IV fluids and oxygen, mother trained and confident; discharge summary given with follow-up date.

I. Safe transport of sick newborns

  • Stabilise before transfer – temperature, airway and breathing, circulation, blood sugar – and communicate with the receiving unit.
  • Transport in kangaroo position with the mother or in a transport incubator, with oxygen, IV fluids, a trained person, the referral note and the mother's breast milk; use the free referral transport (national ambulance services).

J. Records and quality indicators

  • Admission, treatment and discharge records, the SNCU online database, death reviews.
  • Quality indicators – bed occupancy, case fatality rate, rates of sepsis and hospital-acquired infection, hypothermia at admission, exclusive breast-milk feeding rate, KMC coverage, referrals and follow-up attendance – reviewed regularly to improve care.

K. Developmentally supportive and family participatory care

  • Developmental care – dim lights and low noise, covering incubators, clustering of care to allow sleep, nesting and flexed positioning, gentle handling, sucrose and skin-to-skin contact for painful procedures.
  • Family participatory care – mothers (and fathers) are trained and allowed to stay in the unit to provide hand hygiene, breastfeeding and cup feeding, KMC, nappy and skin care, and to observe danger signs; this improves breastfeeding, weight gain and parental confidence, and reduces infection and readmissions.

L. Care and maintenance of equipment

  • Daily checking of warmers, phototherapy units, CPAP machines, pumps, monitors and resuscitation bags; cleaning and disinfection between babies; calibration of thermometers, weighing scales and bilirubinometers; preventive maintenance by biomedical engineers (with an annual maintenance contract); an equipment logbook; and immediate tagging and repair of faulty equipment.

Conclusion Newborn care in India is organised at four levels – NBCC, NBSU, SNCU and NICU. A good neonatal unit is located near the labour room, has separate areas for sick, infected and step-down babies, a KMC ward and milk-expression room, adequate warmers, CPAP, phototherapy, monitors and pumps, trained doctors and nurses in adequate numbers, clear protocols, strict infection control, family participation and follow-up services.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the immediate care of the newborn at birth.
tags: initiation of breastfeeding within one hour
answer_html:
Introduction The first hour after birth – the "Golden Hour" – is critical for the newborn's transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life. Simple, evidence-based essential newborn care at this time prevents hypothermia, infection and asphyxia and promotes breastfeeding.

1. Preparation

  • A warm, draught-free delivery room (about 25–28 °C); radiant warmer switched on; two pre-warmed towels, cap and socks; resuscitation equipment checked; clean hands and sterile delivery kit.

2. At birth

  1. Note the time of birth and the sex of the baby.
  2. Dry the baby immediately and thoroughly with a warm towel (head, body, limbs) and remove the wet towel; drying also stimulates breathing.
  3. Assess breathing and crying – a baby who is crying or breathing well and has good tone needs only routine care; a baby who is not breathing needs resuscitation at once (within the Golden Minute).
  4. Routine suctioning is not done; secretions are wiped from the mouth and nose only if they obstruct breathing.

3. Warmth – skin-to-skin contact

  • Place the baby naked on the mother's abdomen or chest, cover both with a dry cloth, put a cap on the baby's head; this maintains temperature and promotes bonding and breastfeeding.

4. Cord clamping and cutting

  • Delay clamping for at least 1 minute (until pulsations reduce) unless resuscitation is needed – this increases the baby's iron stores.
  • Clamp or tie at about 2–3 cm from the abdomen with a sterile clamp or thread, and cut with a sterile blade; apply nothing on the cord (keep it clean and dry); check for bleeding.

5. Early initiation of breastfeeding

  • Within the first hour, while the baby is in skin-to-skin contact; help the mother with position and attachment; give colostrum – no prelacteal feeds (honey, water, ghutti).

6. APGAR scoring at 1 and 5 minutes, while the baby is with the mother.

7. Identification

  • Identification band on the baby (and mother) with the mother's name, date and time of birth and sex, before leaving the delivery room.

8. Other care (after the first breastfeed, within the first hours)

  • Vitamin K 1 mg IM (0.5 mg for babies below 1,000 g) into the anterolateral thigh to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
  • Eye care – wipe each eye from the inner to the outer canthus with a separate sterile swab.
  • Weight, length and head circumference; quick head-to-toe examination for malformations (cleft lip/palate, spina bifida, imperforate anus, club foot).
  • Birth-dose vaccines – BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B (within 24 hours).
  • Delay the first bath for at least 24 hours (sponge if needed); keep the baby with the mother (rooming-in).

9. Records and observation

  • Record the time of birth, APGAR, weight, interventions and the first breastfeed; observe temperature, breathing, colour, cord and passage of urine and meconium; teach the mother about warmth, breastfeeding and danger signs.

Conclusion Immediate newborn care consists of drying, assessing breathing, skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping with clean cord care, breastfeeding within the first hour, APGAR scoring, identification, Vitamin K, eye care, measurements, birth-dose vaccines, delayed bathing and rooming-in – simple steps that save many newborn lives.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the routine care of a normal newborn and the teaching given to the mother before discharge.
answer_html:
Introduction After the immediate care at birth, a normal newborn needs routine daily care that keeps the baby warm, well fed, clean and safe, and the mother needs to be prepared to care for the baby at home.

1. Rooming-in and warmth

  • Keep the baby with the mother day and night; dress in layers, with cap and socks; cover with a blanket; avoid exposure to cold and draughts; check the baby's warmth by touching the feet and abdomen.

2. Feeding

  • Exclusive breastfeeding on demand (8–12 times in 24 hours), day and night; no water, honey or other feeds; check attachment; burp after feeds.
  • Signs of adequate feeding – the baby passes urine 6 or more times a day, sleeps 2–3 hours between feeds and regains birth weight by 10–14 days.

3. Cord care

  • Keep the cord stump clean and dry; fold the nappy below the stump; apply nothing (oil, ash, turmeric, cow dung); it falls off in 5–10 days; watch for redness, swelling, pus or bleeding.

4. Skin care and bathing

  • First bath after at least 24 hours; then a quick sponge or tub bath in a warm room with warm water, mild soap; dry quickly and dress; do not remove vernix forcibly; avoid applying kajal (surma) to the eyes, and oil in the ears and nose.

5. Nappy (diaper) care

  • Change wet nappies promptly; clean the perineum from front to back; keep the area dry; use soft cotton nappies; watch for nappy rash.

6. Sleep and safety

  • Place the baby on the back to sleep, on a firm surface, without pillows; mother and baby can sleep close together under a mosquito net; never leave the baby alone on a high bed; handle the head carefully.

7. Observation

  • Temperature, breathing, colour (jaundice), feeding, urine and stools, cord, eyes and skin, weight.

8. Screening and preventive care

  • Birth-dose vaccines (BCG, OPV-0, hepatitis B); newborn screening (hypothyroidism and other conditions where available), hearing screening, pulse oximetry screening, eye check; registration of birth.

9. Teaching the mother before discharge

  1. Breastfeeding and expressing milk; maternal nutrition and rest.
  2. Keeping the baby warm; KMC for small babies.
  3. Cord, skin, eye and nappy care; hand washing.
  4. Immunisation schedule and the MCP card; next due date (6 weeks).
  5. Danger signs – seek care immediately if the baby:
    • feeds poorly or cannot suck,
    • breathes fast (60 or more per minute) or has chest indrawing,
    • is cold to touch or has fever,
    • has convulsions or is lethargic,
    • has yellow palms and soles or jaundice in the first day,
    • has umbilical redness spreading to the skin, many skin pustules, or bleeding.
  6. Home visits by the ASHA (home-based newborn care) and follow-up at the health centre.
  7. Avoid harmful customs (prelacteal feeds, applying substances on the cord, early bathing, keeping the baby away from the mother).

Conclusion Routine care of the normal newborn includes rooming-in, warmth, exclusive breastfeeding, clean and dry cord care, delayed and careful bathing, nappy care, safe sleep, observation, immunisation and screening. Before discharge, the mother is taught these practices and the danger signs that need immediate care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)? Explain its types, causes, problems and nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is the failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential in the uterus. At birth such babies are usually small for gestational age (SGA) – birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age. IUGR babies may be term or preterm.

1. Types

  • Symmetrical (proportionate) IUGR (about 20–30%) – growth restriction begins early in pregnancy; weight, length and head circumference are all reduced proportionately; caused by intrinsic factors (chromosomal disorders, congenital infections); poorer prognosis for growth and development.
  • Asymmetrical (disproportionate) IUGR (about 70–80%) – begins late in pregnancy, usually due to placental insufficiency; the head (brain) is relatively spared, but weight is low; the baby looks long and thin with loose, dry skin, reduced subcutaneous fat and a low ponderal index; better catch-up growth.

2. Causes

  • Maternal – undernutrition, anaemia, hypertension and pre-eclampsia, chronic kidney or heart disease, diabetes with vascular disease, tobacco (smoking or chewing), alcohol, drugs, short stature, teenage pregnancy, heavy work, high altitude.
  • Placental – placental insufficiency, infarcts, abnormal implantation, single umbilical artery.
  • Fetal – chromosomal anomalies (trisomies), congenital malformations, intrauterine infections (TORCH), multiple pregnancy.

3. Problems of the IUGR baby

  • Perinatal asphyxia and meconium aspiration.
  • Hypoglycaemia (low glycogen stores) and hypothermia (little fat).
  • Polycythaemia (high haematocrit) leading to jaundice and sluggish circulation.
  • Hypocalcaemia, infections, necrotising enterocolitis.
  • Long-term – poor growth (stunting), developmental problems, and greater risk of diabetes, hypertension and heart disease in adult life.

4. Nursing management

  1. Anticipate – be ready for resuscitation at birth.
  2. Warmth – skin-to-skin contact or KMC, radiant warmer if needed; monitor temperature.
  3. Early and frequent feeding – breastfeeding within one hour and every 2–3 hours; cup or tube feeding with expressed milk if the baby sucks poorly.
  4. Monitor blood glucose at regular intervals in the first 48 hours; treat hypoglycaemia promptly.
  5. Watch for complications – respiratory distress, jaundice, polycythaemia (plethora), feed intolerance, infection.
  6. Infection prevention – hand hygiene, clean cord and skin care.
  7. Daily weight and growth monitoring; record intake and output.
  8. Parent education – feeding, warmth, danger signs, immunisation; follow-up of growth and development.

5. Prevention

  • Good maternal nutrition, treatment of anaemia, avoidance of tobacco and alcohol, regular antenatal care with monitoring of fundal height and ultrasound, management of hypertension, rest, and timely delivery.

Conclusion IUGR is failure of the fetus to reach its growth potential, seen at birth as a small-for-gestational-age baby. It may be symmetrical (early, intrinsic causes) or asymmetrical (late, placental insufficiency). IUGR babies are prone to asphyxia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and polycythaemia, and need warmth, early feeding, glucose monitoring, infection prevention and follow-up.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain kangaroo mother care (KMC).
answer_html:
Definition Kangaroo mother care (KMC) is the care of preterm and low birth weight babies by placing them in continuous, prolonged skin-to-skin contact with the mother (or another family member), along with exclusive breastfeeding, early discharge and close follow-up. It was developed in Bogotá, Colombia (1978) as an alternative to incubator care. WHO now recommends that KMC should begin as soon as possible after birth (immediate KMC) for babies below 2,000 g, even before they are fully stable, in units able to monitor them.

1. Components

  1. Skin-to-skin contact – the baby is placed upright between the mother's breasts.
  2. Exclusive breastfeeding (or expressed breast milk by cup or tube).
  3. Support to the mother–baby pair in the facility and at home.
  4. Early discharge and close follow-up.

2. Benefits

  • Maintains normal temperature (prevents hypothermia) as well as or better than incubators.
  • Reduces mortality and serious infections, and reduces hospital stay.
  • Promotes breastfeeding, better weight gain and more regular breathing (fewer apnoea episodes).
  • Enhances bonding, reduces maternal anxiety and increases her confidence; reduces pain and stress in the baby.
  • Low-cost and possible in any setting.

3. Eligibility

  • All LBW and preterm babies; once a sick baby is stable, KMC is started and continued; intermittent KMC for babies still receiving treatment (IV fluids, oxygen) under supervision.

4. Method (positioning)

  • The mother sits or reclines comfortably in a KMC chair or bed, wearing a front-opening gown.
  • The baby, naked except for a cap, nappy and socks, is placed upright between the breasts in a frog-like position, the chest against the mother's chest, the head turned to one side and slightly extended to keep the airway open.
  • The baby is secured with a binder, wrap or KMC bag; the mother's gown and a blanket cover both.
  • For sleeping, the mother reclines at about 15–30 degrees.

5. Duration

  • As long as possible – ideally 8 to 24 hours a day; sessions shorter than about 1 hour are not advised, as frequent handling disturbs the baby. Fathers and other family members can take turns.
  • Continue until the baby reaches about 2,500 g or 40 weeks, or begins to wriggle out and show discomfort.

6. Feeding – breastfeeding in the KMC position; cup or paladai feeding of expressed milk for babies who cannot suck well.

7. Monitoring

  • Temperature, breathing, colour, feeding and weight; the mother is taught to recognise danger signs (cold, breathing pauses, blue colour, poor feeding).

8. Discharge and follow-up

  • Discharge when the baby is feeding well, gaining weight and the mother is confident in KMC; continue KMC at home; follow-up visits (weekly initially) and home visits by ASHAs.

Conclusion KMC – continuous skin-to-skin contact with exclusive breastfeeding, support and follow-up – keeps preterm and LBW babies warm, reduces deaths and infections, improves breastfeeding and growth, and strengthens bonding. Nurses start it early, teach correct positioning and support mothers and families to continue it at home.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain thermoregulation in the newborn, the prevention of hypothermia (warm chain) and its management.
answer_html:
Introduction Newborns, especially preterm and LBW babies, lose heat rapidly because of a large surface area, thin skin, little subcutaneous fat, wet skin at birth and limited ability to produce heat. Hypothermia increases oxygen consumption and causes hypoglycaemia, acidosis, respiratory distress, infection, sclerema and death.

1. Mechanisms of heat loss

  • Evaporation – from wet skin at birth and during bathing.
  • Conduction – contact with cold surfaces (weighing scale, cold linen).
  • Convection – cool air currents (fans, open windows, draughts).
  • Radiation – to cold walls and windows nearby.

2. Heat production

  • Newborns cannot shiver effectively; they produce heat mainly by non-shivering thermogenesis – breakdown of brown fat (around the neck, shoulders, kidneys), which is scanty in preterm babies.

3. Classification of hypothermia (WHO)

  • Normal axillary temperature – 36.5–37.5 °C.
  • Cold stress (mild hypothermia) – 36.0–36.4 °C.
  • Moderate hypothermia – 32.0–35.9 °C.
  • Severe hypothermia – below 32 °C.
  • Signs – cold feet then cold abdomen, poor feeding, lethargy, weak cry, peripheral cyanosis, slow breathing, hypoglycaemia; red face (cold injury) and hard skin (sclerema) in severe cases.

4. Prevention – the warm chain (ten steps)

  1. Warm delivery room (25–28 °C), free from draughts.
  2. Immediate drying and removal of wet towels.
  3. Skin-to-skin contact with the mother.
  4. Early breastfeeding.
  5. Postponing bathing and weighing (bath after at least 24 hours).
  6. Appropriate clothing and bedding – cap, socks, layers.
  7. Mother and baby together (rooming-in).
  8. Warm transportation (KMC position or transport incubator).
  9. Warm resuscitation (under a radiant warmer).
  10. Training and awareness of health workers and families. A break in any link of the chain puts the baby at risk.

5. Management

  • Cold stress – skin-to-skin contact (KMC), cover with warm clothes and blanket, warm room, breastfeed; recheck temperature after 30 minutes to 1 hour.
  • Moderate hypothermia – KMC or radiant warmer/incubator; remove wet clothes; check every 15–30 minutes until normal.
  • Severe hypothermia – rapid rewarming under a radiant warmer or incubator at a higher setting, IV fluids with glucose, oxygen, check blood glucose, treat suspected sepsis, refer to an SNCU.
  • Avoid hot-water bottles and heaters directly near the baby (burns); avoid hyperthermia during rewarming.

6. Nursing responsibilities

  • Monitor temperature regularly (every 4–6 hours in well babies; more often in sick babies); use servo-controlled warmers correctly; educate mothers on keeping babies warm, KMC and recognising coldness by touching the feet and abdomen.

Conclusion Newborns lose heat by evaporation, conduction, convection and radiation and produce heat mainly from brown fat. Hypothermia (below 36.5 °C) ranges from cold stress to severe hypothermia and is dangerous. It is prevented by the ten steps of the warm chain and managed by skin-to-skin contact, warmers or incubators, glucose and treatment of the cause.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) in the newborn and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also called hyaline membrane disease, is respiratory distress in preterm babies caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, leading to collapse of alveoli (atelectasis), poor gas exchange and formation of hyaline membranes in the airways.

1. Causes and risk factors

  • Prematurity (the main cause – surfactant production matures by about 34–35 weeks); risk increases as gestation decreases.
  • Infants of diabetic mothers, male sex, caesarean section without labour, perinatal asphyxia, second twin, hypothermia.

2. Pathophysiology

  • Lack of surfactant → high surface tension → alveoli collapse at the end of each expiration → reduced lung compliance and increased work of breathing → hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis → damage to the alveolar lining and leakage of protein, forming hyaline membranes.

3. Clinical features

  • Onset within the first few hours (usually within 6 hours) of birth.
  • Tachypnoea (more than 60/min), expiratory grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions (subcostal, intercostal, xiphoid), cyanosis, decreased air entry; apnoea in severe cases.
  • Severity is scored by the Silverman–Anderson score or Downes score.
  • Worsens over 48–72 hours, then improves as the baby makes its own surfactant.

4. Investigations

  • Chest X-ray – ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms ("white-out" in severe cases); blood gases (hypoxia, acidosis); SpO2; blood culture to rule out sepsis.

5. Prevention

  • Antenatal corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (between about 24 and 34 weeks) – betamethasone or dexamethasone, which speed lung maturity; management of maternal diabetes; avoidance of elective caesarean section before 39 weeks.

6. Management

  • Warmth (thermoneutral environment), minimal handling.
  • Oxygen to keep SpO2 about 90–95% (avoid excess oxygen – ROP).
  • Early CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure, about 5–8 cm H2O through nasal prongs) – keeps alveoli open.
  • Surfactant replacement through an endotracheal tube or a thin catheter (LISA, INSURE techniques) in babies needing higher oxygen on CPAP.
  • Mechanical ventilation if CPAP fails.
  • IV fluids initially, then gradual feeds of expressed breast milk; antibiotics until sepsis is excluded.

7. Nursing care

  • Monitor respiratory rate, effort (scoring), colour, SpO2 and blood gases continuously; position with the neck slightly extended; care of CPAP – correct prong size, prevent nasal injury, keep the circuit humidified, orogastric tube to vent air from the stomach; gentle suctioning only when needed; maintain temperature; fluid and glucose monitoring; prevent infection; support parents.

Conclusion RDS is respiratory distress of preterm babies due to surfactant deficiency, presenting within hours of birth with tachypnoea, grunting, flaring, retractions and cyanosis, and a ground-glass chest X-ray. It is prevented by antenatal steroids and treated with warmth, careful oxygen, early CPAP, surfactant and ventilation when needed, along with meticulous nursing care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the metabolic disorders of the newborn – hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia – with their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Newborns have limited energy stores and immature hormonal control, so they easily develop low blood glucose and low calcium, especially when they are small, preterm, sick or born to diabetic mothers. Both can cause convulsions and brain injury if untreated.

A. Neonatal hypoglycaemia Definition – blood glucose below about 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) is generally treated as hypoglycaemia in newborns (operational threshold used in Indian newborn units). Babies at risk

  • Infants of diabetic mothers (high insulin), SGA and IUGR babies, preterm babies, LGA babies, babies with sepsis, asphyxia, hypothermia or polycythaemia, and those who are not feeding well. Clinical features

  • Often none; or jitteriness, tremors, lethargy, poor feeding, weak or high-pitched cry, hypothermia, sweating, cyanosis, apnoea, hypotonia and convulsions. Screening – at-risk babies have blood glucose checked (glucometer, confirmed in the laboratory) about 2 hours after birth and then every few hours for the first 24–48 hours as per protocol, before feeds. Management

  • Asymptomatic, mild – breastfeed or give expressed breast milk at once and recheck in 30–60 minutes.

  • Symptomatic, severe or persistent – IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg as a bolus, followed by a continuous glucose infusion (about 6–8 mg/kg/min), adjusted according to repeat glucose values; continue feeds if possible; investigate persistent hypoglycaemia.
  • Prevent by early and frequent feeding and warmth.

B. Neonatal hypocalcaemia Definition – total serum calcium below about 7 mg/dL (or ionised calcium below about 4 mg/dL / 1 mmol/L). Types

  • Early hypocalcaemia (first 2–3 days) – preterm babies, infants of diabetic mothers, birth asphyxia, IUGR.

  • Late hypocalcaemia (after 5–7 days) – feeding with cow's milk (high phosphate), maternal Vitamin D deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia. Clinical features – often none; jitteriness, irritability, tetany, carpopedal spasm, high-pitched cry, laryngospasm (stridor), apnoea and convulsions. Management

  • 10% calcium gluconate 2 mL/kg IV, given slowly over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring (stop if heart rate falls), followed by maintenance calcium in IV fluids or orally as prescribed.

  • Never give calcium rapidly or mix with bicarbonate; watch the IV site – extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis.
  • Breast milk feeding; avoid undiluted cow's milk; Vitamin D and magnesium if deficient.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Identify at-risk babies; feed early and frequently; monitor glucose and calcium as per protocol; observe for jitteriness and convulsions; give IV dextrose and calcium accurately with infusion pumps and close monitoring; record and report.

Conclusion Neonatal hypoglycaemia (blood glucose below about 45 mg/dL) and hypocalcaemia (serum calcium below about 7 mg/dL) are common in preterm, SGA, asphyxiated and diabetic mothers' babies, and cause jitteriness and convulsions. Early feeding, screening, IV dextrose and slow IV calcium gluconate with careful monitoring prevent brain injury.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain neonatal seizures – causes, types and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Neonatal seizures are the most common neurological emergency in the newborn, usually occurring in the first week. They indicate an underlying brain problem and may cause further injury, so they must be recognised and treated urgently.

1. Causes

  • Hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy (birth asphyxia) – the commonest cause, usually within 24–48 hours.
  • Metabolic – hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia, pyridoxine dependency, inborn errors of metabolism.
  • Infections – meningitis, sepsis, intrauterine (TORCH) infections.
  • Intracranial haemorrhage – intraventricular haemorrhage in preterms, subdural haemorrhage after traumatic delivery.
  • Others – kernicterus, congenital brain malformations, drug withdrawal (maternal opioid use), neonatal epilepsy syndromes.

2. Types

  • Subtle seizures (most common, easily missed) – eye deviation or staring, repeated blinking, lip smacking, sucking, chewing, "cycling" or "swimming" movements of limbs, apnoea.
  • Clonic seizures – rhythmic jerking of one limb (focal) or several limbs (multifocal).
  • Tonic seizures – stiffening of limbs and trunk (common in preterms; may resemble posturing).
  • Myoclonic seizures – sudden single or repeated jerks; often associated with severe brain disease.

3. Differentiating seizures from jitteriness

  • Jitteriness is stopped by gently holding or flexing the limb, is triggered by stimulation, has no eye deviation and no changes in heart rate, breathing or colour; seizures are not stopped by restraint and may have abnormal eye movements and autonomic changes.

4. Investigations

  • Immediate blood glucose, serum calcium, magnesium, sodium; blood gas; sepsis screen and lumbar puncture; cranial ultrasound (haemorrhage), CT or MRI; EEG (preferably continuous or amplitude-integrated EEG).

5. Management

  1. ABC – clear the airway, position on the side, oxygen, ventilation if needed; maintain temperature.
  2. Correct hypoglycaemia at once – 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV; correct hypocalcaemia (10% calcium gluconate 2 mL/kg slowly) and hypomagnesaemia.
  3. Anticonvulsants (as prescribed) – phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV slowly as a loading dose (further doses up to a total of about 40 mg/kg if seizures continue), then phenytoin or levetiracetam, and midazolam infusion for resistant seizures; pyridoxine trial if indicated.
  4. Treat the cause – antibiotics for meningitis, therapeutic hypothermia for eligible babies with HIE, management of haemorrhage.

6. Nursing care

  • Observe and record the type, duration and frequency of seizures, eye movements and accompanying changes (heart rate, SpO2, colour); report immediately.
  • Safety – keep the baby in a warmer or cot with padded sides; do not restrain or put anything in the mouth; suction secretions gently.
  • Monitor vital signs, SpO2, blood glucose and the IV site (phenytoin irritates veins); watch for respiratory depression after anticonvulsants.
  • Feeding by tube or IV until alert; maintain fluid balance and temperature.
  • Support the parents and explain; arrange developmental follow-up.

Conclusion Neonatal seizures are commonly caused by HIE, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, meningitis and haemorrhage. Subtle seizures are the most common and must be distinguished from jitteriness. Management includes ABC, immediate correction of glucose and calcium, phenobarbitone and other anticonvulsants, treatment of the cause, careful observation, safety and follow-up.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).
answer_html:
Definition Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a disorder of the developing blood vessels of the retina in preterm babies, in which abnormal vessels grow at the junction of vascular and avascular retina. Severe ROP can cause retinal detachment and permanent blindness. It is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness, increasing in India as more preterm babies survive.

1. Risk factors

  • Prematurity and low birth weight (the most important), unmonitored or excessive oxygen therapy, fluctuating oxygen levels, sepsis, poor weight gain, blood transfusions, respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage.

2. Pathogenesis (in brief)

  • Retinal vessels grow from the optic disc towards the periphery and are complete only near term. After preterm birth, relative hyperoxia stops their growth; later, the avascular retina becomes hypoxic and releases vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), causing abnormal new vessels and fibrous tissue that can pull the retina off.

3. Stages

  • Stage 1 – demarcation line between vascular and avascular retina.
  • Stage 2 – ridge.
  • Stage 3 – extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation.
  • Stage 4 – partial retinal detachment.
  • Stage 5 – total retinal detachment.
  • Plus disease – dilated and tortuous vessels, indicating active, severe disease needing treatment.

4. Screening

  • In India, screening is recommended for all babies born below 34 weeks and/or below 2,000 g, and for bigger babies with risk factors (prolonged oxygen, sepsis, transfusions).
  • The first examination by about 20–30 days of life (earlier for very small babies), by an ophthalmologist using indirect ophthalmoscopy or retinal imaging, and then repeated until the retina is fully vascularised.

5. Treatment

  • Laser photocoagulation of the avascular retina – standard treatment.
  • Anti-VEGF injections into the eye (for selected cases).
  • Vitreoretinal surgery for retinal detachment (stages 4–5), with poorer results.
  • Treatment is time-critical – it should be given within 48–72 hours of detecting treatment-requiring ROP.

6. Prevention and nursing role

  • Careful oxygen therapy – use air–oxygen blenders and pulse oximeters; keep SpO2 about 90–95% in preterm babies; avoid fluctuations; never give unmonitored oxygen.
  • Prevent and treat sepsis; good nutrition and breast milk; minimise unnecessary transfusions.
  • Identify eligible babies and ensure timely screening before discharge or at follow-up; keep a ROP register; help during examination (dilating drops, swaddling, sucrose, monitoring for apnoea).
  • Educate parents about the importance of follow-up eye examinations; ensure treatment is not delayed.

Conclusion ROP is abnormal retinal vessel growth in preterm babies, worsened by excess or fluctuating oxygen, which can lead to blindness. It is staged from a demarcation line to total retinal detachment. Screening of babies below 34 weeks or 2,000 g from about 3–4 weeks of age, timely laser or anti-VEGF treatment, and careful monitored oxygen therapy prevent blindness.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the methods of feeding preterm and low birth weight babies.
answer_html:
Introduction Breast milk is the best food for preterm and LBW babies – it protects against infection and necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) and promotes growth and brain development. The method of feeding depends on the baby's gestational age, maturity of suck and swallow, and clinical condition.

1. Choice of feeding method

  • Sick or very small babies (usually below about 28–30 weeks or below 1,200 g) – start with IV fluids, then small "trophic" feeds of expressed breast milk by orogastric tube as soon as the baby is stable, increasing gradually.
  • About 28/30–32 weeks – orogastric or nasogastric tube (gavage) feeding of expressed breast milk (no coordinated suck–swallow).
  • About 32–34 weeks – cup, paladai or spoon feeding of expressed breast milk; put to the breast for non-nutritive sucking and practice.
  • About 34 weeks or more – direct breastfeeding, supplemented by cup if needed.
  • Babies move from one method to the next as they mature.

2. Volume and frequency

  • Feeds every 2–3 hours; volume calculated in mL/kg/day as prescribed (starting at about 60–80 mL/kg/day and increased by about 15–30 mL/kg/day to about 150–180 mL/kg/day).

3. Technique of tube (gavage) feeding

  • Measure the tube length (nose or mouth to ear lobe to midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus); insert gently; confirm position before each feed (aspiration of gastric contents, pH check); give milk slowly by gravity from a syringe barrel held about 10–15 cm above the baby; change tubes as per policy.

4. Technique of cup/paladai feeding

  • Hold the baby upright on the lap; place the rim of the cup or paladai lightly on the lower lip; tip it so that milk just touches the lips and let the baby lap or sip at his own pace – never pour milk into the mouth.

5. Expressed breast milk (EBM) and donor milk

  • Help the mother express milk every 2–3 hours by hand or pump; store EBM safely (about 6–8 hours at room temperature, 24 hours in a refrigerator); use donor milk from a human milk bank when the mother's milk is not available.

6. Fortification and supplements (as prescribed)

  • Human milk fortifier for VLBW babies once full feeds are tolerated; Vitamin D (400 IU daily), iron (from about 2 weeks in preterms), calcium and phosphorus, and multivitamins.

7. Monitoring and nursing care

  • Daily weight (target gain about 15–20 g/kg/day after the first week), weekly length and head circumference.
  • Watch for feed intolerance – vomiting, large or bile-stained gastric residues, abdominal distension, blood in stools (NEC).
  • Positioning after feeds (prone or right lateral under monitoring); burping; aspiration precautions; mouth care; intake–output.
  • Involve and train the mother in feeding; support breastfeeding through KMC.

Conclusion Preterm and LBW babies are fed with breast milk by a method suited to their maturity – IV fluids and trophic tube feeds for the very small or sick, tube feeding at 28–32 weeks, cup or paladai at 32–34 weeks, and breastfeeding from about 34 weeks – with gradual increase of volume, fortifiers and supplements, careful monitoring of tolerance and growth, and support for the mother.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the common minor infections of the newborn and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Newborns commonly develop local (minor) infections of the mouth, cord, skin and eyes. They are easily treated, but if neglected they can spread and cause serious sepsis. IMNCI classifies them as "local bacterial infection" when there are no signs of serious illness.

1. Oral thrush (candidiasis)

  • Cause – Candida albicans; from the mother's vagina, unclean feeding bottles or nipples, or after antibiotics.
  • Features – white, curd-like patches on the tongue, cheeks and palate that do not wipe off easily (unlike milk curds); may cause feeding difficulty.
  • Management – nystatin or clotrimazole oral drops/gel applied after feeds, several times a day for about a week; treat the mother's nipples; avoid bottles and pacifiers; hand hygiene.

2. Umbilical sepsis (omphalitis)

  • Features – redness, swelling, pus discharge or foul smell from the cord stump; redness spreading to the surrounding skin is a sign of serious infection.
  • Management – local infection only: clean with clean water or antiseptic and keep dry as advised, apply prescribed local antiseptic; spreading redness, fever or poor feeding – systemic antibiotics and referral.
  • Prevention – clean cutting and tying of the cord, dry cord care, applying nothing on the cord.

3. Skin pustules (pyoderma)

  • Cause – usually Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Features – small pus-filled spots, especially in skin folds (neck, axilla, groin).
  • Management – fewer than 10 pustules: clean with antiseptic and apply local antibiotic; 10 or more pustules, large boils or abscesses, or a sick baby – systemic antibiotics and referral (danger of sepsis).

4. Conjunctivitis (sticky eyes)

  • Features – discharge, redness and swelling of the eyelids.
  • Management – clean eyes with sterile cotton soaked in boiled cooled water or saline from inner to outer canthus; antibiotic eye drops or ointment as prescribed.
  • Ophthalmia neonatorum – purulent conjunctivitis in the first 2–4 weeks, especially gonococcal (severe, early, can cause blindness) or chlamydial; needs systemic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone for gonococcal infection) and treatment of the parents.
  • A blocked tear duct (watering eye with mild discharge) is treated with gentle massage.

5. Nappy (diaper) rash

  • Red, sore skin in the nappy area from wetness and ammonia; Candida infection if satellite lesions are present.
  • Management – frequent nappy changes, cleaning with water, drying, exposure to air, barrier cream (zinc oxide), antifungal cream if candidal.

6. Nursing responsibilities and prevention

  • Hand hygiene; exclusive breastfeeding; clean cord, eye and skin care; avoid harmful practices (kajal, applying substances on the cord); teach mothers to recognise local infections and the danger signs of serious infection (poor feeding, lethargy, fever or low temperature, fast breathing); follow-up within 2 days.

Conclusion Oral thrush, umbilical sepsis, skin pustules, conjunctivitis and nappy rash are common minor infections in newborns. They are treated with local measures and topical drugs, but spreading redness, many pustules, purulent eye discharge in the first weeks or any sign of illness need systemic antibiotics and referral. Hygiene and clean cord and skin care prevent most of them.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the common physiological variations (minor problems) seen in the newborn.
answer_html:
Introduction Many findings in a healthy newborn worry parents but are normal physiological variations due to maternal hormones, adaptation to extrauterine life or the process of birth. The nurse must recognise them, reassure the parents and distinguish them from disease.

1. Physiological weight loss

  • Loss of up to about 10% of birth weight in the first 3–5 days (loss of extracellular fluid and meconium, small early feeds); birth weight is regained by 10–14 days. Greater loss or slow regain needs feeding assessment.

2. Physiological jaundice

  • Appears after 24 hours, peaks on days 3–5 and disappears by 10–14 days; the baby is well and feeding (any jaundice in the first 24 hours or reaching the palms and soles is not normal).

3. Hormonal effects (maternal oestrogen)

  • Breast engorgement in both sexes, sometimes with a few drops of milk ("witch's milk") – do not squeeze or massage (risk of abscess); it subsides in 1–2 weeks.
  • Pseudomenstruation – slight vaginal bleeding in girls around days 3–7, and white mucoid vaginal discharge; resolves on its own.

4. Skin findings

  • Milia – tiny white spots on the nose and chin (blocked sebaceous glands); disappear in weeks.
  • Erythema toxicum – red blotches with small yellow-white centres on the trunk in the first days; harmless and transient.
  • Mongolian spots – bluish-grey patches over the lower back and buttocks, common in Indian babies; fade over the first years; should not be mistaken for bruises.
  • Stork bite (salmon patch) – pink flat marks on the nape, eyelids or forehead; fade.
  • Peeling of skin, especially in post-term babies.
  • Acrocyanosis – blue hands and feet in the first 24–48 hours (central colour pink).
  • Harlequin colour change – one half of the body red and the other pale for a short time (vasomotor instability).

5. Mouth

  • Epstein pearls – small white cysts on the palate; disappear without treatment.

6. Head

  • Moulding of the skull bones and caput succedaneum (soft swelling of the scalp crossing suture lines) – disappear within days.

7. Stools and urine

  • Meconium (dark green, sticky) in the first 1–2 days, transitional stools (greenish-yellow, loose) on days 3–5, then yellow breast-milk stools that may be frequent (with each feed) or infrequent after the first weeks.
  • Pink "brick-dust" staining of the nappy from urate crystals in the first days.

8. Other normal behaviours

  • Sneezing (clearing the nose), hiccups, startles, irregular (periodic) breathing without colour change, crossed eyes (occasional) in the first months.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Recognise these variations, reassure and educate parents, discourage harmful practices (squeezing breasts, applying substances), document findings, and watch for features that suggest disease (jaundice in the first 24 hours, excessive weight loss, bleeding from other sites, persistent central cyanosis).

Conclusion Physiological weight loss and jaundice, breast engorgement and pseudomenstruation, milia, erythema toxicum, mongolian spots, stork bites, Epstein pearls, moulding and caput, acrocyanosis and transitional stools are normal findings in newborns. The nurse reassures parents while remaining alert to abnormal signs.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the APGAR score?
answer_html:
The APGAR score, devised by Dr. Virginia Apgar (1952), is a quick method of assessing the condition of a newborn at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth (and every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if the score is below 7). Five signs are each scored 0, 1 or 2:

  1. Appearance (colour) – blue/pale = 0; body pink, extremities blue = 1; completely pink = 2.
  2. Pulse (heart rate) – absent = 0; below 100/min = 1; 100/min or more = 2.
  3. Grimace (reflex irritability) – no response = 0; grimace = 1; cry, cough or sneeze = 2.
  4. Activity (muscle tone) – limp = 0; some flexion = 1; active movement = 2.
  5. Respiration – absent = 0; weak, irregular = 1; good cry = 2. Interpretation – 7–10 normal; 4–6 moderately depressed; 0–3 severely depressed. Resuscitation is started on the basis of breathing and heart rate and is never delayed to calculate the score.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the Silverman–Anderson score?
answer_html:
The Silverman–Anderson score is used to assess the severity of respiratory distress in newborns (especially preterm babies with RDS). Five signs are each scored 0 (none), 1 (moderate) or 2 (severe):

  1. Upper chest movement – synchronised with abdomen (0), lag on inspiration (1), see-saw movement (2).
  2. Lower chest (intercostal) retraction.
  3. Xiphoid retraction.
  4. Nasal flaring.
  5. Expiratory grunt – absent (0), audible with stethoscope (1), audible with the naked ear (2). Total 0–10 – 0 means no distress; 1–3 mild; 4–6 moderate; 7 or more indicates severe distress and impending respiratory failure. (Note: unlike APGAR, a higher score is worse.) The Downes score is a similar tool that also includes respiratory rate, cyanosis and air entry.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is kernicterus?
answer_html:
Kernicterus is permanent brain damage caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, especially the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei, when serum bilirubin rises to very high levels in newborns.

  • Risk factors – very high bilirubin (haemolytic disease – Rh, ABO, G6PD deficiency), prematurity, sepsis, acidosis, hypoxia, low albumin, drugs that displace bilirubin.
  • Acute signs – lethargy, poor sucking, hypotonia followed by hypertonia, arching of the back (opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, fever, seizures.
  • Long-term effects – athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural deafness, upward gaze palsy, dental enamel defects, intellectual disability.
  • Prevention – early detection of jaundice, measurement of bilirubin, timely phototherapy and exchange transfusion.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: List the danger signs in a newborn.
answer_html:
Danger signs in a newborn (seek care immediately)

  1. Not feeding well or unable to suck.
  2. Convulsions.
  3. Fast breathing (60 or more per minute) or severe chest indrawing, grunting.
  4. Fever (37.5 °C or above) or low body temperature (below 35.5 °C), cold to touch.
  5. Movement only when stimulated or no movement at all (lethargy).
  6. Yellow palms and soles, or jaundice in the first 24 hours.
  7. Umbilical redness extending to the skin, or many or large skin pustules.
  8. Bleeding from any site, central cyanosis, persistent vomiting, abdominal distension. These signs indicate possible serious bacterial infection or other serious illness and need urgent referral.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: How is the umbilical cord cared for in the newborn?
answer_html:
Care of the umbilical cord

  1. At birth – clamp or tie at about 2–3 cm from the abdomen with a sterile clamp or thread and cut with a sterile blade (delayed clamping of at least 1 minute).
  2. Dry cord care – keep the stump clean and dry; leave it exposed to air or loosely covered by clothing; fold the nappy below the stump.
  3. Apply nothing on the cord – no oil, ash, turmeric, cow dung or powder (in settings with very high neonatal mortality, chlorhexidine application may be advised by local policy).
  4. Wash hands before touching the cord; clean with clean water if soiled, and dry.
  5. The stump usually falls off in 5–10 days.
  6. Watch for infection – redness, swelling, pus, foul smell or bleeding; redness spreading to the skin needs urgent treatment.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is necrotising enterocolitis (NEC)?
answer_html:
Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) is a serious inflammatory disease of the intestine in newborns, mainly preterm babies, in which parts of the bowel wall become ischaemic and necrotic, sometimes leading to perforation.

  • Risk factors – prematurity, LBW, formula feeding, rapid increase of feeds, asphyxia, sepsis, exchange transfusion, polycythaemia.
  • Features – feed intolerance, abdominal distension, bile-stained vomiting or gastric residues, blood in stools, abdominal tenderness, lethargy, apnoea, shock.
  • X-ray – gas in the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis), free air if perforated.
  • Management – stop feeds (NPO), orogastric decompression, IV fluids, antibiotics, monitoring of abdominal girth; surgery for perforation.
  • Prevention – breast milk feeding, cautious advancement of feeds, infection control.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is apnoea of prematurity?
answer_html:
Apnoea of prematurity is a pause in breathing lasting 20 seconds or more, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia (heart rate below 100/min) or desaturation/cyanosis, in a preterm baby (usually below 34 weeks), due to immaturity of the respiratory centre in the brain.

  • It differs from periodic breathing (pauses of 5–10 seconds without colour or heart-rate change), which is normal.
  • Other causes (sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, anaemia, seizures, airway obstruction) must be excluded.
  • Management – continuous monitoring (pulse oximeter, apnoea monitor), gentle tactile stimulation (rubbing the back or soles), positioning with the neck slightly extended, avoiding temperature swings and vigorous suctioning, caffeine citrate as prescribed, CPAP or ventilation for severe episodes.
  • It usually resolves by about 36–37 weeks of post-menstrual age.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is dehydration fever (transitional fever) in the newborn?
answer_html:
Dehydration fever is a rise in body temperature (above 37.5 °C) in a newborn, usually on the 2nd–4th day of life, due to inadequate fluid intake (poor breastfeeding) and excess environmental heat (overwrapping, hot room, warmer set too high).

  • Features – fever, irritability or lethargy, dry mouth, sunken fontanelle, reduced urine, excessive weight loss (more than 10%); the baby is otherwise without signs of infection.
  • Management – remove extra clothing, cool the room, frequent breastfeeding (or expressed milk by cup), correct breastfeeding technique; IV fluids if severely dehydrated; check sodium and glucose.
  • Fever in a newborn must always be evaluated for infection before it is considered dehydration fever.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: (a) Define IMNCI and state its objectives. (3 marks) (b) Explain the components of IMNCI and the age groups covered. (4 marks) (c) Describe the IMNCI case management process. (8 marks)
tags: integrated management of neonatal and childhood illness

diagram.caption: IMNCI case management process
labels: feel) – classify the illness using colour-coded charts (pink: urgent referral
green: home care) – identify treatment – treat (first dose
when to return) – give follow-up care

answer_html:
(a) Definition and objectives (3 marks) Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) is the Indian adaptation of the WHO–UNICEF strategy of Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI). It provides a simple, standardised, evidence-based approach for the integrated assessment, classification, treatment and counselling of sick newborns and children up to 5 years, focusing on the main causes of child deaths – neonatal illnesses, pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles and malnutrition. India added the neonatal period to IMCI (hence "N") because most infant deaths occur in the first weeks of life. It was introduced in India in 2003 and scaled up under the National Health Mission; Facility-Based IMNCI (F-IMNCI) extends it to inpatient care at first referral units.

Objectives

  1. To reduce morbidity and mortality among children below 5 years, especially newborns.
  2. To improve the case management skills of health workers at all levels.
  3. To promote growth and development through good feeding practices and immunisation.
  4. To strengthen health systems for child care – drugs, supervision, referral.
  5. To improve family and community practices for child health (care-seeking, home care).

(b) Components and age groups (4 marks) Three components

  1. Improving the case management skills of health workers – training (ANMs, nurses, ASHAs, Anganwadi workers, doctors) in using the IMNCI chart booklet; supervision and follow-up after training.
  2. Improving the overall health system – availability of essential drugs and supplies (ORS, zinc, amoxicillin, gentamicin, antimalarials, Vitamin A, IFA), referral systems, supervision, recording and reporting.
  3. Improving family and community health practices – exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding, immunisation, hand washing, use of ORS, warmth for newborns, recognition of danger signs and timely care-seeking.

Age groups (separate charts)

  • Sick young infant – birth up to 2 months (including newborns up to 7 days at home visits).
  • Sick child – 2 months up to 5 years.

(c) IMNCI case management process (8 marks) The process has six steps, used for every sick child at the health facility (and adapted for home visits).

Step 1 – Assess

  • Greet the mother; ask her about the child's problems, age, whether it is the initial or follow-up visit.
  • Check for general danger signs (sick child) or for possible serious bacterial infection (young infant).
  • Ask about main symptoms – cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever and ear problem (sick child); infection, jaundice, diarrhoea and feeding problem (young infant).
  • Look, listen and feel – count breaths for one full minute, look for chest indrawing, skin pinch, sunken eyes, palmar pallor, oedema, wasting; measure weight, MUAC and temperature.
  • Check nutrition, anaemia, immunisation, feeding and other problems.

Step 2 – Classify

  • Use the colour-coded classification tables of the chart booklet. Each classification is based on a combination of a few clinical signs (not a laboratory diagnosis). A child may have more than one classification.
    • Pink – severe classification needing urgent pre-referral treatment and referral (e.g. severe pneumonia or very severe disease, severe dehydration, possible serious bacterial infection).
    • Yellow – needs specific medical treatment at the facility or at home (antibiotic, ORS, antimalarial) with follow-up (e.g. pneumonia, some dehydration).
    • Green – needs home management advice (e.g. no pneumonia – cough or cold, no dehydration).

Step 3 – Identify treatment

  • For pink classifications – identify urgent pre-referral treatment (first dose of antibiotic, prevention of low blood sugar, keeping warm) and arrange referral.
  • For yellow and green – identify drugs, doses and home care.
  • If referral is not possible, follow national guidelines for treatment at the facility.

Step 4 – Treat

  • Give the first dose of oral or injectable drugs in the clinic; give ORS and zinc; treat local infections (eye, ear, mouth, umbilicus, skin); give Vitamin A, IFA and deworming as indicated.
  • Teach the mother how to give oral drugs at home – how much, how often and for how many days – and check that she has understood.
  • Refer pink cases urgently with a referral note, keeping the child warm and breastfeeding on the way.

Step 5 – Counsel the mother

  • Feeding – assess feeding and give age-appropriate feeding advice (exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months; complementary feeding; feeding during and after illness).
  • Fluids – increase fluids during illness, especially diarrhoea.
  • When to return – immediately if danger signs develop (not able to drink or breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, fast or difficult breathing, blood in stool, drinking poorly), and on the follow-up date.
  • Advise on the mother's own health (nutrition, family planning, immunisation).
  • Use good communication skills – ask and listen, praise, advise, and check understanding; give the mother's card.

Step 6 – Give follow-up care

  • See the child on the specified follow-up day (usually after 2 or 5 days, and 14 days for some problems such as persistent diarrhoea or feeding problems); reassess using the follow-up boxes; change treatment or refer if the child is not improving.

(d) Need for an integrated approach

  • A sick child often has more than one condition at the same time – for example pneumonia with malnutrition and anaemia; a single-disease approach treats one problem and misses the others.
  • The signs of common illnesses overlap – fever with fast breathing may be due to pneumonia or malaria – so assessing the whole child gives better decisions.
  • Most deaths of children below 5 years in India are due to a small number of preventable causes, and a large share occur in the neonatal period.
  • Most sick children are first seen at peripheral facilities without laboratory support, where simple clinical signs must guide treatment.
  • Every visit for illness is an opportunity for prevention – immunisation, Vitamin A, feeding counselling.

(e) Indian adaptation – how IMNCI differs from the generic IMCI

  1. Inclusion of the 0–7 day age group (the first week of life) in the young infant module.
  2. Incorporation of national guidelines on malaria, anaemia, Vitamin A supplementation and the immunisation schedule.
  3. Training begins with the sick young infant (up to 2 months) instead of the older child.
  4. The proportion of training time given to the sick young infant is increased, so that it is almost equal to that for the sick child.
  5. Training is skill-based and includes home visits for young infants by health workers.

(f) Benefits and limitations

  • Benefits – tackles the main killers together; is cost-effective; reduces missed diagnoses and unnecessary antibiotics; links curative care with prevention; strengthens referral and community-based care; empowers mothers through counselling.
  • Limitations – depends on trained, supervised health workers and a regular supply of drugs; families often do not complete referral; assessment takes time in busy clinics; some illnesses (tuberculosis, HIV infection, dengue, heart disease) need assessment beyond the charts; skills fade without refresher training and supportive supervision.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses and ANMs are the main providers of IMNCI at sub-centres and PHCs; correct use of the case management process allows early identification and treatment of sick children close to their homes and timely referral of severely ill ones.

Conclusion IMNCI is India's integrated strategy for managing sick young infants and children below 5 years, aiming to reduce deaths from neonatal illness, pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles and malnutrition. It has three components – health worker skills, health system support and family practices – and follows six steps: assess, classify (pink, yellow, green), identify treatment, treat, counsel the mother and give follow-up care.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the IMNCI management of the sick young infant (birth up to 2 months) – assessment, classification and treatment.

diagram.caption: IMNCI classification for the sick young infant
labels: possible serious bacterial infection (pink – first dose antibiotic
refer); local bacterial infection (yellow – oral antibiotic
follow-up 2 days); severe disease or local infection unlikely (green – home care); severe jaundice (pink)
no jaundice (green); feeding problem or low weight (yellow)

answer_html:
Introduction Young infants (below 2 months) can become seriously ill very quickly, often with non-specific signs. Their illnesses are mainly bacterial infections, jaundice, diarrhoea and feeding problems, and they need assessment with a separate IMNCI chart.

A. Check for possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) and local bacterial infection Ask – Is the infant having difficulty in feeding? Has the infant had convulsions? Look and feel

  • Count breaths in one minute – repeat if 60 or more; fast breathing = 60 or more breaths per minute.
  • Look for severe chest indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting.
  • Look and feel for a bulging fontanelle.
  • Look at the umbilicus – red or draining pus; redness extending to the skin.
  • Measure temperature – fever (37.5 °C or above, or feels hot) or low temperature (below 35.5 °C, or feels cold).
  • Look for skin pustules – many or severe.

  • See if the infant is lethargic or unconscious; look at movements – fewer than normal. Classification

  • Possible serious bacterial infection (pink) – any of: not able to feed, convulsions, fast breathing, severe chest indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting, bulging fontanelle, umbilical redness extending to the skin, fever or low temperature, many or severe skin pustules, lethargy or unconsciousness, less than normal movement.

    • Treatment – give the first dose of antibiotics as per national guidelines (e.g. injection gentamicin with ampicillin or oral amoxicillin); treat to prevent low blood sugar (breastfeed or give expressed milk or sugar water); keep the infant warm (skin-to-skin) on the way; refer urgently; if referral is refused or not possible, follow the national guideline for treatment with simplified antibiotic regimens at the facility, with close follow-up.
  • Local bacterial infection (yellow) – umbilicus red or draining pus, or skin pustules (few).
    • Treatment – oral antibiotic (amoxicillin) for 5 days, teach the mother to treat local infections at home (clean the umbilicus or pustules and apply gentian violet or antiseptic as advised), home care, follow-up in 2 days.
  • Severe disease or local infection unlikely (green) – none of the above; home care advice.

B. Check for jaundice

  • Severe jaundice (pink) – any jaundice in an infant below 24 hours old, or yellow palms and soles at any age, or jaundice lasting 14 days or more – refer urgently, prevent low blood sugar, keep warm.
  • Jaundice (yellow) – jaundice appearing after 24 hours, palms and soles not yellow – advise feeding, follow-up in 2 days, return immediately if palms and soles become yellow.
  • No jaundice (green) – home care.

C. Diarrhoea in the young infant

  • Assess for dehydration – movement (only when stimulated or not at all), restlessness and irritability, sunken eyes, skin pinch (goes back very slowly or slowly).
  • Severe dehydration (pink) – two of the signs: movement only when stimulated or no movement, sunken eyes, skin pinch very slow – give IV fluids (Plan C) if possible or refer urgently with mother giving ORS sips on the way; continue breastfeeding.
  • Some dehydration (yellow) – restless and irritable, sunken eyes, skin pinch slow – Plan B (ORS in the clinic), continue breastfeeding.
  • No dehydration (green) – Plan A (extra breastfeeds, ORS after each stool if the infant is receiving other fluids, zinc as per guidelines, when to return).
  • Diarrhoea for 14 days or more, or blood in the stool, in a young infant – refer.

D. Check for feeding problem or low weight Ask – Is the infant breastfed? How many times in 24 hours? Does he receive other foods or drinks (water, honey, animal milk)? What is used to feed? Look – weight for age on the growth chart (low weight); oral thrush (white patches). Assess breastfeeding (if no indication for urgent referral and a feeding problem or low weight is present)

  • Has the infant breastfed in the previous hour? If not, ask the mother to breastfeed and observe for 4 minutes.
  • Attachment – chin touching the breast, mouth wide open, lower lip turned outward, more areola visible above than below the mouth.

  • Effective suckling – slow, deep sucks, sometimes pausing. Classification

  • Not able to feed – possible serious bacterial infection (pink) – not able to feed, no attachment at all or not suckling at all – refer.

  • Feeding problem or low weight (yellow) – not well attached, not suckling effectively, fewer than 8 breastfeeds in 24 hours, receives other foods or drinks, low weight for age, thrush, breast or nipple problems – advise on correct positioning and attachment, increase breastfeeding frequency, stop other feeds, treat thrush, follow-up in 2 days (14 days for low weight).
  • No feeding problem (green) – praise the mother, advise on continuing exclusive breastfeeding.

E. Check immunisation status – give vaccines due (BCG, OPV, hepatitis B at birth; pentavalent, OPV, rotavirus, PCV and IPV from 6 weeks) – sickness is not a reason to delay (except in infants being referred).

F. Home care for the young infant (counselling)

  1. Breastfeed frequently, as often and for as long as the infant wants, day and night, during sickness and health; give only breast milk.
  2. Keep the young infant warm – skin-to-skin contact (especially for LBW infants), cap and socks, avoid bathing a cold infant.
  3. Hygiene – hand washing, clean cord and skin care.
  4. When to return immediately – breastfeeding or drinking poorly, becomes sicker, develops fever or feels cold, fast or difficult breathing, blood in stool, yellow palms and soles.

G. Follow-up

  • Local bacterial infection, jaundice, diarrhoea and feeding problems are reviewed after 2 days; low weight after 14 days; any infant who is worse is referred.

H. Points to remember while assessing a young infant

  • Examine the infant in a warm room, keeping him covered as much as possible; undress only the part being examined.
  • The infant should be calm (asleep or quiet) when breaths are counted and chest indrawing is looked for. Mild chest indrawing is normal in young infants because the chest wall is soft; only severe chest indrawing (very deep and easy to see) is a danger sign.
  • Count breaths for a full minute and repeat the count if it is 60 or more, because young infants often breathe irregularly.
  • A low temperature is as dangerous as fever in a young infant.
  • Observe a breastfeed rather than relying only on the mother's report.
  • Look for jaundice in natural daylight, pressing the skin of the forehead, chest, palms and soles.

I. Home visits for young infants

  • IMNCI provides home visits to all newborns – within 24 hours of birth, on day 3–4 and on day 7–10 – with three more visits (days 14, 21 and 28) for low birth weight babies.
  • Under Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC), the ASHA visits on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 after an institutional delivery (6 visits), and also on day 1 after a home delivery (7 visits), with extra visits for preterm, LBW and SNCU-discharged babies.
  • At each visit the infant is weighed and checked for danger signs, warmth and breastfeeding, and the mother is counselled; infants with danger signs are referred.

Nursing importance

  • During home-based newborn care visits and at health facilities, nurses and ANMs who use the young infant chart correctly can identify sick newborns early, start life-saving treatment and refer, which is the key to reducing neonatal mortality.

Conclusion The sick young infant is assessed for possible serious bacterial infection and local infection, jaundice, diarrhoea with dehydration, and feeding problems or low weight, and immunisation status is checked. Infants with pink classifications receive pre-referral antibiotics, warmth and prevention of low blood sugar and are referred urgently; those with yellow classifications receive specific treatment and follow-up in 2 days; and mothers are counselled on frequent breastfeeding, warmth, hygiene and when to return.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the IMNCI management of the sick child aged 2 months to 5 years with general danger signs, cough or difficult breathing, and diarrhoea.

diagram.caption: IMNCI assessment of dehydration in a child with diarrhoea
labels: severe dehydration (two of: lethargic or unconscious
not able to drink or drinking poorly
skin pinch goes back very slowly) – Plan C; some dehydration (two of: restless and irritable
skin pinch goes back slowly) – Plan B; no dehydration – Plan A

answer_html:
Introduction Pneumonia and diarrhoea together cause a large share of deaths in Indian children below 5 years. IMNCI provides a step-wise approach to recognise the severely ill child and to treat others close to home.

A. Check for general danger signs (in every sick child) Ask – Is the child able to drink or breastfeed? Does the child vomit everything? Has the child had convulsions during this illness? Look – Is the child lethargic or unconscious? Is the child convulsing now?

  • A child with any general danger sign needs urgent attention, completion of the assessment quickly, pre-referral treatment and urgent referral.

B. Cough or difficult breathing Ask – for how long? Look and listen (child calm)

  • Count the breaths in one minute. Fast breathing is:
    • 50 or more per minute in a child aged 2 months up to 12 months,
    • 40 or more per minute in a child aged 12 months up to 5 years.
  • Look for chest indrawing (lower chest wall goes in when the child breathes in).
  • Look and listen for stridor (harsh noise on breathing in) and wheeze.

  • Check oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter where available. Classification and treatment

  • Severe pneumonia or very severe disease (pink) – any general danger sign, or stridor in a calm child, or low oxygen saturation:

    • First dose of an appropriate antibiotic (injectable or oral as per guidelines), oxygen if available, treat to prevent low blood sugar, keep warm, refer urgently.
  • Pneumonia (yellow) – fast breathing and/or chest indrawing (without danger signs):
    • Oral amoxicillin for 5 days (dose by weight, twice daily), soothe the throat and relieve cough with a safe home remedy, treat wheeze with an inhaled bronchodilator if present, advise when to return, follow-up in 2 days (3 days for some guidelines).
  • No pneumonia: cough or cold (green) – no signs of pneumonia:
    • Soothe the throat with a safe remedy (warm fluids, honey for children above 1 year, tulsi or ginger tea), keep the nose clear, continue feeding, follow-up in 5 days if not improving.
  • Cough for more than 14 days, or recurrent wheeze – refer for assessment of tuberculosis, asthma or other causes.

C. Diarrhoea Ask – for how long? Is there blood in the stool? Look and feel

  • General condition – lethargic or unconscious, or restless and irritable.
  • Sunken eyes.
  • Offer fluid – not able to drink or drinking poorly, or drinking eagerly, thirsty.
  • Skin pinch of the abdomen – goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds) or slowly.

Classification of dehydration and treatment

  1. Severe dehydration (pink) – two or more of: lethargic or unconscious, sunken eyes, not able to drink or drinking poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly.
    • Plan C – IV Ringer's lactate (or normal saline) 100 mL/kg:
      • Infants below 12 months – 30 mL/kg in 1 hour, then 70 mL/kg in 5 hours.
      • Children 12 months to 5 years – 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes, then 70 mL/kg in 2½ hours.
    • Reassess every 1–2 hours; give ORS (about 5 mL/kg/hour) as soon as the child can drink; if IV is not possible, ORS by nasogastric tube (20 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours) or refer urgently with the mother giving sips of ORS on the way.
  2. Some dehydration (yellow) – two or more of: restless and irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly or thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly.
    • Plan B – ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours in the clinic (more if the child wants), continue breastfeeding, give zinc, reassess after 4 hours and move to Plan A or C.
  3. No dehydration (green) – not enough signs for the above.
    • Plan A (home treatment) – four rules:
      1. Give extra fluids – as much as the child will take; ORS after each loose stool – 50–100 mL for a child below 2 years, 100–200 mL for a child 2 years or older; continue breastfeeding.
      2. Give zinc – 10 mg daily for infants 2–6 months, 20 mg daily for children above 6 months, for 14 days.
      3. Continue feeding.
      4. Know when to return – drinking poorly, becomes sicker, develops fever, blood in stool.

Persistent diarrhoea and dysentery
