  • Severe persistent diarrhoea (pink) – diarrhoea for 14 days or more with dehydration – treat dehydration and refer.
  • Persistent diarrhoea (yellow) – 14 days or more without dehydration – feeding advice, multivitamins and minerals (with zinc), follow-up in 5 days.
  • Dysentery (yellow) – blood in the stool – an oral antibiotic recommended for Shigella (e.g. ciprofloxacin) for 3 days, zinc, follow-up in 2 days.

D. Then assess the other main symptoms (fever, ear problem), nutrition, anaemia, immunisation and feeding, and counsel the mother.

E. Pre-referral treatment for pink classifications

  • First dose of an appropriate antibiotic (injectable or oral, as shown in the chart).
  • First dose of an antimalarial (injectable or rectal artesunate, as per the national drug policy) for very severe febrile disease in a malaria area.
  • Convulsions – clear the airway, turn the child on the side and give rectal diazepam as per the chart.
  • Prevent low blood sugar – breastfeed, or give 30–50 mL of milk or sugar water (4 level teaspoons – about 20 g – of sugar in 200 mL of clean water) before departure; by nasogastric tube if the child cannot swallow.
  • Paracetamol for high fever (38.5 °C or above); Vitamin A and tetracycline eye ointment in severe complicated measles; sips of ORS on the way for dehydration; keep the child warm.
  • Explain the need for referral to the mother, write a referral note and arrange transport.

F. Teaching the mother to prepare and give ORS

  • Wash hands; dissolve one packet of low-osmolarity ORS in 1 litre of clean drinking water; stir well; use within 24 hours and discard the rest.
  • WHO low-osmolarity ORS contains (per litre) sodium 75 mmol, chloride 65 mmol, glucose 75 mmol, potassium 20 mmol and citrate 10 mmol, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L.
  • Give small, frequent sips from a cup or spoon; if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly.
  • Avoid antidiarrhoeal drugs, antiemetics and routine antibiotics for simple watery diarrhoea, and cough syrups containing codeine, antihistamines or sedatives for cough and cold.

G. Follow-up

  • Pneumonia (after 2 days) – breathing slower, less fever and eating better: complete 5 days of amoxicillin; the same: change to the second-line antibiotic or refer; worse or a danger sign: refer urgently.
  • Dysentery (after 2 days) – fewer stools, less blood and eating better: complete the treatment; the same or worse: change the antibiotic or refer.
  • Persistent diarrhoea (after 5 days) – diarrhoea stopped: give the usual feeding advice for age; not stopped: reassess fully and refer.

Note for examinations – older IMNCI charts classified chest indrawing as "severe pneumonia". Under the revised WHO guidance (2014), followed in India's standard treatment guidelines and the SAANS initiative (Social Awareness and Action to Neutralise Pneumonia Successfully, 2019), chest indrawing without danger signs is classified as pneumonia and treated with oral amoxicillin, and ASHAs can give a pre-referral dose of amoxicillin. SAANS aims to reduce child deaths due to pneumonia to less than 3 per 1,000 live births by 2025.

Nursing importance

  • Correct counting of the respiratory rate for a full minute in a calm child, and skilled assessment of dehydration, are the key nursing skills that allow early treatment of pneumonia and diarrhoea and save children's lives.

Conclusion Every sick child aged 2 months to 5 years is first checked for general danger signs. Cough or difficult breathing is classified as severe pneumonia or very severe disease (refer), pneumonia (fast breathing or chest indrawing – oral amoxicillin) or cough or cold (home care), using age-specific breathing cut-offs. Diarrhoea is classified by dehydration into severe (Plan C), some (Plan B – ORS 75 mL/kg in 4 hours) or no dehydration (Plan A – fluids, zinc for 14 days, feeding and when to return), with special management for persistent diarrhoea and dysentery.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Write the principles of IMNCI.
answer_html:
Introduction IMNCI is based on a set of principles that make it simple, practical and effective for health workers with limited diagnostic facilities, especially at sub-centres and PHCs.

Principles of IMNCI

  1. All sick young infants and children are examined for signs of serious illness – general danger signs in children (2 months to 5 years) and signs of possible serious bacterial infection in young infants – that need immediate referral or admission.
  2. Children are routinely assessed for the main symptoms – cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever and ear problems in children; bacterial infection, jaundice, diarrhoea and feeding problems in young infants.
  3. All sick children are routinely assessed for nutritional and immunisation status, feeding problems and other potential problems – every contact is used to prevent future illness, not only to treat the present one.
  4. Only a limited number of carefully selected clinical signs are used – signs that have good sensitivity and specificity and can be checked by health workers without laboratory tests (e.g. respiratory rate, chest indrawing, skin pinch, palmar pallor).
  5. A combination of individual signs leads to a classification rather than a diagnosis – classifications indicate the severity of illness and the action needed, and a child can have more than one classification at the same time (integrated approach).
  6. Classifications are colour-coded:
    • Pink – urgent pre-referral treatment and referral.
    • Yellow – specific treatment (antibiotic, antimalarial, ORS) at the facility or at home.
    • Green – home management.
  7. Management uses a limited number of essential drugs and simple treatment procedures, with active participation of the caretaker (mother taught to give drugs and ORS at home).
  8. Counselling of caretakers about home care – feeding, fluids, recognising danger signs and when to return – is an essential part of every visit.
  9. Follow-up at specified intervals ensures that treatment is working and that children who do not improve are referred.
  10. Neonatal focus (Indian adaptation) – care of the young infant, including the first week of life and home visits, receives special emphasis.

Advantages

  • Treats the whole child, not a single disease; reduces missed diagnoses and unnecessary antibiotics; promotes rational drug use; strengthens prevention (immunisation, nutrition) and family practices.

Conclusion The principles of IMNCI are: assessment of every sick child for danger signs, routine assessment of main symptoms, nutrition, immunisation and feeding, use of a few reliable clinical signs, colour-coded classifications instead of diagnoses, limited essential drugs with caretaker participation, counselling, follow-up and a special focus on newborns.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the IMNCI assessment and classification of fever and ear problems in a child aged 2 months to 5 years.
answer_html:
Introduction Fever is one of the commonest complaints in children. In IMNCI it is assessed for very severe febrile disease (including meningitis), malaria and measles, and ear problems are assessed for mastoiditis and acute or chronic ear infection.

A. Fever Assess

  • Decide the malaria risk – high or low risk area (and travel history).
  • Ask – for how long (if more than 7 days, has fever been present every day?); has the child had measles within the last 3 months?
  • Look and feel – stiff neck; runny nose; signs of measles – generalised rash with one of cough, runny nose or red eyes; look for mouth ulcers (deep or extensive), pus from the eyes, clouding of the cornea.
  • Test for malaria – rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or blood smear in all febrile children in high-risk areas (and when no other cause is found in low-risk areas).

Classify and treat

  • Very severe febrile disease (pink) – any general danger sign or stiff neck – first dose of antibiotic and of an antimalarial (in a malaria area), paracetamol for high fever, prevent low blood sugar, refer urgently.
  • Malaria (yellow) – fever with a positive malaria test – treat according to the national drug policy (artemisinin-based combination therapy for P. falciparum; chloroquine plus primaquine for P. vivax), paracetamol for high fever, follow-up in 2–3 days if fever persists.
  • Fever – malaria unlikely / no malaria (green) – look for other causes; paracetamol for high fever; follow-up in 2 days if fever persists; fever every day for more than 7 days – refer.
  • Severe complicated measles (pink) – measles with a general danger sign, clouding of the cornea, or deep or extensive mouth ulcers – Vitamin A, first dose of antibiotic, tetracycline eye ointment if clouding, refer.
  • Measles with eye or mouth complications (yellow) – pus from the eyes or mouth ulcers – Vitamin A, treat the eyes with tetracycline ointment and mouth ulcers with gentian violet, follow-up in 2 days.
  • Measles (green) – Vitamin A and home care.
  • Vitamin A doses in measles – 50,000 IU below 6 months, 1,00,000 IU for 6–12 months and 2,00,000 IU above 12 months, given on day 1 and day 2.

B. Ear problem Assess – ear pain; ear discharge and for how long; look for pus draining from the ear; feel for tender swelling behind the ear.

Classify and treat

  • Mastoiditis (pink) – tender swelling behind the ear – first dose of antibiotic, paracetamol for pain, refer urgently.
  • Acute ear infection (yellow) – pus seen draining from the ear for less than 14 days, or ear pain – oral amoxicillin for 5 days, paracetamol for pain, dry the ear by wicking, follow-up in 5 days.
  • Chronic ear infection (yellow) – pus draining for 14 days or more – dry the ear by wicking, topical antibiotic (quinolone) ear drops, follow-up in 5 days (refer for hearing assessment).
  • No ear infection (green) – no additional treatment.
  • Wicking – roll a clean, absorbent cloth or tissue into a wick, insert into the ear, remove when wet and replace; repeat until the wick comes out dry; do this 3 times daily; nothing else is put in the ear, and the child should not swim.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Accurate temperature recording, performing RDTs, giving first doses, teaching mothers to give drugs, Vitamin A and wicking at home, and ensuring follow-up.

Conclusion In IMNCI, fever is classified as very severe febrile disease, malaria or fever without malaria, and measles as severe complicated, with eye or mouth complications, or uncomplicated, each with specific treatment including Vitamin A. Ear problems are classified as mastoiditis (refer), acute ear infection (amoxicillin and wicking) or chronic ear infection (wicking and quinolone drops).

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the IMNCI assessment of malnutrition and anaemia, immunisation status and feeding in a sick child.
answer_html:
Introduction Malnutrition and anaemia are the hidden causes behind many child deaths. IMNCI requires that every sick child be checked for malnutrition, anaemia, immunisation status and feeding, whatever the reason for the visit.

A. Malnutrition Look and feel

  • Visible severe wasting, oedema of both feet (bilateral pitting oedema).
  • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) in children 6–59 months.
  • Weight-for-height/length (z-score) and weight-for-age on the growth chart.
  • For children with severe acute malnutrition – check for medical complications (danger signs, pneumonia, dehydration, severe anaemia) and do the appetite test with ready-to-use therapeutic food where available.

Classify and treat

  • Complicated severe acute malnutrition (pink) – oedema of both feet, or MUAC below 11.5 cm or weight-for-height below –3 SD with a medical complication or failed appetite test – prevent low blood sugar, keep warm, first dose of antibiotic, refer to a Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC) or hospital.
  • Uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition (yellow) – the same anthropometric criteria, without complications and with good appetite – community-based management where available, antibiotics, feeding counselling, close follow-up (weekly).
  • Moderate acute malnutrition (yellow) – MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm or weight-for-height between –3 and –2 SD – assess feeding and counsel the mother, supplementary nutrition through the Anganwadi (ICDS), follow-up in 14–30 days.
  • No acute malnutrition (green) – praise the mother; feeding advice if the child is below 2 years.

B. Anaemia Look – palmar pallor (compare the child's palm with your own and with other children).

  • Severe anaemia (pink) – severe palmar pallor – refer urgently.
  • Anaemia (yellow) – some palmar pallor – give iron (IFA syrup) for 14 days and follow-up, albendazole if the child is 1 year or older and has not had a dose in 6 months, antimalarial if the malaria test is positive, feeding advice.
  • No anaemia (green) – routine IFA prophylaxis under Anemia Mukt Bharat.

C. Immunisation status and Vitamin A

  • Check the MCP card; give all vaccines that are due – the only exception is a child being referred urgently (who is immunised at the referral facility); illness, mild fever, diarrhoea or malnutrition are not contraindications.
  • Give Vitamin A if due (from 9 months, every 6 months up to 5 years).

D. Feeding assessment and counselling (for children below 2 years, children with anaemia or malnutrition, and when feeding problems are suspected)

  • Ask – breastfeeding (frequency, at night), other foods and fluids (type, frequency, how given – bottle or cup), the child's own serving, who feeds the child, changes in feeding during illness.
  • Identify feeding problems – not breastfeeding enough, using a feeding bottle, thin or watery foods, too few meals, no active feeding.
  • Advise according to age – exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months; from 6 months, continued breastfeeding with thick, energy-dense complementary foods (mashed rice and dal with ghee or oil, vegetables, eggs), increasing in quantity and frequency with age; feed actively and patiently; extra meal daily for 2 weeks after illness.

Conclusion Every sick child under IMNCI is assessed for malnutrition (visible wasting, bilateral oedema, MUAC and weight-for-height – complicated SAM is referred to an NRC), anaemia (palmar pallor – severe anaemia is referred, some pallor is treated with iron and deworming), immunisation and Vitamin A status (all due doses given), and feeding problems (age-appropriate counselling) – so that each visit also prevents future illness.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the counselling of the mother in IMNCI.
answer_html:
Introduction Counselling is the step that makes treatment work at home. A mother who understands how to give medicines, feed and give fluids, and when to return, can save her child's life. IMNCI therefore makes counselling the mother an essential step in every visit.

1. Communication skills (the key steps)

  • Ask and listen – find out what the mother is doing and what her problems are.
  • Praise – praise her for what she is doing well (breastfeeding, coming early).
  • Advise – give relevant, simple advice; use local language and practical examples; demonstrate where possible.
  • Check understanding – ask open questions ("How will you give this medicine?") rather than questions answered by yes or no.
  • Use the mother's card – a picture card that reminds her of feeding, fluids and danger signs.

2. Teaching the mother to give oral drugs at home

  • Show the drug and explain the dose, how often, and for how many days; give the first dose in the clinic; demonstrate how to crush and mix a tablet or measure syrup; label and package the drug; explain to finish the course even if the child improves; check her understanding.
  • Teach treatment of local infections – wicking the ear, cleaning eyes and applying ointment, treating mouth ulcers, the umbilicus or skin pustules.

3. Advice on feeding

  • Exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months; continued breastfeeding with complementary foods from 6 months; age-appropriate frequency and amounts; active feeding; hygiene in food preparation.
  • During illness – continue feeding; offer small, frequent feeds; breastfeed more often; after illness – one extra meal a day for at least 2 weeks.

4. Advice on fluids

  • Increase fluids during any illness; for diarrhoea, give ORS and other fluids as in Plan A; continue breastfeeding more often and for longer.

5. When to return

  • Immediately if the child – is not able to drink or breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever; for a child with cough or cold – fast or difficult breathing; for diarrhoea – blood in stool or drinking poorly.
  • For a young infant – breastfeeding or drinking poorly, becomes sicker, develops fever or feels cold, fast or difficult breathing, diarrhoea with blood, yellow palms and soles.
  • Follow-up visits – on the date given (for example 2 days for pneumonia, dysentery and malaria; 5 days for persistent diarrhoea or ear infection; 14 days for anaemia or feeding problems).
  • Next immunisation date.

6. Counselling the mother about her own health

  • Her nutrition and rest, treatment of her own illness, breast problems, family planning and birth spacing, her immunisation (Td), and support from the family.

7. Barriers and how to overcome them

  • Shyness, illiteracy, belief in traditional practices, family pressure; overcome them by respect, simple words, demonstration, involving family members and repeating key messages.

Conclusion IMNCI counselling uses the skills of asking and listening, praising, advising and checking understanding, supported by the mother's card. The mother is taught to give oral drugs and treat local infections, to feed and give extra fluids during and after illness, to recognise when to return immediately and when to come for follow-up, and to care for her own health.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the implementation of IMNCI.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses and ANMs are the backbone of IMNCI in India – at sub-centres, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, PHCs, CHCs and first referral units, and during home visits.

1. Case management at the facility

  • Assess, classify, identify treatment, treat, counsel and follow up sick young infants and children using the IMNCI chart booklet and recording forms.
  • Give first doses of drugs, ORS and zinc, Vitamin A, IFA and deworming; perform RDTs for malaria; treat local infections.

2. Home-based care

  • Home visits to newborns (with ASHAs under HBNC) – assess for danger signs, warmth, breastfeeding, cord care; extra visits for LBW babies.
  • Follow up children after illness or discharge.

3. Referral

  • Identify children with pink classifications, give pre-referral treatment, keep the child warm, prevent low blood sugar, write a referral note, arrange transport (national ambulance service) and follow up on the outcome.

4. Counselling and health education

  • Counsel mothers on feeding, fluids, home care and when to return; educate families and communities on key practices – exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding, immunisation, hand washing, sanitation, use of ORS, bed nets, recognising danger signs early.

5. Facility-based IMNCI

  • In first referral units, nurses provide emergency triage, oxygen, IV fluids, feeding of severely malnourished children (in NRCs) and monitoring of admitted children, as per F-IMNCI protocols.

6. Training and supervision

  • Train and supervise ASHAs and Anganwadi workers; conduct on-the-job mentoring; ensure correct use of charts.

7. Logistics

  • Ensure availability of drugs (amoxicillin, gentamicin, ORS, zinc, antimalarials, Vitamin A, IFA, albendazole), equipment (timer or watch with a second hand, weighing scale, MUAC tape, thermometer, pulse oximeter) and forms; maintain stock registers.

8. Records, reports and monitoring

  • Maintain IMNCI recording forms, registers and follow-up lists; report in HMIS; track indicators (number of sick children managed, referrals, follow-up completion, deaths); participate in child death reviews.

9. Coordination and community participation

  • Coordinate with medical officers, ICDS, schools and Panchayati Raj institutions; use Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days and mothers' meetings to promote child health.

Conclusion The nurse implements IMNCI through facility and home-based case management, pre-referral treatment and referral, counselling and community education, facility-based care, training and supervision of community workers, logistics management, record keeping and coordination – making IMNCI available to children close to their homes.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: List the general danger signs in IMNCI.
answer_html:
General danger signs (child aged 2 months to 5 years)

  1. Not able to drink or breastfeed.
  2. Vomits everything.
  3. Has had convulsions during this illness.
  4. Lethargic or unconscious.
  5. Convulsing now. How each sign is checked – not able to drink or breastfeed: the child is too weak to suck or swallow when offered the breast or a drink; vomits everything: the child cannot hold anything down at all; lethargic: drowsy, not alert, not interested in what is happening; unconscious: cannot be wakened. A child with any general danger sign has a serious problem and needs urgent pre-referral treatment and referral to hospital; the assessment is completed quickly so that referral is not delayed.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: What are the respiratory rate cut-offs for fast breathing in IMNCI?
answer_html:
Fast breathing according to age (count for one full minute in a calm child)

  • Young infant (below 2 months) – 60 breaths per minute or more (repeat the count if 60 or more; if the second count is also 60 or more, the infant has fast breathing).
  • Child aged 2 months up to 12 months – 50 breaths per minute or more.
  • Child aged 12 months up to 5 years – 40 breaths per minute or more. Fast breathing is a sign of pneumonia; in a young infant it is a sign of possible serious bacterial infection.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: How is Plan B (some dehydration) given under IMNCI?
answer_html:
Plan B – treatment of some dehydration with ORS in the clinic

  1. Give ORS about 75 mL/kg over 4 hours (use the child's weight; if weight is not known, use the age chart – for example 200–400 mL below 4 months, 400–700 mL for 4–12 months, 700–900 mL for 12 months–2 years, 900–1,400 mL for 2–5 years).
  2. Give more if the child wants more; give frequent small sips from a cup or spoon; if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly.
  3. Continue breastfeeding; start zinc.
  4. Reassess after 4 hours – classify again and move to Plan A (no dehydration), continue Plan B, or Plan C (severe dehydration).

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI)
question: What do the colours pink, yellow and green indicate in IMNCI?
answer_html:
In IMNCI, classifications are colour-coded to show the severity of illness and the action needed:

  • Pink – severe classification – needs urgent pre-referral treatment and referral to hospital (e.g. severe pneumonia or very severe disease, severe dehydration, possible serious bacterial infection, severe anaemia).
  • Yellow – needs specific treatment at the health facility or at home, such as an oral antibiotic, antimalarial, ORS (Plan B), iron, with follow-up (e.g. pneumonia, some dehydration, malaria, acute ear infection).
  • Green – no specific medical treatment; the mother is advised about home care (e.g. cough or cold, no dehydration).

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Master Aarav, a 7-year-old boy, is admitted with repeated attacks of sore throat, fever and difficulty in swallowing, and is diagnosed with chronic tonsillitis. He is posted for tonsillectomy. (a) Define tonsillitis and explain its causes and clinical features in children. (4 marks) (b) Explain the complications of tonsillitis in children and the indications for tonsillectomy. (3 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative preparation and post-operative nursing care of Aarav. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Positioning a child after tonsillectomy
labels: child lying on the side (semi-prone) with the head turned to one side and slightly lower than the chest

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and clinical features (4 marks) Definition Tonsillitis is inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually as part of an infection of the pharynx (tonsillopharyngitis). The tonsils are lymphoid tissue that is largest between about 3 and 7 years of age, which is why tonsillitis is so common in school-going children. It may be acute, recurrent acute (repeated attacks, as in Aarav) or chronic (persistent infection with enlarged or scarred tonsils).

Causes

  • Viruses (the most common cause, especially below 3 years) – adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza, Coxsackie virus and Epstein–Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).
  • Bacteria – group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is the most important bacterial cause in school-age children; others are Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae; diphtheria must be remembered in unimmunised children (greyish membrane).
  • Predisposing factors – crowding in homes and schools, poor oral hygiene and dental caries, malnutrition, exposure to tobacco smoke and smoke from wood or dung fuel, allergic rhinitis, and incomplete courses of antibiotics.

Clinical features in children

  • Sore throat and pain on swallowing; a young child may simply refuse feeds, drool or cry while eating.
  • Fever, often high, with malaise, headache and irritability.
  • Abdominal pain and vomiting – common in children with streptococcal sore throat.
  • Referred ear pain.
  • Enlarged, red tonsils, sometimes with yellowish exudate in the crypts (follicular tonsillitis).
  • Tender, enlarged jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph nodes below the angle of the jaw.
  • Bad breath and coated tongue.
  • In chronic tonsillitis and adenotonsillar enlargement – repeated sore throats, persistent bad breath, snoring, mouth breathing and pauses in breathing during sleep, restless sleep, daytime sleepiness, bedwetting, poor attention and school performance, poor appetite and poor weight gain, and a muffled voice.

Investigations – throat swab culture or rapid antigen test for streptococcus, complete blood count, ASO titre (evidence of past streptococcal infection) and, before surgery, Hb, bleeding and clotting tests.

Medical treatment of an acute attack (in brief) – rest, plenty of cold fluids and soft food, paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever (never aspirin in children – Reye syndrome), warm saline gargles for an older child, and for streptococcal infection oral penicillin V or amoxicillin for a full 10 days (azithromycin if allergic). Completing the 10-day course is what prevents rheumatic fever.

(b) Complications and indications for tonsillectomy (3 marks) Complications

  1. Suppurative (local) complications
    • Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – more common in older children and adolescents (severe one-sided throat pain, trismus, "hot potato" voice).
    • Retropharyngeal abscess – mainly in children below 5 years, whose retropharyngeal lymph nodes are still present (fever, drooling, neck stiffness, noisy breathing).
    • Parapharyngeal abscess, acute otitis media, sinusitis and cervical lymphadenitis.
  2. Non-suppurative (post-streptococcal) complications
    • Acute rheumatic fever about 2–3 weeks after an untreated streptococcal sore throat, which may lead to rheumatic heart disease.
    • Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis about 1–2 weeks after the infection (smoky urine, puffiness of the face, hypertension).
    • Scarlet fever.
  3. Complications of chronic enlargement – obstructive sleep apnoea, poor growth, behavioural and learning problems and, rarely, pulmonary hypertension; feeding difficulty; repeated school absence.

Indications for tonsillectomy in children

  • Obstructive sleep-disordered breathing (sleep apnoea) due to enlarged tonsils and adenoids – now the commonest indication in children.
  • Recurrent tonsillitis that is frequent and well documented (for example seven or more attacks in one year, five or more a year for two years, or three or more a year for three years – the Paradise criteria), causing school absence.
  • Peritonsillar abscess, especially if repeated.
  • Chronic tonsillitis not responding to treatment; suspected tumour (one-sided enlargement – rare).
  • Surgery is usually postponed for 2–3 weeks after an acute attack, and is generally avoided in the presence of a bleeding disorder, anaemia or an uncontrolled illness.

(c) Pre-operative preparation and post-operative nursing care of Aarav (8 marks) A. Pre-operative preparation

  1. Psychological preparation suited to his age
    • A 7-year-old thinks in concrete terms – explain honestly and simply, with pictures, dolls or a teddy bear, what he will see, hear and feel (gown, cap, mask, the "special sleep", waking up with a sore throat).
    • Therapeutic play – let him handle a mask and stethoscope; show the ward and recovery area if possible.
    • Tell him that his throat will hurt for some days, that he will get medicine and cold drinks, and that a parent will be with him.
    • Avoid frightening words ("cut", "put to sleep"); encourage questions; allow a favourite toy to go with him.
    • Allow a parent to stay until induction and in the recovery room; explain the plan of care to the parents.
  2. Assessment
    • History of a recent sore throat, fever or cough – inform the surgeon, as surgery may be postponed.
    • History of bleeding in the child or family, and of aspirin or other drug use.
    • Loose milk (deciduous) teeth – common at this age; note and report them, as a loose tooth can be dislodged and aspirated during intubation.
    • Allergies, weight (for drug doses), baseline vital signs and history of snoring or sleep apnoea (such children need closer breathing observation after surgery).
  3. Investigations – Hb, total and differential count, bleeding and clotting time, PT/INR, urine examination, blood grouping and cross-matching.
  4. Fasting as instructed by the anaesthetist – usually no solid food or milk for about 6 hours, and clear fluids allowed until 1–2 hours before anaesthesia; avoid unnecessarily long fasting, which makes children hypoglycaemic, dehydrated and irritable.
  5. Consent – written informed consent from the parents or legal guardian, with Aarav's assent after an age-appropriate explanation.
  6. Physical preparation – bath and clean gown, mouth care, removal of ornaments, identification band, recording of weight and vital signs, local anaesthetic cream on the cannulation site (atraumatic care), pre-medication as ordered (e.g. oral midazolam for anxiety), and emptying the bladder before shifting.

B. Immediate post-operative care

  1. Position – the tonsillar (semi-prone) position until fully awake: lying on his side, head turned to one side and slightly lower than the chest, with a pillow under the chest – so that blood and saliva drain out of the mouth and are not aspirated. When awake, sit him up (semi-Fowler's position).
  2. Airway – keep suction ready; suction gently from the mouth only, without touching the tonsillar beds; monitor respiratory rate, SpO2 and colour; watch for stridor or laryngospasm; children with sleep apnoea need continuous pulse oximetry on the first night.
  3. Watch for haemorrhage – the most serious complication
    • Primary/reactionary haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours; secondary haemorrhage usually between the 5th and 10th day (infection and separation of the slough).
    • Signs in a child – frequent swallowing (the earliest and most important sign, especially when asleep), restlessness, clearing the throat, pallor, rising pulse, fresh blood in the mouth or nose, and vomiting of dark (swallowed) blood. A fall in blood pressure is a late sign in children.
    • Action – inform the surgeon at once, keep the child on his side and calm, suction, maintain the IV line, monitor vital signs every 15 minutes, send blood for grouping and cross-matching, and prepare for return to the operation theatre.
  4. Vital signs – every 15 minutes until stable, then half-hourly and hourly; temperature 4-hourly.
  5. Pain relief
    • Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen as prescribed; assess pain with an age-appropriate tool such as the Wong–Baker FACES scale.
    • Codeine is not used in children after tonsillectomy (danger of fatal breathing depression in some children who metabolise it very fast).
    • Ice collar or cold compress over the neck, distraction with stories or cartoons, and the parent's presence.
  6. Fluids and diet
    • When fully awake and swallowing well, start sips of cold water, then cold fluids; avoid red or brown coloured drinks (blood is difficult to recognise) and citrus juices (sting).
    • Then soft, cool foods – ice cream, custard, jelly, curd rice, mashed banana – moving on to normal soft food as tolerated; eating and swallowing actually help healing and reduce pain.
    • Avoid hot, spicy and rough foods (chips, toast) for about 2 weeks.
    • Continue IV fluids until he drinks adequately; keep an intake–output chart and watch for dehydration (dry mouth, less urine).
  7. Prevent strain on the operation site – discourage coughing, clearing the throat, vigorous gargling, blowing the nose forcefully and drinking through straws in the first days.
  8. Mouth care – rinse the mouth gently with water after feeds; gentle tooth brushing.
  9. Nausea and vomiting – antiemetic as ordered; observe the vomitus for blood.
  10. Explain normal findings to the parents – a white or yellowish layer (slough) over the tonsil beds from the second day, bad breath for about a week, ear pain and a slight change in voice are normal and not signs of infection.

C. Discharge teaching for Aarav's parents

  • Rest at home for about a week; keep him away from school for about 10–14 days and from crowded places and people with colds.
  • Give pain medicines regularly as prescribed; no aspirin.
  • Give plenty of fluids and soft food as advised.
  • Report immediately – any bleeding from the mouth or nose (even a little), frequent swallowing, vomiting of blood, fever above 38.5 °C, refusal to drink, or reduced urine. Explain that bleeding is most likely around the 5th to 10th day.
  • Follow-up visit after about one week.
  • Good oral hygiene and hand washing; treat future sore throats early and complete antibiotic courses.

Nursing diagnoses (examples)

  1. Fear and anxiety (child and parents) related to hospitalisation and surgery.
  2. Risk for aspiration and ineffective airway clearance related to blood and secretions after surgery.
  3. Risk for bleeding related to the surgical wound.
  4. Acute pain related to the operation.
  5. Risk for deficient fluid volume related to painful swallowing.
  6. Deficient knowledge of the parents regarding home care.

Nursing importance

  • Careful age-appropriate preparation, close watch for frequent swallowing and other early signs of bleeding, safe pain relief and clear teaching of parents make tonsillectomy in children safe, and timely treatment of streptococcal sore throat protects children from rheumatic heart disease.

Conclusion Tonsillitis is inflammation of the palatine tonsils, common in school children, caused by viruses and by group A streptococcus. It may lead to abscesses, rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis and, when the tonsils stay enlarged, sleep apnoea. Tonsillectomy is indicated for sleep-disordered breathing, frequent documented attacks and peritonsillar abscess. For Aarav, nursing care includes honest age-appropriate preparation with play, assessment of infection, bleeding risk and loose teeth, correct fasting and consent; after surgery – the tonsillar position, airway care, close watch for haemorrhage (frequent swallowing), regular paracetamol and ibuprofen without codeine, cold fluids and soft diet, and thorough discharge teaching for the parents.

question: (a) What is pneumonia? Explain the common causative organisms of pneumonia in children according to age. (3 marks) (b) Describe the clinical features of pneumonia in infants and children and the assessment of its severity. (4 marks) (c) Prepare a nursing care plan for a child admitted with severe pneumonia. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Signs of pneumonia in a young child
labels: count breaths for one full minute (fast breathing by age)
lethargy; pulse oximeter on the finger or toe showing SpO2

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causative organisms (3 marks) Definition Pneumonia is acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma – the alveoli and the smallest airways – usually due to infection, in which the alveoli fill with inflammatory fluid and cells and gas exchange is impaired. Pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in children below 5 years in India and the world.

Types

  • Bronchopneumonia (patchy, around the bronchioles) – commonest in infants and young children.
  • Lobar pneumonia (consolidation of a whole lobe) – more in older children.
  • Interstitial pneumonia – viral and Mycoplasma infections.
  • Aspiration pneumonia – children with feeding difficulty, cerebral palsy, or after kerosene ingestion (hydrocarbon pneumonitis).

Common organisms according to age

  • Newborns (first month) – group B streptococcus, E. coli and other Gram-negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, Listeria.
  • 1–3 months – respiratory viruses (RSV), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis (afebrile pneumonia), Bordetella pertussis, S. aureus.
  • 3 months to 5 years – viruses are most common (RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus); the commonest bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae type b; S. aureus after measles or influenza (abscesses, pneumatoceles, empyema).
  • 5 years and above – Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and S. pneumoniae.
  • Any age – Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Pneumocystis jirovecii in HIV-infected infants.

Risk factors – low birth weight and prematurity, malnutrition, lack of exclusive breastfeeding, incomplete immunisation (measles, pertussis, Hib, pneumococcal vaccine), indoor air pollution (wood or dung smoke, tobacco smoke), overcrowding, Vitamin A and zinc deficiency, HIV infection and congenital heart disease.

(b) Clinical features and assessment of severity (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Cough and fever (fever may be absent in young infants, who may be hypothermic).
  • Fast breathing – the most sensitive sign; count for one full minute when the child is calm: 60 or more below 2 months, 50 or more at 2–12 months, 40 or more at 1–5 years.
  • Lower chest wall indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting (infants), head nodding, use of accessory muscles.
  • Poor feeding or inability to breastfeed, vomiting, irritability or lethargy; apnoea in young infants.
  • Central cyanosis in severe disease.
  • On examination – reduced air entry, crackles, bronchial breathing over consolidation and dullness on percussion; abdominal pain in lower lobe pneumonia and neck stiffness in upper lobe pneumonia in older children.
  • Mycoplasma (atypical) pneumonia – gradual onset, headache, sore throat, dry cough and few chest signs.

Assessment of severity

  • Pneumonia – cough or difficult breathing with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, without danger signs – oral amoxicillin and home care.
  • Severe pneumonia – cough or difficult breathing with any general danger sign (not able to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness), central cyanosis or SpO2 below 90%, stridor in a calm child, or severe respiratory distress (grunting, very severe chest indrawing) – hospital admission.
  • Other reasons for admission – age below 2 months, severe malnutrition, dehydration, failure of oral treatment, and complications (effusion, empyema).

Investigations – pulse oximetry (essential), complete blood count, CRP, chest X-ray (consolidation, effusion, pneumatoceles), blood culture, blood gases in severe cases, serum electrolytes, gastric aspirate or sputum for TB (CBNAAT) when suspected, nasopharyngeal swab for viruses, and HIV testing when indicated.

Medical management (in brief)

  • Oxygen when SpO2 is below 90% or the child has emergency signs.
  • Antibiotics as prescribed – for severe pneumonia, injectable ampicillin (or penicillin) with gentamicin, with ceftriaxone as an alternative; cloxacillin when Staphylococcus is suspected; azithromycin for atypical pneumonia.
  • Fluids (avoiding overload), paracetamol for fever, bronchodilator if there is wheeze, and chest tube drainage for empyema.

(c) Nursing care plan for a child with severe pneumonia (8 marks) 1. Impaired gas exchange related to inflammation and fluid in the alveoli

  • Goal – the child maintains SpO2 of at least 92–95%, with pink colour and less distress.
  • Interventions
    • Place the child in a propped-up position (head and chest raised about 30°; an infant can be held upright on the mother's lap); loosen clothing.
    • Give humidified oxygen as prescribed – nasal prongs are preferred (about 0.5–1 L/min in young infants and 1–2 L/min in older infants and children), or a face mask; use the correct size.
    • Monitor respiratory rate, chest indrawing, grunting, heart rate, colour and SpO2 at least every 1–2 hours, and continuously in severe distress.
    • Minimal handling and clustering of care to reduce oxygen demand.
  • Evaluation – breathing slower and easier, SpO2 maintained.

2. Ineffective airway clearance related to secretions

  • Clear the nose with saline drops and gentle suction, especially before feeds (infants breathe through the nose).
  • Change position 2-hourly; ensure good hydration to keep secretions thin.
  • Encourage older children to cough and take deep breaths – blowing bubbles or a pinwheel makes it a game.
  • Chest physiotherapy is not routinely needed in acute pneumonia.

3. Hyperthermia related to infection

  • Monitor temperature 4-hourly; light clothing; tepid sponging with lukewarm (not cold) water; paracetamol as prescribed; extra fluids.
  • Watch for febrile convulsions in children of 6 months to 5 years.

4. Risk for deficient fluid volume and imbalanced nutrition related to fast breathing and poor intake

  • Continue breastfeeding in small, frequent feeds.
  • If the child is in severe distress or cannot feed, give expressed breast milk by nasogastric tube or IV fluids as ordered – do not force oral feeds (risk of aspiration).
  • Avoid fluid overload (severe pneumonia may cause fluid retention); maintain an intake–output chart and daily weight; check urine output.
  • After recovery, give an extra meal daily for at least 2 weeks.

5. Fatigue and activity intolerance related to increased work of breathing

  • Provide rest in a quiet environment; plan care to allow sleep; allow quiet play (stories, music) as the child improves.

6. Risk for complications – empyema, pneumothorax, respiratory failure, septic shock, convulsions

  • Report increasing distress, sudden worsening, one-sided reduced breath sounds, cyanosis, drowsiness or poor perfusion at once; keep resuscitation equipment ready; care of a chest drain if inserted.
  • Give antibiotics exactly on time and watch for side effects (gentamicin – check urine output).

7. Anxiety of the child and parents

  • Explain procedures; allow parents to stay and take part in care; comfort the child with favourite toys.

8. Infection control – hand hygiene, droplet precautions where required, and separation from other high-risk children.

9. Deficient knowledge of the parents – health education before discharge

  • Complete the full course of antibiotics; recognise fast breathing, chest indrawing and inability to feed and return immediately; follow-up after 2–3 days.
  • Prevention – the "Protect, Prevent, Treat" approach (WHO–UNICEF):
    • Protect – exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, good complementary feeding, Vitamin A.
    • Prevent – complete immunisation (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, pentavalent vaccine with Hib and pertussis, measles–rubella vaccine), hand washing, clean cooking fuel and a smoke-free home, avoiding overcrowding.
    • Treat – early care-seeking, correct antibiotics and oxygen.

Nursing importance

  • Correct counting of the respiratory rate, use of pulse oximetry, careful oxygen therapy and feeding, and teaching mothers the signs of pneumonia are the nurse's main tools in reducing pneumonia deaths in children.

Conclusion Pneumonia is acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma and the leading infectious killer of children below 5 years. The organisms vary with age – group B streptococcus and Gram-negative bacilli in newborns, viruses, pneumococcus and Hib in young children, and Mycoplasma in school children. It presents with cough, fever, fast breathing and chest indrawing, and severe pneumonia is recognised by danger signs, cyanosis or low SpO2. Nursing care focuses on oxygenation, airway clearance, fever control, safe feeding and fluids, rest, early detection of complications, parental support and prevention through breastfeeding, immunisation and clean air.

question: (a) Define oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula and list their types. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing management of a newborn with tracheo-oesophageal fistula. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula (Gross classification)
labels: A – atresia without fistula (about 8%); B – atresia with proximal fistula (rare); C – proximal blind pouch with distal fistula to the trachea (most common
about 85%); D – atresia with both proximal and distal fistulas (rare); E – H-type fistula without atresia (about 4%)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (3 marks) Definitions

  • Oesophageal atresia (OA) is a congenital interruption of the oesophagus, in which the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch and is not continuous with the lower oesophagus and stomach.
  • Tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal communication between the trachea and the oesophagus.
  • The two usually occur together. The defect arises in about the 4th week of fetal life from faulty separation of the foregut into trachea and oesophagus. It occurs in about 1 in 3,000–4,500 live births; about one-third of affected babies are preterm or of low birth weight.

Types (Gross classification)

  • Type A – oesophageal atresia without fistula (pure atresia, about 8%); the gap between the two ends is usually long.
  • Type B – atresia with a proximal fistula (upper pouch to trachea) – rare.
  • Type C – proximal blind pouch with a distal fistula between the trachea and the lower oesophagus – the most common (about 85%).
  • Type D – atresia with both proximal and distal fistulas – rare.
  • Type E (H-type) – fistula without atresia (about 4%).

Associated anomalies – present in about half the babies; the VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies), cardiac defects being the most important; also chromosomal disorders (trisomy 18, 21).

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks) Antenatal clues – polyhydramnios (the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid), a small or absent stomach bubble on ultrasound.

Clinical features at birth

  • Excessive frothy saliva bubbling from the mouth and nose, and drooling – the earliest sign; saliva collects in the blind pouch.
  • The "3 Cs" with the first feed – choking, coughing and cyanosis – as milk overflows from the pouch into the trachea; feeds are regurgitated immediately.
  • Respiratory distress – from aspiration of saliva from above and reflux of gastric acid through the distal fistula into the lungs (aspiration pneumonia).
  • Abdominal distension in type C – air passes from the trachea through the fistula into the stomach, especially when the baby cries or is ventilated.
  • Scaphoid, gasless abdomen in pure atresia (type A).
  • H-type fistula – no atresia; coughing and choking with feeds, recurrent pneumonia and abdominal distension, often diagnosed late.

Diagnosis

  1. Inability to pass an orogastric tube – a firm 10 Fr tube meets resistance about 10–12 cm from the gums. Every baby born after polyhydramnios, and every baby with excessive salivation, should have this check before the first feed.
  2. X-ray of chest and abdomen with the tube in place – the tube is seen coiled in the upper pouch; air in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal fistula, while a gasless abdomen indicates pure atresia. Contrast studies are avoided, as contrast can be aspirated.
  3. Screening for associated anomalies – echocardiography (also shows the side of the aortic arch, important for the surgical approach), renal ultrasound, X-rays of the spine and limbs, and examination of the anus.
  4. Bronchoscopy (often at the start of surgery) to locate the fistula; for an H-type fistula, a prone tube oesophagogram or bronchoscopy.

(c) Pre-operative and post-operative nursing management (8 marks) A. Pre-operative nursing management – goals: keep the airway clear, prevent aspiration pneumonia and maintain warmth, fluids and glucose.

  1. Keep the baby nil by mouth – no feeds of any kind.
  2. Continuous suction of the upper pouch with a double-lumen Replogle tube (about 10 Fr) connected to low, continuous suction; flush the irrigation lumen with small volumes of saline as per unit policy to keep it patent; check that it is working and record the amount and nature of secretions. If a Replogle tube is not available, suction the mouth and pouch every 10–15 minutes.
  3. Position – head and chest elevated about 30–45° (prone or supine) to reduce reflux of gastric juice through the fistula into the trachea; change position regularly.
  4. Respiratory care – monitor respiratory rate, effort, colour and SpO2; oxygen as needed; avoid bag-and-mask ventilation and CPAP where possible – air is forced through the fistula into the stomach, causing gross distension that splints the diaphragm and may perforate the stomach. If ventilation is unavoidable, it is done by an expert with gentle pressures.
  5. Warmth – radiant warmer or incubator; monitor temperature.
  6. IV fluids with dextrose; monitor blood glucose, electrolytes and urine output.
  7. Antibiotics as prescribed (to prevent or treat aspiration pneumonia); Vitamin K.
  8. Investigations and preparation – blood grouping and cross-matching, complete blood count, screening for associated anomalies; identification band; consent from the parents.
  9. Transport to a neonatal surgical centre in a transport incubator, with the Replogle tube on suction and the head raised, with a trained nurse or doctor.
  10. Support to the parents – explain the condition, the surgery and the good outcome; help the mother to express and store breast milk for later feeds.

Surgery (in brief)

  • Usually done within the first days when the baby is stable: through a right-sided thoracotomy (often extrapleural) or by thoracoscopy, the fistula is divided and closed and the two ends of the oesophagus are joined (primary end-to-end anastomosis). A fine transanastomotic tube is often left across the join for feeding.
  • Long-gap atresia (usually type A) – a gastrostomy is made for feeding, the upper pouch is kept on suction, and the ends are joined later (delayed primary anastomosis, after a few months of growth); if joining is not possible, an oesophageal replacement (gastric pull-up or colon interposition) is done, sometimes with a cervical oesophagostomy in the meantime.

B. Post-operative nursing management

  1. Respiratory care
    • Ventilator or oxygen care as needed; monitor SpO2, breath sounds and blood gases.
    • Suction only with a catheter marked to a measured length (to stop short of the anastomosis), since deep suction can damage the join.
    • Avoid hyperextension of the neck, which puts tension on the anastomosis; keep the head end raised.
  2. Chest drain care (if present) – closed system, record drainage; saliva or milky fluid in the drain, air leak or sudden respiratory distress suggests an anastomotic leak – report at once.
  3. Nutrition
    • Parenteral nutrition or feeds through the transanastomotic tube or gastrostomy as ordered; the transanastomotic tube must be well secured and never removed or reinserted blindly.
    • A contrast swallow is usually done around the 5th–7th day; if there is no leak, oral feeds are started slowly – small, frequent feeds of expressed breast milk, with the baby upright, watching for choking, coughing or cyanosis.
    • Give non-nutritive sucking (pacifier) to maintain the sucking reflex; in long-gap babies with an oesophagostomy, sham feeding helps them learn oral feeding.
  4. Gastrostomy care – keep the site clean and dry, check the tube's position, vent the tube for air, and record feeds.
  5. Pain relief, warmth, fluid balance and blood glucose – as for any neonatal surgery; maintain an intake–output chart.
  6. Wound care and infection prevention.
  7. Observe for complications
    • Anastomotic leak – early; fever, saliva in the drain, pneumothorax, sepsis.
    • Anastomotic stricture – common; difficulty in swallowing, drooling, choking and regurgitation of feeds; treated by oesophageal dilatation.
    • Recurrent fistula – coughing and choking with feeds, recurrent pneumonia.
    • Gastro-oesophageal reflux – very common; upright positioning, small feeds, medicines; fundoplication if severe.
    • Tracheomalacia – a characteristic barking ("TOF") cough, stridor, and sometimes sudden cyanotic or "dying" spells during feeds.
  8. Support and involvement of the parents – encourage holding, kangaroo care when stable, and participation in feeding.

C. Discharge teaching

  • Feeding technique – upright position, small and frequent feeds, burping, keeping the baby upright for 20–30 minutes after feeds.
  • Recognise choking, cyanosis, difficulty in swallowing and drooling (stricture or recurrent fistula) and seek help early; parents should learn infant CPR and the management of choking.
  • Care of the gastrostomy or oesophagostomy, if present.
  • Later, introduce solids carefully, cut food small and teach the child to chew well; avoid hard foods such as whole nuts.
  • Regular follow-up for growth, dilatations, reflux and breathing problems; immunisation as per schedule.

Nursing diagnoses (examples)

  1. Risk for aspiration related to the blind upper pouch and the fistula.
  2. Ineffective airway clearance related to excessive secretions.
  3. Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements related to inability to feed orally.
  4. Risk for infection related to aspiration and surgery.
  5. Anxiety and interrupted family processes related to a critically ill newborn.

Prognosis – survival is now over 90% in babies of good birth weight without major cardiac anomalies; low birth weight and serious heart defects reduce survival.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse is often the first to notice excessive frothy saliva or choking with the first feed. Passing an orogastric tube before the first feed in suspected babies, keeping the pouch on suction with the head raised, and avoiding bag-and-mask ventilation prevent aspiration pneumonia and save lives.

Conclusion Oesophageal atresia is a blind-ending upper oesophagus and TEF an abnormal connection between the trachea and oesophagus; type C (upper pouch with distal fistula) is the commonest. The newborn shows frothy saliva and choking, coughing and cyanosis with feeds, and the diagnosis is confirmed when an orogastric tube cannot be passed and is seen coiled on X-ray. Pre-operatively the baby is kept nil by mouth with continuous pouch suction (Replogle tube), head raised, warm and on IV fluids; after surgery, careful respiratory care with marked-length suction, chest drain and feeding-tube care, gradual feeding and watch for leak, stricture, reflux and tracheomalacia, with full parent teaching, ensure a good outcome.

unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: (a) Define juvenile (type 1) diabetes mellitus and explain its causes. (3 marks) (b) Describe its clinical features and diagnosis in children. (4 marks) (c) Explain the management and nursing care of a child with type 1 diabetes, including education of the child and family. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Insulin injection sites in a child
labels: back of the upper arms; rotation within each site to prevent lipohypertrophy; pinch-up of skin with a short needle in thin children

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Definition Type 1 (juvenile) diabetes mellitus is a chronic disorder in which autoimmune destruction of the beta cells of the pancreas leads to absolute insulin deficiency and hyperglycaemia. It is the commonest type of diabetes in children and adolescents; onset peaks around 4–6 years and 10–14 years (puberty), and the child needs insulin for life. India has one of the largest numbers of children with type 1 diabetes in the world.

Causes

  • Genetic susceptibility – certain HLA types (DR3, DR4); risk is higher in siblings and children of people with type 1 diabetes.
  • Autoimmunity – T-cell destruction of beta cells, marked by autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin and zinc transporter 8 antibodies) that may appear years before symptoms.
  • Environmental triggers – viral infections (enteroviruses such as Coxsackie B, congenital rubella) and other factors in genetically susceptible children.
  • Stages – stage 1: autoantibodies with normal glucose; stage 2: autoantibodies with abnormal glucose but no symptoms; stage 3: clinical diabetes.

Other types seen in children – type 2 diabetes in obese adolescents (with acanthosis nigricans, family history); monogenic diabetes – MODY (strong family history in several generations) and neonatal diabetes (onset before 6 months); secondary diabetes – in thalassaemia with iron overload, cystic fibrosis, fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes and drugs such as steroids.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia with weight loss in spite of eating well.
  • Bedwetting in a child who was previously dry (secondary nocturnal enuresis) – an important early clue.
  • Tiredness, irritability, poor school performance and behaviour change.
  • Recurrent infections – candidal nappy rash in toddlers, vulvovaginal candidiasis in girls, skin infections.
  • Blurred vision; poor growth if poorly controlled.
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis at first presentation is common (especially in young children and in India) – vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, fruity breath and drowsiness; it is often mistaken for gastroenteritis, pneumonia or an "acute abdomen".

Diagnosis

  • Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms, or
  • Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL, or
  • 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL in an oral glucose tolerance test (glucose 1.75 g/kg, maximum 75 g), or
  • HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (not needed in a symptomatic child).
  • Supporting tests – urine glucose and ketones, blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate), venous blood gas if unwell, autoantibodies, C-peptide (low).
  • At diagnosis, screen for associated autoimmune diseases – thyroid function (hypothyroidism) and coeliac antibodies.

(c) Management and nursing care (8 marks) Goals – near-normal blood glucose without frequent hypoglycaemia, normal growth, development and puberty, prevention of DKA and long-term complications, and a normal school and social life. ISPAD (2022) recommends HbA1c below 7% and time in the target glucose range above 70% where continuous monitoring is used.

1. Insulin therapy

  • Total daily dose – roughly 0.5–1.0 unit/kg/day in pre-pubertal children, rising to about 1.0–1.5 units/kg/day in puberty; it is lower in the early "honeymoon" phase.
  • Regimens
    • Basal–bolus (multiple daily injections) – a long-acting analogue (glargine, detemir, degludec) once daily as basal insulin (about 40–50% of the daily dose), plus rapid-acting insulin (lispro, aspart, glulisine) or regular insulin before each meal (bolus) – the preferred regimen, allowing flexible meals.
    • Twice-daily split-mixed regimen – a mixture of intermediate-acting (NPH) and regular insulin before breakfast (about two-thirds of the dose) and before dinner (one-third) – still used where resources are limited; needs regular meals and snacks.
    • Insulin pump (continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion), with or without automated (hybrid closed-loop) control, where available.
  • Injection technique for children
    • Use U-100 syringes with half-unit markings or pens with short (4 mm) needles; in thin children, lift a skin fold.
    • Sites – abdomen, thighs, buttocks and upper arms; rotate within a site to prevent lipohypertrophy (lumps that cause erratic absorption); do not inject into lumps.
    • Inject rapid-acting insulin 0–15 minutes and regular insulin about 20–30 minutes before meals.
  • Storage – unopened insulin in the refrigerator door (2–8 °C), never in the freezer; the vial or pen in use can be kept at room temperature (below about 25–30 °C) for about 4 weeks, away from sunlight; where there is no refrigerator, a clay pot (matka) with water keeps insulin cool in Indian summers; carry insulin in an insulated pouch when travelling.

2. Monitoring

  • Self-monitoring of blood glucose at least 4–6 times a day (before meals and at bedtime, and at 2–3 a.m. when needed), or continuous glucose monitoring (CGM); record in a diary.
  • Target glucose about 70–180 mg/dL; check ketones when glucose is above about 250 mg/dL or the child is ill.
  • HbA1c every 3 months; height, weight and pubertal stage at every visit.

3. Nutrition

  • No special "diabetic diet" – a healthy, balanced family diet with enough energy for growth; regular meals; whole grains, dals, vegetables, fruits, milk and curd; limit sugary drinks, sweets and fried snacks.
  • Carbohydrate counting (matching rapid-acting insulin to the carbohydrate in a meal) for children on basal–bolus or pumps; consistent meal timing and snacks on the split-mixed regimen.

4. Exercise

  • Daily physical activity of about 60 minutes is encouraged; check glucose before exercise, take extra carbohydrate or reduce insulin as advised, carry glucose tablets, and watch for delayed (night-time) hypoglycaemia after heavy exercise.

5. Hypoglycaemia (blood glucose below 70 mg/dL) – the commonest acute problem

  • Signs in children – shakiness, sweating, hunger, pallor, headache, sudden irritability, crying, unusual behaviour, poor concentration, nightmares; in severe cases convulsions and unconsciousness. Young children may not recognise or report symptoms.
  • Treatment – give fast-acting sugar (about 0.3 g/kg glucose) – glucose tablets, sugar or glucose dissolved in water, or fruit juice; recheck after 15 minutes and repeat if still low; then a snack.
  • Severe hypoglycaemia (unconscious or fitting) – nothing by mouth; glucagon injection (0.5 mg below 25 kg, 1 mg for heavier children) or nasal glucagon; IV dextrose in hospital.

6. Sick-day management – never stop insulin; check glucose and ketones every 2–3 hours, give extra fluids and extra rapid-acting insulin as advised, and seek help for persistent vomiting, high ketones, abdominal pain, fast breathing or drowsiness.

7. School and psychosocial care

  • A written school diabetes care plan; teachers trained to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia; permission for glucose checks, snacks, insulin and toilet visits; a hypoglycaemia kit at school; full participation in sports and trips.
  • Support for adjustment and emotional problems – fear of injections, diabetes-related distress, depression, disturbed eating and insulin omission in adolescents; peer support groups and diabetes camps.
  • Gradual transfer of self-care with age – parents manage toddlers; school-age children learn to test and recognise hypoglycaemia; adolescents take over injections and decisions, with guidance on risk-taking and alcohol.

8. Screening for complications

  • From about 11 years of age (or puberty) with 2–5 years of diabetes – yearly eye examination (retinopathy), urine albumin (nephropathy), blood pressure and lipids; foot examination in adolescents; thyroid and coeliac screening every 1–2 years.

Nursing care plan (main diagnoses)

  1. Risk for unstable blood glucose related to insulin, diet and activity – monitor glucose as ordered, give insulin accurately and on time, coordinate meals with insulin, recognise and treat hypoglycaemia promptly.
  2. Deficient knowledge (child and family) related to a new diagnosis – teach "survival skills" first (insulin injection, glucose testing, recognising and treating hypoglycaemia, sick-day rules, basic food plan), using demonstration and return demonstration; continue education at each visit.
  3. Fear and anxiety related to injections and a lifelong disease – practise on a doll, use fine needles, praise, involve the child in choosing sites.
  4. Risk for infection – hygiene, skin care, foot care, good glucose control.
  5. Disturbed body image and ineffective coping (adolescent) – listen, counsel, link with peers and support groups.

Nursing importance

  • Most of the care of a diabetic child happens at home and at school, so the nurse's teaching of injection technique, monitoring, hypoglycaemia management and sick-day rules decides how well the child grows and how often emergencies occur.

Conclusion Type 1 diabetes in children results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency. It presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and new bedwetting, often with DKA, and is diagnosed by blood glucose criteria. Management combines lifelong insulin (basal–bolus or split-mixed), regular monitoring with an HbA1c target below 7%, healthy family meals, exercise, prompt treatment of hypoglycaemia, sick-day rules, school support, psychosocial care and screening for complications – with the nurse educating and supporting the child and family at every step.

unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a defect in the diaphragm through which abdominal organs (stomach, intestines, spleen, part of the liver) herniate into the chest during fetal life, compressing the developing lungs. It occurs in about 1 in 3,000 births.

Types

  • Bochdalek hernia – posterolateral defect, about 85–90% of cases, mostly on the left side.
  • Morgagni hernia – anterior (retrosternal) defect; rare and often milder.
  • Central or hiatal defects – rare.

Pathophysiology

  • The herniated organs prevent normal growth of the lungs, causing pulmonary hypoplasia (small lungs with fewer airways and vessels) on both sides, more on the affected side, and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. These two problems, not the hernia itself, decide survival.

Clinical features

  • Often detected on antenatal ultrasound (stomach or bowel in the chest, polyhydramnios).
  • Severe respiratory distress and cyanosis at or soon after birth.
  • Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and barrel-shaped chest.
  • Reduced breath sounds on the affected side; bowel sounds heard in the chest.
  • Heart sounds shifted to the right in a left-sided hernia (mediastinal shift).

Diagnosis – chest X-ray shows loops of bowel in the chest, mediastinal shift and the tip of a nasogastric tube in the chest; echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension and heart defects.

Management

  1. Delivery in a tertiary centre when diagnosed antenatally.
  2. Immediate care at birth
    • Avoid bag-and-mask ventilation – it inflates the stomach and bowel in the chest and worsens lung compression.
    • Immediate endotracheal intubation and gentle ventilation with low pressures, accepting somewhat lower oxygen saturation and higher CO2 to avoid lung injury.
    • Insert a large orogastric/nasogastric tube on suction to decompress the stomach and bowel.
  3. Stabilisation – IV access (umbilical lines), fluids and glucose, sedation, minimal handling, warmth; treatment of pulmonary hypertension (inhaled nitric oxide, sildenafil), inotropes, high-frequency ventilation and ECMO in specialised centres.
  4. Surgery – delayed repair after the baby is stable (usually after a few days): the organs are returned to the abdomen and the defect is closed directly or with a patch.

Nursing care

  • Position – head and chest elevated; positioning the baby on the affected side allows the unaffected lung to expand.
  • Continuous monitoring of SpO2 (pre- and post-ductal), heart rate, blood pressure and blood gases; careful suctioning; maintain the gastric tube on suction.
  • Thermoregulation, fluid balance, blood glucose and pain relief; skin and eye care in the sedated baby.
  • After surgery – respiratory monitoring, wound care, gradual feeding (gastro-oesophageal reflux is common), watch for recurrence and infection.
  • Support to the parents – explain the condition and the uncertain course, encourage visiting and expressing breast milk.
  • Long-term follow-up – chronic lung disease, reflux and feeding problems, hearing and developmental assessment.

Conclusion CDH is herniation of abdominal organs into the chest through a diaphragmatic defect, usually left posterolateral (Bochdalek), causing pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension. It presents with respiratory distress at birth, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest. Management includes avoiding bag-and-mask ventilation, immediate intubation, gastric decompression, gentle ventilation and stabilisation before delayed surgical repair, with intensive nursing care and family support.

question: Explain croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis) in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis) is an acute viral infection of the larynx, trachea and bronchi, causing swelling below the vocal cords (subglottic oedema) and narrowing of the upper airway. It affects children of 6 months to 3 years (peak around 2 years), mostly in autumn and winter.

Cause – parainfluenza virus (type 1 commonest); also RSV, influenza, adenovirus, measles and SARS-CoV-2.

Why young children are affected – the subglottic area (cricoid ring) is the narrowest part of a child's airway, and even 1 mm of swelling greatly reduces the airway lumen and increases resistance.

Clinical features

  • 1–2 days of cold and mild fever, followed by:
  • Barking ("seal-like") cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor.
  • Respiratory distress – chest retractions, nasal flaring; worse at night and when the child cries or is agitated.
  • Usually improves within 2–3 days and resolves in about a week.

Assessment of severity

  • The Westley croup score (stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis and level of consciousness) grades croup as mild, moderate, severe or impending respiratory failure.
  • Stridor at rest, marked retractions, agitation, cyanosis or decreasing consciousness mean severe croup.
  • Warning – a child whose stridor and retractions decrease while he becomes tired, drowsy or pale may be exhausted and near respiratory failure, not improving.

Diagnosis – clinical; a neck X-ray (not routinely needed) shows the "steeple sign" of subglottic narrowing.

Management

  1. Keep the child calm – on the parent's lap, in a comfortable position; avoid distressing procedures (examining the throat with a spatula, unnecessary injections).
  2. Corticosteroids – a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15–0.6 mg/kg, as prescribed) for all grades; nebulised budesonide as an alternative.
  3. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) for moderate to severe croup – acts within minutes but wears off in about 2 hours, so the child must be observed for at least 2–3 hours afterwards.
  4. Humidified oxygen if SpO2 is low.
  5. Intubation (with a tube smaller than usual) and PICU care for impending respiratory failure.
  6. Antibiotics are not needed (viral illness); cool mist is not proven to help.

Nursing care

  • Monitor respiratory rate, stridor, retractions, heart rate (rising rate indicates hypoxia), SpO2, colour, restlessness and level of consciousness frequently.
  • Give medicines and nebulisation as ordered; record the response.
  • Hydration – frequent small drinks; IV fluids if the child cannot drink.
  • Paracetamol for fever; rest and cluster care; keep emergency airway equipment ready.
  • Teach parents – croup is often worse at night; keep the child calm; return at once if there is stridor at rest, difficulty in breathing, drooling, blue lips or drowsiness.

Conclusion Croup is a viral (mainly parainfluenza) infection causing subglottic swelling in children of 6 months to 3 years, with barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor. Management is keeping the child calm, oral dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline for moderate to severe cases, oxygen and close observation for signs of exhaustion.

question: Explain bronchiolitis in infants and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Bronchiolitis is an acute viral infection of the bronchioles (small airways) in children below 2 years (peak at 2–6 months), causing inflammation, swelling, mucus and cell debris that block the small airways, with air trapping and areas of collapse.

Cause – respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in most cases; also rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, adenovirus and influenza. It spreads by contact with secretions (hands, toys, surfaces) and droplets.

Infants at risk of severe disease – age below 3 months, prematurity, chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, Down syndrome, exposure to tobacco smoke and lack of breastfeeding.

Clinical features

  • 1–3 days of cold, cough and mild fever, then:
  • Fast breathing, chest retractions and nasal flaring.
  • Wheeze and fine crackles; hyperinflated chest.
  • Poor feeding (breathlessness and nasal blockage) and fewer wet nappies.
  • Apnoea – may be the first sign in young or preterm infants.
  • The illness is worst around days 3–5; the cough may last 2–3 weeks.

Diagnosis – clinical; pulse oximetry; nasopharyngeal swab for RSV (helps in cohorting); chest X-ray only if the diagnosis is unclear (hyperinflation, patchy collapse).

Management – mainly supportive

  1. Clear the nose – saline drops and gentle suction before feeds and as needed (avoid deep suction).
  2. Oxygen if SpO2 stays below about 90–92%; humidified high-flow nasal cannula or CPAP for moderate to severe distress; ventilation for repeated apnoea or respiratory failure.
  3. Feeding and hydration – small, frequent breastfeeds; nasogastric or orogastric feeds if the infant cannot feed enough; IV fluids if needed.
  4. Not recommended routinely – bronchodilators (salbutamol), adrenaline, corticosteroids, antibiotics (unless there is a bacterial infection) and chest physiotherapy.
  5. Position – head end slightly raised; loose clothing; minimal handling.

Nursing care

  • Monitor respiratory rate, work of breathing, SpO2, heart rate and temperature; apnoea monitoring in young and preterm infants.
  • Assess hydration – intake–output, wet nappies, weight.
  • Infection control – hand hygiene is the most important measure; contact and droplet precautions; cohort RSV-positive infants; clean toys and surfaces; restrict visitors with colds.
  • Support and teach the parents.
  • Discharge advice – return if there is fast or difficult breathing, feeding less than half the usual amount, few wet nappies, pauses in breathing or blue colour; avoid smoke exposure.

Prevention

  • Hand washing, breastfeeding, avoiding smoke and crowded places for young infants.
  • For high-risk infants – RSV monoclonal antibodies (palivizumab given monthly through the RSV season, or a single dose of a long-acting antibody such as nirsevimab) where available; maternal RSV vaccination in pregnancy is used in some countries.

Conclusion Bronchiolitis is a viral, mostly RSV, infection of the small airways in infants below 2 years, presenting after a cold with fast breathing, retractions, wheeze, crackles, poor feeding and sometimes apnoea. Treatment is supportive – nasal suction, oxygen, feeding support and monitoring – with strict hand hygiene to prevent spread and antibody prophylaxis for high-risk infants.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain the common upper respiratory tract infections in children and their nursing management.
tags: avoid cough and cold medicines under 2 years
answer_html:
Introduction Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are the most common illnesses of childhood – a young child may have 6–8 colds a year, especially after starting a crèche or school. They are mostly viral and self-limiting, but infants become distressed because they breathe mainly through the nose, and some children develop complications.

Common URTIs

  1. Common cold (acute nasopharyngitis) – rhinovirus and other viruses; nasal blockage and discharge, sneezing, mild fever, cough, irritability and difficulty in feeding in infants; lasts about 7–10 days.
  2. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis – sore throat, fever, painful swallowing; group A streptococcal infection needs a full 10-day antibiotic course to prevent rheumatic fever.
  3. Acute otitis media – common in infants and young children because their Eustachian tube is short, wide and horizontal; follows a cold; ear pain, pulling or rubbing the ear, crying at night, fever, irritability and discharge if the drum perforates. Complications – chronic ear discharge, hearing loss affecting speech development, mastoiditis.
  4. Sinusitis – in older children; nasal discharge or cough lasting more than 10 days, facial pain or headache.
  5. Acute laryngitis and croup – hoarseness, barking cough, stridor.

Nursing management
