  1. Assess – respiratory rate (count for one minute), chest indrawing, danger signs, temperature, hydration, ear discharge and feeding, to separate a simple cold from pneumonia or another serious illness.
  2. Keep the nose clear – saline nose drops and gentle suction with a bulb syringe before feeds and sleep; wipe the nose with a soft cloth; protect the skin around the nostrils.
  3. Position – head slightly raised for sleep; hold the infant upright for feeds.
  4. Fluids and feeding – continue breastfeeding, offer frequent small feeds and extra fluids.
  5. Fever and pain – paracetamol or ibuprofen as advised; tepid sponging; never aspirin (Reye syndrome).
  6. Avoid unnecessary medicines – over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are not given below 2 years (and are of little benefit in older children); antibiotics are not used for viral colds; honey soothes cough in children above 1 year; warm fluids (tulsi or ginger with honey) for older children.
  7. Ear care – analgesics, prescribed antibiotics for otitis media, dry the ear by wicking if there is discharge (nothing else put into the ear); no swimming until healed.
  8. Rest and a humid, smoke-free room.
  9. Prevent spread – hand washing, covering the mouth while coughing, disposal of tissues, keeping the sick child home from school or crèche until better.
  10. Health education – when to return – fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, inability to drink, high fever beyond 3 days, ear discharge, drowsiness or a stiff neck.

Prevention

  • Exclusive breastfeeding; avoid bottle-feeding in the lying position (bottle propping), which favours otitis media; avoid tobacco and kitchen smoke; good nutrition and Vitamin A; complete immunisation (pneumococcal, Hib, measles, influenza where recommended); hand hygiene.

Conclusion Common cold, pharyngitis, otitis media, sinusitis and laryngitis are the usual URTIs of childhood, mostly viral and self-limiting. Nursing management consists of careful assessment for pneumonia and danger signs, keeping the nose clear with saline and suction, fluids and feeding, safe fever and pain control without aspirin, avoiding cough-cold medicines in infants, ear care, prevention of spread and teaching parents when to return.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain the management of bronchial asthma in children, with special reference to inhaler devices and the asthma action plan.
answer_html:
Introduction Bronchial asthma is the most common chronic disease of childhood – a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways causing recurrent wheeze, cough (often at night or with exercise), breathlessness and chest tightness, which vary over time and are reversible.

Common triggers in children – viral colds (the commonest in young children), house dust mite, cockroaches, pollen, pets, tobacco and wood or dung smoke, mosquito coils and incense, cold air, exercise, strong smells and emotional upset.

Diagnosis – the history of recurrent symptoms and response to treatment; in children above about 5–6 years, spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction or variable peak flow; in younger children, diagnosis rests on the pattern of symptoms and a trial of controller medicine.

Long-term management (stepwise, as in GINA guidelines)

  • Reliever – salbutamol (short-acting beta-2 agonist) by inhaler for symptoms; in older children, inhaled corticosteroid–formoterol may be used as a reliever in some steps.
  • Controller – inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as budesonide or fluticasone, the mainstay; add a long-acting beta-agonist (with ICS) or montelukast at higher steps.
  • Treatment is stepped up if control is poor (after checking technique, adherence and triggers) and stepped down after about 3 months of good control; refer if not controlled.
  • Low-dose ICS has only a small effect on growth – the benefit far outweighs the risk; monitor height.

Inhaler devices suited to age

  • Below about 4 years – pressurised metered-dose inhaler (pMDI) with a spacer (valved holding chamber) and a face mask.
  • About 4–6 years – pMDI with a spacer and mouthpiece.
  • Above about 6 years – pMDI with spacer, or a dry powder inhaler if the child can inhale quickly and deeply.
  • Nebuliser – for severe attacks or when a spacer cannot be used; a pMDI with spacer is as effective as a nebuliser for most attacks.
  • Where a spacer is not available, a 500 mL plastic bottle modified as a spacer can be used.
  • Technique (pMDI with spacer and mask) – shake the inhaler; fit it to the spacer; place the mask firmly over the nose and mouth; press one puff; let the child take 5–6 normal breaths; wait about 30–60 seconds before the next puff; rinse the mouth (or give water) after ICS; wash the spacer with mild detergent and let it air-dry.

Acute attack (exacerbation)

  • Salbutamol by spacer (or nebuliser) repeated every 20 minutes in the first hour, oxygen to keep SpO2 about 94–98%, oral prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg for 3–5 days) as prescribed, ipratropium and IV magnesium sulphate in severe attacks.
  • Danger signs – unable to speak or feed, drowsiness, cyanosis, a "silent chest" – need emergency care.

Asthma action plan (written, given to parents and school)

  • Green zone (doing well) – no symptoms; take the controller daily.
  • Yellow zone (getting worse) – cough, wheeze, night waking, peak flow 50–80% of best – take the reliever and follow the plan; contact the doctor.
  • Red zone (medical alert) – very short of breath, unable to talk, lips blue, reliever not helping, peak flow below 50% – take the reliever and go to hospital immediately.
  • A peak flow meter is useful for children above about 5–6 years.

Nursing role and education

  • Teach and check inhaler technique at every visit; stress daily use of the controller even when the child is well.
  • Trigger control – damp dusting, washing bedding weekly in hot water and drying in sunlight, no smoking at home, a smoke-free kitchen, pets out of the bedroom.
  • Encourage normal activity and sports (reliever before exercise if advised); inform the school; influenza vaccination; follow-up every 3 months.

Conclusion Childhood asthma is managed with inhaled corticosteroids as controllers and salbutamol as a reliever, stepped up or down by control. The correct age-appropriate device – pMDI with spacer and mask in young children – and good technique are essential. A written green–yellow–red action plan, trigger avoidance and regular follow-up keep the child well and attending school.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain oxygen therapy in children, with the devices used and the nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Hypoxaemia (low oxygen in the blood) is the main cause of death in children with pneumonia, bronchiolitis, severe asthma and other serious illnesses. Oxygen is a drug: it must be given when needed, in the right amount, with the right device, and monitored.

Indications

  • SpO2 below 90% (at sea level) in a child with an acute illness.
  • Children with emergency signs – obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, shock, coma or convulsions – during resuscitation (aim for SpO2 of about 94% or more).
  • Severe pneumonia, bronchiolitis, acute asthma, heart failure, shock, sepsis and neonatal respiratory distress.
  • Clinical signs suggesting hypoxaemia (where no oximeter is available) – central cyanosis, grunting, severe chest indrawing, head nodding, inability to feed and lethargy.

Detecting hypoxaemia – pulse oximetry

  • Use a probe of the correct size (neonatal or infant wrap on the foot or hand); read only when the waveform is good and the child is still.

Sources – oxygen cylinders, oxygen concentrators (reliable where electricity is available), and piped oxygen from plants; an air–oxygen blender for newborns.

Devices

  1. Nasal prongs (binasal cannula) – the preferred method for most children; comfortable and allow feeding; flow about 0.5–1 L/min in newborns and 1–2 L/min in infants and young children; humidification is not needed at these low flows.
  2. Nasal catheter – a fine catheter passed into the nostril up to a measured depth (from the side of the nostril to the inner end of the eyebrow); similar flows.
  3. Face mask – simple mask (at least 5 L/min to prevent rebreathing CO2) or a mask with a reservoir bag (10–15 L/min) for high concentrations in emergencies; young children often resist masks.
  4. Head box (oxygen hood) – for newborns and young infants; needs high flows to wash out CO2; less used now.
  5. Humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and CPAP (including low-cost bubble CPAP in SNCUs) for children with severe respiratory distress.
  6. Bag–valve–mask and ventilators – for resuscitation and respiratory failure.

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Check the order – device, flow rate and target SpO2.
  2. Explain to the parents and child; let the child touch the prongs or mask (play) to reduce fear; a parent can hold the child.
  3. Clear the nose (saline and gentle suction) before starting; keep the child in a comfortable propped-up position.
  4. Fix the prongs or catheter securely; check the tubing, flowmeter and oxygen supply; ensure the cylinder has enough oxygen and a back-up is available.
  5. Monitor SpO2, respiratory rate, chest indrawing, heart rate, colour and alertness at least every 3 hours (continuously in severe illness); record.
  6. Humidify oxygen given by mask, head box or high flows; keep the nostrils clean; check the skin under prongs, tapes and masks for pressure injury.
  7. Prevent hazards
    • Retinopathy of prematurity and lung damage in preterm babies – use a blender and keep SpO2 about 90–95%; avoid unmonitored oxygen.
    • Fire – no smoking, flames or oil-based products near oxygen; keep cylinders upright and secured.
    • Drying of mucosa, nasal trauma, gastric distension with high flows (an orogastric tube may be needed with CPAP).
  8. Feeding – continue breastfeeding with nasal prongs; tube feeds if the child is too breathless.
  9. Weaning – once the child is stable, try him off oxygen each day; stop oxygen when SpO2 stays at 90% or above in room air.
  10. Clean and maintain equipment (concentrator filters, humidifier bottles) as per policy.

Conclusion Oxygen therapy in children is given for SpO2 below 90% or emergency signs, detected by pulse oximetry. Nasal prongs at low flows are the preferred device, with masks, head boxes, high-flow nasal cannula and CPAP for special situations. The nurse ensures the correct device and flow, a clear airway, regular monitoring, humidification where needed, prevention of ROP, fire and skin injury, and timely weaning.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in children and its management, with special reference to cerebral oedema.
tags: insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units per kg per hour
answer_html:
Definition Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute, life-threatening complication of diabetes due to severe insulin deficiency, causing hyperglycaemia, breakdown of fat into ketones, metabolic acidosis and dehydration. In children it is a common first presentation of type 1 diabetes and the commonest cause of diabetes-related death.

Biochemical criteria (ISPAD 2022)

  • Blood glucose above 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L),
  • Venous pH below 7.3 or serum bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, and
  • Ketonaemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 3 mmol/L) or moderate/large ketonuria.
  • Severity – mild: pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18; moderate: pH below 7.2 or bicarbonate below 10; severe: pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L.

Causes – new-onset diabetes (especially in young children), missed insulin doses (common in adolescents), infections and other illnesses, and insulin pump failure.

Clinical features – polyuria and polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, weight loss, dehydration, deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, fruity (acetone) breath, tachycardia, drowsiness and coma.

Investigations – blood glucose (hourly), venous blood gas, electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride), urea and creatinine, blood ketones, urine ketones, complete blood count, cultures if infection is suspected, and an ECG for potassium changes.

Management (as per the hospital DKA protocol)

  1. ABC, oxygen if shocked; two IV lines; accurate weight.
  2. Fluids – shocked children receive 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline boluses; others an initial 10–20 mL/kg of 0.9% saline over 20–30 minutes, then the remaining deficit evenly over 24–48 hours with maintenance fluids – avoiding rapid fluid shifts.
  3. Insulin – regular insulin by continuous IV infusion at 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/hour, started about 1 hour after fluids are begun; no IV insulin bolus (it increases the risk of cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia).
  4. Glucose – when blood glucose falls to about 250–300 mg/dL, add dextrose to the IV fluids, so that insulin can continue until acidosis clears without causing hypoglycaemia.
  5. Potassium – total body potassium is low even if the blood level is normal; add potassium to the fluids (about 40 mmol/L) once urine output is confirmed and the level is not high; monitor the ECG.
  6. Bicarbonate is not given routinely – only in very severe acidosis with cardiovascular compromise.
  7. Treat the cause (e.g. infection) and change to subcutaneous insulin when acidosis has resolved and the child can eat; give the first subcutaneous dose before stopping the infusion.

Cerebral oedema – the most dangerous complication

  • Occurs in about 0.5–1% of children with DKA, usually 4–12 hours after starting treatment, and has a high mortality.
  • Risk factors – young age, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, high urea, very low pCO2, bicarbonate therapy and an insulin bolus or large early fluid volumes.
  • Warning signs – headache, recurrence of vomiting, irritability, falling level of consciousness, inappropriate slowing of the heart rate, rising blood pressure, abnormal breathing, unequal pupils and incontinence.
  • Immediate management – raise the head end to 30°, reduce the IV fluid rate, give mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg IV over 10–15 minutes) or 3% hypertonic saline (2.5–5 mL/kg) as ordered, call for PICU care and support the airway; CT scan after stabilisation.

Nursing care

  • Hourly vital signs, neurological observations (GCS), capillary blood glucose and intake–output (urinary catheter if unconscious); 2–4-hourly electrolytes, blood gas and ketones; record on a DKA flow chart.
  • Use infusion pumps for insulin and fluids; label lines; cardiac monitoring.
  • Nil by mouth initially; mouth care; skin and eye care in the drowsy child; prevent hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.
  • Support the family and, before discharge, teach sick-day rules, never omitting insulin and early recognition of DKA.

Conclusion Paediatric DKA (glucose above 200 mg/dL, pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18, with ketones) is treated with careful fluid replacement over 24–48 hours, low-dose IV insulin infusion started after fluids and without a bolus, added dextrose and potassium, and close hourly monitoring. Cerebral oedema – signalled by headache, falling consciousness and bradycardia – must be recognised early and treated with mannitol or hypertonic saline.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Explain congenital hypothyroidism – causes, clinical features, newborn screening and management.
answer_html:
Definition Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is deficiency of thyroid hormone present from birth. It is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability, because thyroid hormone is essential for brain development in the first 2–3 years of life. Indian newborn screening studies show it is more frequent in India (roughly 1 in 1,000–2,500 newborns) than in many Western countries.

Causes

  • Thyroid dysgenesis – absent (agenesis), small (hypoplasia) or misplaced (ectopic, e.g. lingual) gland – the commonest cause in most countries.
  • Dyshormonogenesis – inherited defects in thyroid hormone synthesis (often with goitre).
  • Iodine deficiency in the mother (endemic cretinism).
  • Transient CH – maternal antithyroid drugs or antibodies, iodine exposure (antiseptics) in preterm babies.
  • Central (pituitary/hypothalamic) hypothyroidism – rare.

Clinical features

  • Most babies look normal at birth (some maternal hormone crosses the placenta) – which is why screening is essential.
  • Early signs – prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, excessive sleepiness, constipation, hoarse cry, hypothermia and cold mottled skin, large posterior fontanelle, umbilical hernia, large tongue (macroglossia), dry skin, puffy face and hypotonia.
  • If untreated – delayed milestones, intellectual disability, short stature with delayed bone age, coarse features (cretinism).

Newborn screening

  • Heel-prick blood on filter paper (dried blood spot) for TSH (with or without T4), ideally at 48–72 hours of age (or cord blood TSH in many Indian hospitals when babies are discharged early).
  • An abnormal screen is confirmed by serum TSH and free T4; thyroid ultrasound or scan helps find the cause.
  • Indian guidelines (Indian Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Endocrinology, 2018) recommend universal newborn screening for CH.

Treatment

  • Levothyroxine 10–15 micrograms/kg/day, started as early as possible – ideally within the first 2 weeks of life – once daily.
  • The tablet is crushed and mixed with a small amount of breast milk or water and given by spoon (not added to a bottle of feed); not given with soy formula, iron or calcium, which reduce absorption.
  • Monitoring – serum T4 and TSH at 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment, then every 1–2 months in the first 6 months, every 3–4 months until 3 years and less often thereafter; dose adjusted with growth.
  • Treatment is lifelong for permanent CH; children suspected of transient CH are re-evaluated after 3 years of age.
  • With early, adequate treatment, children achieve normal growth and intelligence.

Nursing role

  • Ensure screening of every newborn; correct sample technique (warm the heel, prick the side of the heel, fill each circle completely from one side, dry flat away from heat and sunlight, send promptly); trace and recall screen-positive babies quickly.
  • Teach parents – give the medicine every day at the same time; do not stop it; if a dose is missed, give it as soon as remembered; recognise signs of under-treatment (sleepiness, constipation, poor growth) and over-treatment (irritability, fast heart rate, poor sleep, loose stools); keep follow-up appointments.
  • Monitor growth and development; refer for early intervention if there is delay; promote iodised salt and maternal iodine nutrition.

Conclusion Congenital hypothyroidism, usually due to thyroid dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis, causes few signs at birth but leads to intellectual disability and short stature if untreated. Newborn screening by heel-prick TSH, confirmation by serum TSH and free T4, and early daily levothyroxine (10–15 µg/kg/day) with regular monitoring allow normal growth and development.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What is the VACTERL association?
answer_html:
VACTERL association is a non-random occurrence of a group of congenital anomalies together in the same baby. The letters stand for:

  • V – Vertebral defects (hemivertebrae, fused vertebrae).
  • A – Anal atresia (imperforate anus).
  • C – Cardiac defects (VSD, ASD, tetralogy of Fallot).
  • TE – Tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia.
  • R – Renal anomalies (renal agenesis, dysplasia, reflux).
  • L – Limb anomalies, especially of the radial side (absent radius or thumb). At least three features are usually present. Every baby with TEF or anal atresia is screened for the others – examination of the anus and limbs, echocardiography, renal ultrasound and spine X-ray.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What is a Replogle tube?
answer_html:
A Replogle tube is a double-lumen sump catheter (about 10 Fr in a term baby) placed through the mouth or nose into the blind upper oesophageal pouch of a baby with oesophageal atresia, before surgery.

  • One lumen is connected to low continuous suction to remove saliva; the other lumen lets air in (and is used for flushing), which prevents the tube from sticking to the pouch wall.
  • It prevents aspiration of saliva into the lungs.
  • Nursing care – keep the baby's head raised, check that the suction is working, flush the irrigation lumen with small amounts of saline as per policy, record the secretions, secure the tube and keep it in place during transport.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Differentiate between croup and epiglottitis.
answer_html:
Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) vs Epiglottitis

  • Cause – croup: viral (parainfluenza); epiglottitis: bacterial, Haemophilus influenzae type b (now rare because of Hib vaccine).
  • Age – croup: 6 months–3 years; epiglottitis: usually 2–7 years.
  • Onset – croup: gradual, after a cold; epiglottitis: sudden and rapidly progressive.
  • Cough and voice – croup: barking cough, hoarse voice; epiglottitis: little cough, muffled voice.
  • Drooling and posture – croup: absent, any position; epiglottitis: drooling, child sits up leaning forward (tripod position).
  • Fever and look – croup: low fever, not toxic; epiglottitis: high fever, toxic appearance.
  • X-ray – croup: steeple sign; epiglottitis: thumb sign.
  • Treatment – croup: dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline; epiglottitis: secure the airway (in OT or ICU), IV antibiotics. Never examine the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What is acute bronchitis in children?
answer_html:
Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi, usually following a viral cold; sometimes caused by Mycoplasma or pertussis.

  • Features – cough, at first dry and then productive, which may last 1–3 weeks; low-grade fever; rhonchi on auscultation; no fast breathing or chest indrawing (which helps to separate it from pneumonia).
  • Care – plenty of fluids, rest, humid air, paracetamol for fever, honey for cough in children above 1 year; antibiotics are not needed unless there is bacterial infection; avoid cough suppressants in young children.
  • Parents are advised to return if the child develops fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, high fever or cannot drink.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What is Reye syndrome?
answer_html:
Reye syndrome is a rare but serious acute encephalopathy with fatty degeneration of the liver in children, associated with use of aspirin during a viral illness such as influenza or chickenpox.

  • Features – a few days after the viral illness: persistent vomiting, lethargy, confusion, irritability, seizures and coma; raised liver enzymes and blood ammonia, hypoglycaemia; no jaundice.
  • Treatment – intensive care to control raised intracranial pressure, correct glucose and support the liver.
  • Prevention – do not give aspirin to children and adolescents (except under medical supervision, e.g. Kawasaki disease); use paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and pain.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What is the honeymoon phase in type 1 diabetes?
answer_html:
The honeymoon (partial remission) phase is a period soon after diagnosis and starting insulin in type 1 diabetes when the remaining beta cells recover temporarily and produce some insulin.

  • Insulin requirement falls (often below 0.5 unit/kg/day) and blood glucose is easier to control.
  • It begins within days to weeks of starting insulin and lasts weeks to months (occasionally up to 1–2 years).
  • Nursing significance – parents must understand that it is not a cure; insulin must not be stopped, but doses are reduced to prevent hypoglycaemia; glucose monitoring continues, and insulin needs rise again when the phase ends.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: What are the sick-day rules for a child with type 1 diabetes?
answer_html:
Sick-day rules (during fever, vomiting, diarrhoea or other illness):

  1. Never stop insulin – the body needs more insulin during illness, even if the child eats less.
  2. Check blood glucose every 2–3 hours and ketones (blood or urine) every few hours.
  3. Give extra rapid-acting insulin as advised when glucose and ketones are high.
  4. Give plenty of fluids in small, frequent sips – sugar-free if glucose is high, sugar-containing if glucose is low or the child cannot eat.
  5. Offer easily digestible carbohydrate foods; treat fever.
  6. Seek medical help immediately for persistent vomiting, rising or high ketones, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness, or glucose that stays high or low.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
unit_title: Nursing Management in Common Childhood Diseases
question: Differentiate between the Somogyi effect and the dawn phenomenon.
answer_html:
Both cause high blood glucose in the early morning, but for different reasons:

  • Somogyi effect (rebound hyperglycaemia) – night-time hypoglycaemia (around 2–3 a.m.), usually from too much evening insulin, triggers counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone), causing a rebound high glucose in the morning. Management – reduce the evening/bedtime insulin or give a bedtime snack.
  • Dawn phenomenon – a rise in glucose between about 4 and 8 a.m. due to the early-morning surge of growth hormone and cortisol (marked in puberty), without night-time hypoglycaemia. Management – adjust the dose or timing of basal insulin.
  • Differentiation – check blood glucose at 2–3 a.m.: low in the Somogyi effect, normal or high in the dawn phenomenon.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Explain the chain of survival and how cardiac arrest in children differs from that in adults. (3 marks) (b) Describe paediatric basic life support for an infant and a child as per the AHA 2025 guidelines. (6 marks) (c) Explain the paediatric advanced life support management of cardiac arrest and post-cardiac arrest care. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Paediatric cardiac arrest algorithm (AHA 2025, simplified)
labels: CPR with epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg every 3–5 min and advanced airway
shock at least 4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose)
CPR with amiodarone 5 mg/kg or lidocaine 1 mg/kg; non-shockable (asystole/PEA): epinephrine as soon as possible
treat reversible causes; ROSC – post-cardiac arrest care

answer_html:
(a) Chain of survival and differences from adult cardiac arrest (3 marks) Chain of survival (AHA 2025) The 2025 guidelines use a single chain of survival for adults and children, in and out of hospital, with six links:

  1. Recognition and emergency activation.
  2. High-quality CPR.
  3. Defibrillation.
  4. Advanced resuscitation.
  5. Post-cardiac arrest care.
  6. Recovery and survivorship. For children, prevention – early recognition and treatment of respiratory failure and shock – remains the most effective way to improve survival.

How cardiac arrest in children differs

  • Most paediatric arrests are secondary (asphyxial) – the end result of progressive respiratory failure or shock (pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma, drowning, choking, dehydration, sepsis, trauma). Hypoxia leads to bradycardia, then asystole or pulseless electrical activity (PEA).
  • Sudden primary cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation (VF) is less common – seen more in adolescents and in children with heart disease or channelopathies.
  • Therefore ventilation is an essential part of CPR in children ("breaths matter"), and a child with a pulse below 60/min and poor perfusion needs chest compressions.
  • Drugs, energies and equipment are weight-based; outcome after arrest, especially out of hospital, is poor, so recognition of the seriously ill child before arrest (paediatric early warning scores, rapid response) is crucial.

(b) Paediatric basic life support – AHA 2025 (6 marks) Age definitions – infant: below 1 year (beyond the newborn period); child: 1 year to puberty (breast development in girls, axillary hair in boys); after the onset of puberty, adult guidelines apply.

Steps

  1. Ensure scene safety.
  2. Check responsiveness – tap and shout ("Are you all right?"); for an infant, tap the sole of the foot.
  3. Shout for help; activate the emergency response system (mobile phone on speaker) and send someone for an AED.
  4. Check breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds – look for no breathing or only gasping; feel the brachial pulse in an infant and the carotid or femoral pulse in a child.
  5. Act on the findings
    • Breathing normally with a pulse – place in the recovery position and monitor.
    • Not breathing normally but pulse present – give rescue breaths, 1 every 2–3 seconds (20–30 per minute); check the pulse every 2 minutes; if the heart rate is below 60/min with signs of poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation and oxygenation, start CPR.
    • No breathing (or only gasping) and no pulse – start CPR immediately.
    • Lone rescuer without a phone – if the collapse was witnessed and sudden, leave to activate the emergency system and get an AED first; if unwitnessed, give 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call for help.
  6. High-quality CPR
    • Rate 100–120 compressions per minute.
    • Depth at least one-third of the front-to-back diameter of the chest – about 4 cm in infants and about 5 cm in children.
    • Infant technique – the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, just below the nipple line, or the two-thumb encircling hands technique (with two rescuers). The two-finger technique is no longer recommended (AHA 2025).
    • Child technique – heel of one or two hands on the lower half of the sternum.
    • Allow full chest recoil; keep interruptions under 10 seconds; avoid excessive ventilation; change compressors every 2 minutes.
    • Compression–ventilation ratio – 30:2 for a single rescuer; 15:2 with two rescuers for infants and children before puberty (30:2 after puberty).
    • Airway – head tilt–chin lift (in infants, a neutral "sniffing" position – overextension can block the soft airway); jaw thrust if injury is suspected.
    • Breaths – each over about 1 second, just enough to make the chest rise; mouth-to-mouth-and-nose for an infant; bag–mask by trained rescuers.
  7. AED – use as soon as it arrives; for infants and children below 8 years use paediatric pads or a dose attenuator if available (otherwise adult pads, placed front and back so they do not touch); a manual defibrillator is preferred for infants. Resume CPR immediately after each shock.
  8. Continue until advanced help takes over or the child shows signs of life.

Choking (foreign-body airway obstruction) – AHA 2025 – if the infant or child cannot cough, cry or breathe: infant – alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; child – alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts; if the child becomes unresponsive, start CPR, look in the mouth before giving breaths and remove a visible object; no blind finger sweeps.

(c) Paediatric advanced life support and post-cardiac arrest care (6 marks) PALS cardiac arrest algorithm (AHA 2025)

  1. Start CPR, give oxygen, attach the monitor/defibrillator; obtain IV or intraosseous (IO) access (IO in the proximal tibia if IV access is not quickly obtained).
  2. Check the rhythm – is it shockable?
    • Shockable (VF/pulseless VT)
      • Shock 2 J/kg → CPR for 2 minutes and obtain IV/IO access.
      • Shock 4 J/kg → CPR for 2 minutes; epinephrine every 3–5 minutes; consider an advanced airway.
      • Subsequent shocks at least 4 J/kg (maximum 10 J/kg or the adult dose) → CPR; amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus (maximum 300 mg; may be repeated up to 3 doses) or lidocaine 1 mg/kg; treat reversible causes.
    • Non-shockable (asystole/PEA)
      • Epinephrine as soon as possible (early epinephrine improves outcome), then every 3–5 minutes, with 2-minute cycles of CPR; consider an advanced airway and capnography; treat reversible causes.
  3. Drug doses
    • Epinephrine IV/IO 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL solution), maximum 1 mg.
    • Amiodarone 5 mg/kg (maximum 300 mg); lidocaine 1 mg/kg.
  4. Airway and ventilation
    • Good bag–mask ventilation is effective; an advanced airway (cuffed endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway) should not delay other interventions. Approximate cuffed tube size (internal diameter, mm) = age in years ÷ 4 + 3.5.
    • With an advanced airway – continuous compressions with 1 breath every 2–3 seconds; avoid hyperventilation.
    • ETCO2 (capnography) to confirm tube placement and monitor CPR quality.
  5. Reversible causes (Hs and Ts) – Hypovolaemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypoglycaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary).
  6. Weight – use a length-based tape or estimate (age + 4) × 2 kg for children of 1–10 years, to calculate doses and equipment sizes.

Post-cardiac arrest care (after return of spontaneous circulation)

  • Oxygenation – keep SpO2 about 94–99%, avoiding both hypoxaemia and excessive oxygen.
  • Ventilation – aim for normal carbon dioxide levels; avoid hyperventilation.
  • Blood pressure – keep systolic and mean pressure above the 5th percentile for age; fluids, inotropes or vasopressors as needed.
  • Temperature control – continuous temperature monitoring; prevent and treat fever; targeted temperature management in comatose children as per protocol.
  • Glucose and electrolytes – monitor and correct; treat hypoglycaemia.
  • Seizures – EEG monitoring where available; treat seizures promptly.
  • Find and treat the cause; careful neurological assessment; avoid early decisions about prognosis.
  • Recovery and survivorship – follow-up of physical, cognitive and emotional needs, rehabilitation and support for school re-entry; support and counselling for the family.

Nursing role

  • Early recognition of the deteriorating child (respiratory distress, shock, altered consciousness) using paediatric early warning scores; summoning the rapid response team.
  • Paediatric resuscitation trolley with all sizes of masks, airways, tubes and pads; a weight-based drug chart prepared in advance.
  • Taking assigned roles (compressions, airway, drugs, recording) with closed-loop communication; accurate timing and documentation.
  • Supporting the parents – allowing family presence where appropriate with a dedicated staff member; team debriefing after the event.

Conclusion Paediatric cardiac arrest is usually asphyxial, following respiratory failure or shock, so prevention and early ventilation are vital. The AHA 2025 guidelines use a single six-link chain of survival; paediatric BLS uses compressions of at least one-third of the chest depth at 100–120/min, with the heel of one hand or two-thumb technique in infants (two fingers no longer), 30:2 for one rescuer and 15:2 for two, and early AED use. In PALS, shockable rhythms receive 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg and higher shocks with epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg and amiodarone or lidocaine, while non-shockable rhythms need epinephrine as soon as possible; post-arrest care maintains oxygenation, ventilation, blood pressure, temperature and glucose, with follow-up for recovery.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: (a) Define an accident and list the common accidents in children. (3 marks) (b) Explain why children are prone to accidents and the common accidents at different ages. (4 marks) (c) Describe the prevention of accidents in children and the role of the nurse. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Common home hazards for young children and their prevention
labels: open water drums and buckets (cover or empty)
floor-level chulha and hot vessels (raised platform
kerosene in a soft-drink bottle (labelled locked storage)
medicines on a low shelf (high locked cupboard)
small objects and coins on the floor (keep away from under-threes)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and common accidents (3 marks) Definition An accident has been defined by WHO as "an unpremeditated event resulting in recognisable damage." Today the term unintentional injury is preferred, because injuries are predictable and largely preventable rather than chance events. Injuries are a leading cause of death and disability in children after the first year of life, and many survivors are left with disabilities.

Common accidents in children

  1. Falls – the commonest cause of non-fatal injury (from beds, stairs, terraces, trees, play equipment).
  2. Road traffic injuries – as pedestrians, cyclists and passengers on two-wheelers.
  3. Drowning – in buckets, tubs, water tanks, wells, ponds, rivers and canals.
  4. Burns and scalds – hot liquids, chulhas, kerosene lamps, firecrackers, electricity.
  5. Poisoning – kerosene, medicines, household chemicals, pesticides.
  6. Foreign bodies and choking – coins, seeds, groundnuts, beads, button batteries.
  7. Suffocation – pillows, plastic bags, overlaying of infants.
  8. Electric injuries – open sockets, loose wires, kites on overhead lines.
  9. Animal bites and stings – dog bites, snake bites, scorpion stings.
  10. Others – cuts from glass-coated kite string, injuries from farm machinery (threshers, chaff cutters), sports injuries.

(b) Why children are prone to accidents, and accidents by age (4 marks) Reasons

  • Developmental factors – curiosity and the urge to explore; putting things in the mouth (infants and toddlers); increasing mobility without the judgement of danger; imitation of adults; limited understanding of cause and effect; in adolescents, risk-taking and peer pressure.
  • Physical factors – small size (not seen by drivers), a large head (falls head-first), narrow airways, thin skin.
  • Lack of supervision – busy or working parents, young siblings looking after babies, crowded homes.
  • Environmental hazards – open wells, ponds and water drums, unprotected stairs and terraces, floor-level cooking, kerosene stored in soft-drink bottles, medicines and pesticides within reach, heavy traffic without footpaths.
  • Child and family factors – hyperactivity, fatigue, hunger or illness, family stress, poverty and lack of safety awareness.

Common accidents at different ages

  • Infants (0–1 year) – falls from beds, suffocation, choking on food or small objects, scalds from hot drinks or bath water, drowning in buckets, injuries while carried on two-wheelers.
  • Toddlers (1–3 years) – falls from stairs and terraces, poisoning (medicines, kerosene, cleaners), drowning in buckets, tanks and ponds, burns from hot liquids and chulhas, foreign bodies, electric shocks, dog bites.
  • Preschool children (3–6 years) – pedestrian road injuries, falls from heights and play equipment, drowning, burns from matches and firecrackers, dog bites.
  • School-age children (6–12 years) – road injuries as cyclists and pedestrians, drowning while swimming in rivers and ponds, sports injuries, firecracker injuries, kite-flying accidents (falls from terraces, electrocution, cuts from kite string), snake bites.
  • Adolescents – two-wheeler accidents (no helmet, underage driving, speeding), drowning, sports injuries, injuries at work or on farms.

(c) Prevention of accidents and the role of the nurse (8 marks) Principles of prevention – the "three Es":

  • Education – of parents, children, teachers and the community.
  • Engineering (environmental modification) – making the environment and products safer.
  • Enforcement – laws and regulations, and their implementation. Injury prevention also plans for before, during and after the event (Haddon's approach) – preventing the event, reducing injury when it occurs, and providing good first aid and emergency care.

Prevention of specific accidents

  1. Falls
    • Never leave an infant alone on a bed, table or changing surface; keep cot sides up.
    • Gates at stairs, railings on terraces and balconies (especially during kite-flying season), grills on windows.
    • Safe playgrounds with soft surfaces; avoid baby walkers.
  2. Drowning
    • Constant, "within arm's reach" supervision of young children near water.
    • Empty buckets and tubs after use; cover water drums, tanks and wells; fence ponds and open water near homes.
    • Safe day care (crèches/Anganwadi) for young children away from water in rural areas.
    • Teach swimming and water safety to school-age children; life jackets on boats; train community members in safe rescue and CPR.
  3. Burns and scalds
    • Keep hot liquids and vessels out of reach; do not hold a child while drinking tea or cooking; turn pan handles inward.
    • Raised cooking platforms instead of floor-level chulhas; keep children out of the kitchen while cooking.
    • Store matches, lighters and kerosene safely; replace kerosene lamps; cotton clothing near fire.
    • Check bath water temperature with the elbow; cover electric sockets.
    • Firecrackers only under adult supervision, at a distance, with a bucket of water ready.
    • First aid – cool the burn under running water for 20 minutes.
  4. Poisoning
    • Store medicines, kerosene, pesticides, acids and cleaners in original labelled containers, locked and out of reach; never in soft-drink bottles.
    • Child-resistant packaging; never call medicines "sweets"; safe disposal of unused medicines; safe storage of pesticides on farms.
  5. Foreign bodies and choking
    • Keep coins, buttons, beads, button batteries, magnets and small toy parts away from children below 3 years; age-appropriate toys.
    • Avoid whole groundnuts, nuts, hard sweets and whole grapes for young children; supervise eating; no running, laughing or playing with food in the mouth.
  6. Suffocation – firm mattress, back to sleep, no pillows or soft toys in an infant's bed, plastic bags out of reach.
  7. Road traffic injuries
    • Child restraints in cars (infant and child seats, rear seat); never carry a child in the front seat or on the lap.
    • Helmets for children on two-wheelers – under the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019, helmets are compulsory for all riders and pillion passengers above 4 years, and later rules require a crash helmet and safety harness for children of 9 months to 4 years riding pillion.
    • No underage driving (parents or owners are liable under the 2019 Act); road-safety education, safe routes to school, safe school transport, play areas away from roads.
  8. Electric injuries – socket covers, no loose wires, no kite-flying near overhead lines.
  9. Animal bites – teach children not to tease or approach stray dogs; vaccinate pets; wash bite wounds with soap and running water for 15 minutes and get anti-rabies vaccine. To prevent snake bites, children should sleep on a cot under a mosquito net rather than on the floor (kraits bite at night), and use footwear and a torch outdoors at night.
  10. Kite-string and farm injuries – avoid glass-coated or synthetic (nylon) kite string, which has been banned; keep children away from threshers, chaff cutters and pesticide spraying.

Role of the nurse

  1. Assessment – identify hazards during home visits using a home safety checklist; identify high-risk children (hyperactive children, previous injuries, families under stress).
  2. Anticipatory guidance at every well-child visit and immunisation contact, according to the next developmental stage (for example, stair gates before the child starts crawling).
  3. Health education – parents, grandparents, older siblings (child-to-child approach), teachers and the community through mothers' meetings, Anganwadi, VHSNDs, school health programmes and mass media.
  4. First aid training – choking, CPR, cooling of burns, what not to do in poisoning (no induced vomiting), bleeding control.
  5. Safe hospital environment – cot sides up, identification bands, safe storage of medicines and chemicals, no small objects within reach, supervised play.
  6. Emergency care and referral – prompt first aid, triage and transport.
  7. Advocacy and coordination – with Panchayats, schools, traffic police and municipal bodies for fencing ponds, crèches, speed limits, helmets, safe playgrounds.
  8. Recognition of non-accidental injury – injuries not matching the history or the child's developmental stage, or repeated injuries, must be reported as per law.
  9. Records and research – injury surveillance and data to plan prevention.

Nursing importance

  • Most childhood injuries happen at home and on the roads and are preventable; nurses who give stage-appropriate anticipatory guidance and teach first aid can prevent deaths and lifelong disability.

Conclusion Accidents, now called unintentional injuries, are a leading cause of death and disability in children after infancy. Falls, road injuries, drowning, burns, poisoning, foreign bodies, suffocation, electric injuries and animal bites are common, and their pattern changes with the child's developmental stage, curiosity, supervision and environment. Prevention uses education, engineering and enforcement – supervision, safe storage, barriers around water, raised cooking platforms, helmets and child restraints, safe toys and food – with the nurse providing assessment, anticipatory guidance, health education, first aid training, a safe hospital environment and advocacy.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain accidental poisoning in children – common poisons, management and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Poisoning is a common childhood emergency. In children below 5 years it is usually accidental – a curious toddler swallows a small amount of a single substance found at home. In adolescents poisoning is more often intentional and needs a mental health assessment as well as medical care.

Common poisons in Indian children

  • Kerosene and other hydrocarbons (often stored in soft-drink bottles) – among the commonest.
  • Household products – toilet and floor cleaners (acids and alkalis), bleach, detergents.
  • Medicines – iron (IFA) tablets, paracetamol, anticonvulsants, antihistamines, antidepressants, antidiabetic tablets, and adults' blood pressure medicines.
  • Insecticides and pesticides – organophosphates and carbamates, liquid mosquito repellents, and rat poisons (yellow phosphorus or zinc phosphide pastes).
  • Plants and seeds – datura, oleander, jatropha (ratanjot) seeds, castor seeds; camphor (seizures) and naphthalene balls (haemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
  • Envenomation – snake bite and scorpion sting.

Assessment

  • History – what substance (ask for the container), how much, when, by which route, symptoms since, and first aid already given.
  • Examination – ABC, consciousness, pupils, temperature, skin (sweating or dryness), smell (kerosene), burns around the mouth (corrosives), breathing (aspiration), seizures.
  • Toxidromes – e.g. cholinergic (salivation, small pupils, sweating, bradycardia – organophosphates), anticholinergic (dry hot skin, dilated pupils, delirium – datura), opioid (small pupils, slow breathing).
  • Investigations – blood glucose, blood gases, electrolytes, renal and liver function, drug levels (paracetamol, iron), cholinesterase, ECG, chest X-ray (hydrocarbons), X-ray abdomen (iron tablets, batteries).

Management

  1. Stabilise ABCDE – airway, oxygen, IV access, treat shock and seizures, and always check blood glucose.
  2. Decontamination
    • Skin and eyes – remove contaminated clothes, wash the skin with soap and water (staff wear gloves), irrigate eyes for 15–20 minutes.
    • Do not induce vomiting (fingers, ipecac, salt water) – it causes aspiration; salt water can cause fatal hypernatraemia in children.
    • Activated charcoal (1 g/kg) within about 1 hour for substances it binds, only if the airway is protected – not for hydrocarbons, corrosives, iron or alcohols.
    • Gastric lavage is rarely indicated in children; whole-bowel irrigation for iron or sustained-release tablets in selected cases.
  3. Antidotes where available – N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol), atropine and pralidoxime (organophosphates), desferrioxamine (iron), naloxone (opioids), vitamin K (warfarin-type rat poisons), anti-snake venom (snake bite), prazosin (scorpion sting).
  4. Supportive care and observation – fluids, oxygen, temperature, nutrition; observe children who look well for the expected period (e.g. at least 6 hours after kerosene ingestion).
  5. Seek expert advice – a poisons information centre (for example the National Poisons Information Centre at AIIMS, New Delhi).
  6. Psychosocial care – avoid blaming parents; assess supervision and home hazards; look for repeated poisoning or neglect; adolescents need counselling and psychiatric evaluation.

Prevention

  • Store medicines, kerosene, chemicals and pesticides in original labelled containers, locked and out of children's reach; never in food or drink bottles.
  • Child-resistant containers; do not take medicines in front of children or call them "sweets"; dispose of unused medicines safely.
  • Keep IFA tablets out of reach; safe storage of pesticides on farms; teach older children about poisonous plants and seeds.

Conclusion Childhood poisoning is mostly accidental in toddlers and involves kerosene, household chemicals, medicines (especially iron), pesticides and plant seeds. Management is stabilisation, careful history and examination, appropriate decontamination without induced vomiting, specific antidotes, supportive care and observation, with psychosocial assessment – and above all prevention by safe storage.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain foreign body aspiration and ingestion in children and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Foreign body (FB) accidents are commonest at 1–3 years, because young children explore by putting objects in the mouth, do not have molar teeth to chew properly, have immature swallowing coordination, and often run, laugh or cry while eating.

A. Foreign body aspiration (into the airway) Common objects – groundnuts and other nuts, seeds (gram, maize, custard apple), beads, small toy parts, pen caps, whistles. Clinical features

  • Sudden choking, coughing, gagging and breathlessness while eating or playing – often witnessed.
  • Stridor (laryngeal or tracheal FB), unilateral wheeze and reduced air entry on one side (bronchial FB).
  • A symptom-free interval may follow, so the event is forgotten; later the child presents with persistent cough, recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia in the same lobe, or unexplained unilateral wheeze.

  • Any child with sudden onset of respiratory symptoms should be suspected of FB aspiration. Investigations

  • Chest X-ray – radio-opaque objects are seen; organic objects (nuts, seeds) are not, but indirect signs appear – obstructive emphysema (hyperinflation) on the affected side (inspiratory and expiratory films), collapse or consolidation; CT in doubtful cases.

  • Rigid bronchoscopy – both diagnostic and therapeutic. Emergency first aid (AHA 2025)

  • Partial obstruction with effective cough – let the child cough; do not interfere; take to hospital.

  • Severe obstruction (cannot cough, cry or breathe) – infant: alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; child: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts, until the object comes out or the child becomes unresponsive.
  • Unresponsive – start CPR; look in the mouth before giving breaths and remove a visible object; no blind finger sweeps. Treatment – removal by rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in a centre with expertise. Post-bronchoscopy care – monitor breathing and SpO2, watch for stridor (laryngeal oedema), give oxygen, humidified air or nebulisation and steroids as prescribed, antibiotics for infection, nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns.

B. Foreign body ingestion (into the food passage)

  • Common objects – coins (most common), button batteries, magnets, safety pins, hair clips, small toys, fish or chicken bones.
  • Features – often none; drooling, refusal of feeds, vomiting, painful or difficult swallowing, chest or neck pain, coughing (pressure on the trachea).
  • X-ray (neck, chest and abdomen) – a coin in the oesophagus is usually seen face-on (as a disc) on a front view; a button battery shows a "double ring" (halo) edge, which distinguishes it from a coin.
  • Management
    • Button battery in the oesophagus is an emergency – it can burn through the oesophageal wall within 2 hours, causing perforation or fistula; it is removed endoscopically at once. For a child above 1 year who swallowed it within 12 hours, honey (10 mL every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses) may be given on the way to hospital to reduce injury – without delaying removal.
    • Multiple magnets (or a magnet with a metal object) can attract across loops of bowel and cause perforation – urgent removal.
    • Coins and blunt objects stuck in the oesophagus – endoscopic removal; objects that have reached the stomach usually pass in the stools (parents check stools; repeat X-ray if not passed).
    • Sharp objects – early endoscopic removal if within reach; close observation otherwise.
    • Do not induce vomiting.
  • Ear and nose – a one-sided foul-smelling nasal discharge in a child suggests a nasal FB; a button battery in the ear or nose is also an emergency.

Prevention and nursing education

  • Keep small objects, coins, batteries and magnets away from children below 3 years; check toys for small detachable parts; secure battery compartments of remotes and toys.
  • Avoid giving whole groundnuts, nuts, hard sweets and whole grapes to young children; seat children while eating and supervise.
  • Teach parents first aid for choking and infant/child CPR.

Conclusion FB aspiration presents with sudden choking, stridor or unilateral wheeze and may later cause recurrent pneumonia; it is treated by first aid for choking and removal by rigid bronchoscopy. FB ingestion – coins most commonly – often passes harmlessly, but button batteries in the oesophagus and multiple magnets are emergencies needing immediate removal. Prevention through supervision and keeping small objects away from young children is the nurse's key message.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the special features of burns in children and their management.
tags: urine output 1 mL per kg per hour
first aid cool running water 20 minutes
answer_html:
Introduction Burns are a common cause of injury, disability and death in children. Scalds from hot liquids (tea, milk, dal, bath water) are commonest in children below 5 years; older children suffer flame burns (chulhas, kerosene stoves and lamps, firecrackers), electrical burns (sockets, wires, kites touching overhead lines), chemical burns (toilet cleaners) and contact burns (irons, cooking vessels).

Why burns are more serious in children

  • Thinner skin – deeper burns at lower temperatures and shorter exposure.
  • Larger body surface area for weight – greater loss of fluid and heat; shock and hypothermia develop with smaller burns (IV fluid resuscitation is usually needed for burns above about 10% of body surface area, compared with about 15–20% in adults).
  • Different body proportions – the head is relatively large and the legs small, so the adult rule of nines is inaccurate; the Lund and Browder chart (age-adjusted) or the palm method (the child's palm with fingers ≈ 1% of body surface) is used.
  • Low glycogen stores – hypoglycaemia, so maintenance fluids contain dextrose.
  • Immature immunity – infection and sepsis; toxic shock syndrome may follow even small burns (fever, rash, diarrhoea and shock on day 2–4).
  • Narrow airways – swelling from inhalation injury obstructs breathing quickly.
  • Growth – scars and contractures restrict growth and movement; lasting psychological effects for child and family.
  • Non-accidental burns – suspect child abuse when the pattern does not fit the history: glove- or stocking-like scalds with sharp lines, cigarette burns, burns on the buttocks and perineum, or delay in seeking care.

First aid

  • Stop the burning; remove clothing and ornaments (unless stuck); for electrical burns, switch off the power before touching the child.
  • Cool the burn under cool running tap water for 20 minutes (useful up to 3 hours after the burn); do not apply ice, toothpaste, ghee, oil or ink.
  • Cool the burn but keep the child warm – cover the rest of the body; cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean cloth.
  • Chemical burns – irrigate with plenty of water.
  • Give pain relief and take the child to hospital.

Hospital management

  1. Airway and breathing – suspect inhalation injury if there are facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth, hoarseness or stridor; early intubation by an expert; oxygen.
  2. Assess extent and depth – Lund and Browder chart; superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted.
  3. Fluid resuscitation (burns above about 10%)
    • Parkland formula – 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % burn of Ringer's lactate in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn and half in the next 16 hours, plus maintenance fluid with dextrose for children.
    • Adjust to keep urine output about 1 mL/kg/hour in children (urinary catheter); monitor blood glucose, temperature and electrolytes.
  4. Pain relief – adequate analgesia (IV morphine, ketamine for dressings); age-appropriate distraction and play therapy during procedures.
  5. Wound care – cleaning, removal of blisters and dead tissue, topical antimicrobials (silver sulfadiazine – not for infants below 2 months), silver or hydrocolloid dressings; early excision and skin grafting for deep burns; check tetanus immunisation.
  6. Nutrition – high-energy, high-protein diet; early enteral (nasogastric) feeding; vitamins and zinc; weekly weight.
  7. Prevent complications – infection control, watch for toxic shock and sepsis, stress ulcers, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia; elevation of burned limbs.
  8. Rehabilitation – positioning and splinting to prevent contractures, physiotherapy, pressure garments for scars, play, schooling during hospital stay, psychological support for the child and parents (who often feel guilty), and later reconstructive surgery.

Prevention

  • Keep hot liquids out of reach; do not hold a child while drinking tea; raised cooking platforms; keep children out of the kitchen while cooking; safe storage of kerosene and matches; check bath water temperature; socket covers; adult supervision with firecrackers.

Conclusion Burns in children – mostly scalds in toddlers – are more serious because of thin skin, large surface area, different body proportions, low glycogen stores, immature immunity and growth. Correct first aid (cool running water for 20 minutes, keep the child warm), assessment with the Lund and Browder chart, fluid resuscitation for burns above 10% with Parkland plus maintenance fluids and a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hour, good pain relief, wound care, nutrition, rehabilitation and vigilance for abuse are essential.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain the recognition and emergency management of haemorrhage and shock in children.
tags: fluid bolus 10 to 20 mL per kg
septic shock antibiotics within one hour
answer_html:
Introduction A child's blood volume is only about 80 mL/kg (about 800 mL in a 10 kg child), so even a small loss is significant – 200 mL is a quarter of a toddler's blood volume. Children compensate well, keeping their blood pressure normal until late, and then deteriorate suddenly. Early recognition of shock is therefore vital.

Causes of haemorrhage in children

  • Trauma – road accidents, falls, cuts.
  • Epistaxis – common, usually from the front of the nose (Little's area) due to nose picking, dry air or colds.
  • Post-operative bleeding (tonsillectomy, circumcision).
  • Bleeding disorders – haemophilia, ITP, Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in infants, leukaemia.
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding – oesophageal varices, Meckel's diverticulum (painless rectal bleeding), peptic ulcer.

Recognition of shock in children

  • Compensated shock (blood pressure still normal) – tachycardia (the earliest sign), capillary refill time above 2 seconds, cool and mottled extremities, weak peripheral pulses, irritability or anxiety, reduced urine output (below 1 mL/kg/hour).
  • Hypotensive (decompensated) shock – low blood pressure is a late and ominous sign: systolic BP below 70 mmHg + (2 × age in years) in children of 1–10 years (below 70 mmHg in infants, below 90 mmHg above 10 years); lethargy, weak central pulses, bradycardia – arrest is near.
  • Types – hypovolaemic (the commonest in children – dehydration from diarrhoea, haemorrhage, burns), distributive (septic, anaphylactic), cardiogenic and obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade).

First aid for bleeding

  • External bleeding – firm direct pressure with a clean cloth for at least 10 minutes, elevation of the limb, pressure bandage; a tourniquet above the wound for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control (note the time).
  • Nosebleed – sit the child up, leaning forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes while breathing through the mouth; a cold compress over the nose; do not tilt the head back (blood is swallowed or aspirated); seek care if bleeding continues beyond about 20 minutes or recurs often.

Emergency management of shock

  1. ABC – open the airway, give high-flow oxygen, call for help.
  2. Vascular access – two IV cannulas or intraosseous access if IV fails quickly; take blood for grouping and cross-matching, glucose, haemoglobin and electrolytes.
  3. Fluid bolus – 10–20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or Ringer's lactate) over 5–20 minutes, reassessing after each bolus (heart rate, capillary refill, BP, consciousness, urine) and watching for fluid overload (crackles, enlarging liver, increasing work of breathing).
  4. Haemorrhage – early blood transfusion (packed red cells 10–20 mL/kg) if shock persists after 1–2 boluses; control the source (pressure, surgery); tranexamic acid in major trauma as prescribed.
  5. Septic shock – antibiotics within the first hour, fluid boluses, and vasoactive drugs (adrenaline or noradrenaline) for fluid-refractory shock.
  6. Anaphylactic shock – intramuscular adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (1 mg/mL) into the thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed, plus fluids and oxygen.
  7. Cardiogenic shock – smaller, cautious boluses (5–10 mL/kg) and inotropes.
  8. Severe acute malnutrition – shock is treated with smaller, slower boluses (about 15 mL/kg over 1 hour) as per WHO guidelines, because of the risk of heart failure.
  9. Check and correct blood glucose; keep the child warm.

Nursing care

  • Lay the child flat (legs slightly raised if no injury), keep warm, minimise distress, allow a parent to stay.
  • Monitor heart rate, capillary refill, BP, respiratory rate, SpO2, consciousness, temperature and hourly urine output (catheter if needed); record all fluids accurately with infusion pumps or burettes.
  • Observe for transfusion reactions; avoid intramuscular injections in children with bleeding disorders.
  • Educate parents about first aid for bleeding, nosebleeds and early signs of dehydration.

Conclusion Because children have a small blood volume and compensate well, shock must be recognised early by tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool mottled skin and reduced urine output – hypotension is a late sign. Bleeding is controlled by direct pressure (and correct nosebleed first aid), and shock is treated with oxygen, IV/IO access, 10–20 mL/kg fluid boluses with reassessment, early blood for haemorrhage, antibiotics for sepsis, adrenaline for anaphylaxis and close nursing monitoring.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Explain Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) for sick children.
answer_html:
Introduction Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) is a WHO approach for rapidly sorting sick children as soon as they arrive at a hospital and treating life-threatening conditions immediately. Many children die in hospital within the first 24 hours, often while waiting to be seen; ETAT reduces such deaths. Triage is done before registration or payment, and should take only a short time for each child.

Three triage categories

  1. Emergency signs (E) – need immediate treatment.
  2. Priority signs (P) – need rapid assessment and treatment without waiting in the queue.
  3. Non-urgent (Q – queue) – wait their turn for routine assessment.

1. Emergency signs – assess "ABCD"

  • A, B – Airway and Breathing – obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis.
  • C – Circulation – signs of shock: cold hands with capillary refill longer than 3 seconds and a weak, fast pulse.
  • C – Coma and Convulsions – coma (responds only to pain or not at all on AVPU) or convulsing now.
  • D – Dehydration (severe) – in a child with diarrhoea, any two of lethargy, sunken eyes and a very slow skin pinch.

2. Priority signs – remembered as "3TPR-MOB"

  • Tiny baby (below 2 months); Temperature – very high; Trauma or other urgent surgical condition.
  • Pallor (severe); Poisoning (history); Pain (severe).
  • Respiratory distress; Restless, continuously irritable or lethargic; Referral (urgent).
  • Malnutrition – visible severe wasting; Oedema of both feet; Burns (major).

3. Non-urgent – children with none of the above.

Immediate treatment of emergency signs

  • Airway – position the head (neutral in infants, head tilt–chin lift in older children; no neck movement if trauma is suspected); clear secretions with suction; manage choking.
  • Breathing – give oxygen; support breathing with a bag and mask if needed.
  • Circulation – stop bleeding; give oxygen; keep the child warm; insert an IV (or IO) line; give IV fluids rapidly (in a child without severe malnutrition, 20 mL/kg Ringer's lactate or normal saline); smaller, slower fluids in severe malnutrition.
  • Coma or convulsions – manage the airway; place in the recovery position if no trauma; give diazepam (rectal or IV) for convulsions; check blood glucose and give 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV if it is low.
  • Severe dehydration – rapid IV fluids as per Plan C.
  • After emergency treatment, call a senior clinician and complete the assessment.

ETAT+ – the extended course also covers the admission management of severe pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, severe malnutrition and sick newborns.

Role of the nurse

  • Work as the triage nurse at the entrance – see every child on arrival, identify emergency and priority signs and start treatment at once.
  • Keep a triage/emergency area ready with oxygen, suction, bag and mask, IV and IO sets, fluids, dextrose, diazepam, glucometer and weighing scale.
  • Use colour-coded triage (red – emergency, yellow – priority, green – queue), document findings and re-triage waiting children regularly.
  • Work as a team with pre-assigned roles; communicate with parents and keep them with the child.

Conclusion ETAT sorts sick children on arrival into emergency (ABCD signs – airway and breathing, circulation, coma and convulsions, severe dehydration), priority (3TPR-MOB) and non-urgent groups, and gives immediate treatment – airway care, oxygen, fluids, glucose and anticonvulsants – to those with emergency signs. Nurses performing triage at the hospital entrance can prevent many early deaths.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the Lund and Browder chart?
answer_html:
The Lund and Browder chart is an age-adjusted chart for estimating the percentage of body surface area burned, more accurate than the rule of nines in children.

  • It allows for the changing body proportions with age – the head is relatively large in infants (about 19% of body surface at birth, compared with about 7% in adults), while the thighs and legs are smaller (one thigh about 5.5% at birth and 9.5% in adults; one lower leg about 5% at birth and 7% in adults).
  • The burned areas are shaded on the chart and the percentages for the child's age are added.
  • Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted, not simple redness.
  • For small or scattered burns, the palm method is used – the child's palm with fingers is about 1% of the body surface.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: What is the paediatric assessment triangle?
answer_html:
The paediatric assessment triangle (PAT) is a rapid "across the room" assessment of a sick child, done in 30–60 seconds by looking and listening, without touching the child.

  1. Appearance – the child's general look, remembered as TICLS: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, Speech or cry.
  2. Work of breathing – abnormal sounds (stridor, grunting, wheeze), abnormal positioning (tripod or sniffing position), retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing.
  3. Circulation to the skin – pallor, mottling, cyanosis. Interpretation – abnormal work of breathing alone suggests respiratory distress; with abnormal appearance, respiratory failure; abnormal circulation alone suggests compensated shock; with abnormal appearance, decompensated shock; all three abnormal indicate cardiopulmonary failure – immediate resuscitation.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Write the features and management of kerosene poisoning in children.
answer_html:
Kerosene (hydrocarbon) poisoning is one of the commonest poisonings in Indian children, usually when kerosene stored in a soft-drink or water bottle is drunk by mistake.

  • Main danger – aspiration chemical pneumonitis: kerosene has low viscosity and spreads easily into the lungs even in small amounts.
  • Features – coughing, choking and gasping soon after ingestion, fast breathing, chest retractions, fever, vomiting, smell of kerosene, drowsiness or convulsions in severe cases.
  • Management – do not induce vomiting; no gastric lavage or activated charcoal; remove contaminated clothes and wash the skin; oxygen if breathing is fast or SpO2 is low; observe for at least 6 hours (with a chest X-ray) before sending home; supportive care for pneumonitis.
  • Prevention – store kerosene in labelled containers out of reach, never in drink bottles.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: Write the features and management of iron poisoning in children.
answer_html:
Iron poisoning occurs when children swallow iron and folic acid (IFA) tablets, which look like sweets.

  • Toxic dose – serious toxicity is expected above about 60 mg/kg of elemental iron; less than 20 mg/kg is usually harmless.
  • Stages – (1) 0–6 hours: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, haematemesis; (2) 6–24 hours: apparent improvement; (3): shock and metabolic acidosis; (4) 2–5 days: liver failure; (5) 2–6 weeks: scarring and narrowing of the stomach outlet.
  • Management – ABC and fluids; X-ray abdomen (tablets are radio-opaque); serum iron at 4–6 hours; activated charcoal does not bind iron; whole-bowel irrigation in selected cases; IV desferrioxamine for severe poisoning (urine turns reddish, "vin rosé").
  • Prevention – keep IFA tablets locked and out of children's reach.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: List the measures for child-proofing a home.
answer_html:
Measures for child-proofing a home

  1. Store medicines, kerosene, cleaners and pesticides locked, high up, in labelled original containers – never in drink bottles.
  2. Keep matches, lighters, knives, sharp tools and plastic bags out of reach.
  3. Cover electric sockets; no loose or exposed wires.
  4. Gates at stairs, railings on terraces and balconies, grills on windows.
  5. Empty buckets and tubs; cover water drums, tanks and wells.
  6. Cook on a raised platform; turn pan handles inward; keep hot liquids away from table edges.
  7. Keep small objects – coins, buttons, beads, button batteries and magnets – away from children below 3 years.
  8. Secure heavy furniture and television sets so they cannot topple over.
  9. Keep emergency numbers handy and learn first aid.

subject: Child Health Nursing I (including ENBC, FBNC, IMNCI and PLS modules)
question: State the differences in CPR between an infant, a child and an adult (AHA 2025).
answer_html:
Differences in CPR (AHA 2025)

  • Pulse check – infant: brachial; child: carotid or femoral; adult: carotid.
  • Compression technique – infant: heel of one hand or two-thumb encircling hands (two-finger technique no longer recommended); child: heel of one or two hands; adult: two hands.
  • Depth – at least one-third of the chest depth: about 4 cm in infants, about 5 cm in children; adults 5–6 cm.
  • Rate – 100–120 per minute for all.
  • Compression–ventilation ratio – adult: 30:2; infant and child: 30:2 for one rescuer and 15:2 for two rescuers (before puberty).
  • Airway – neutral "sniffing" position in infants; head tilt–chin lift in children and adults.
  • AED – paediatric pads or dose attenuator for children below 8 years if available.
  • Choking – infant: back blows and chest thrusts; child and adult: back blows and abdominal thrusts.
